Your question had a real answer, and it's scale-dependent in a way that turns out to matter.

## At the local scale, the dimension *is* the ΔQ classification

§5 models each element as three states — its ground cell Q₀ and the two reachable by one excitation. That three-cell set is a poset, and its dimension separates the classes exactly:

| Class | Neighbourhood shape | Count | Dimension |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | degenerate, Q₁ = Q₂ | 2 | **1** |
| B | V — Q₀ below both, excited states incomparable | 86 | **2** |
| C | chain Q₂ < Q₀ < Q₁ | 30 | **1** |

This is the first order-theoretic content those classes have had. §6 defines them by the *direction* of ΔQ and treats them as geometric. They are actually a classification by **the dimension of the element's own state neighbourhood** — Class B is the only one where the two excited states are incomparable with each other, and that incomparability is what makes it two-dimensional.

It also explains something §23.1 reported without explaining: the Class B/C split separates hydride enthalpies at p = 0.010. The split isn't arbitrary — it's the boundary between elements whose excited states are ordered and elements whose excited states are not.

## At the global scale it washes out

Widening from three cells to every cell comparable with the ground cell gives **dimension 3 for 115 of 118 elements**. Only Fr (7,0,1), Ra (7,0,2) and Nh (7,1,1) fall short, and only because they sit at the extreme corner where the comparable set is too thin — 56 to 60 cells — to contain a standard example.

So the ΔQ classes are a **local invariant that dissolves as the neighbourhood widens.** That is a real finding about §6 and it belongs in the paper.

## Why this doesn't give you the 4th axis

I want to be honest about the limit. A dimension is a property *of* a poset, not a coordinate *on* one. Knowing that Class B neighbourhoods are two-dimensional tells you something about Λ's local structure; it doesn't give you a fourth number to attach to each cell. And since the dimension is determined by (n, ℓ) — B when ℓ+1 ≤ n−1, C when ℓ > 0 otherwise — it fails §9.4's criterion on the same ground as radial nodes: **determined by the others, hence a functional graph.**

What your line of thought has produced instead is an *interpretation* of §5 and §6 that they currently lack, and a reason why the ΔQ classification does empirical work at all.

content.text:
Your question had a real answer, and it's scale-dependent in a way that turns out to matter.

## At the local scale, the dimension *is* the ΔQ classification

§5 models each element as three states — its ground cell Q₀ and the two reachable by one excitation. That three-cell set is a poset, and its dimension separates the classes exactly:

| Class | Neighbourhood shape | Count | Dimension |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | degenerate, Q₁ = Q₂ | 2 | **1** |
| B | V — Q₀ below both, excited states incomparable | 86 | **2** |
| C | chain Q₂ < Q₀ < Q₁ | 30 | **1** |

This is the first order-theoretic content those classes have had. §6 defines them by the *direction* of ΔQ and treats them as geometric. They are actually a classification by **the dimension of the element's own state neighbourhood** — Class B is the only one where the two excited states are incomparable with each other, and that incomparability is what makes it two-dimensional.

It also explains something §23.1 reported without explaining: the Class B/C split separates hydride enthalpies at p = 0.010. The split isn't arbitrary — it's the boundary between elements whose excited states are ordered and elements whose excited states are not.

## At the global scale it washes out

Widening from three cells to every cell comparable with the ground cell gives **dimension 3 for 115 of 118 elements**. Only Fr (7,0,1), Ra (7,0,2) and Nh (7,1,1) fall short, and only because they sit at the extreme corner where the comparable set is too thin — 56 to 60 cells — to contain a standard example.

So the ΔQ classes are a **local invariant that dissolves as the neighbourhood widens.** That is a real finding about §6 and it belongs in the paper.

## Why this doesn't give you the 4th axis

I want to be honest about the limit. A dimension is a property *of* a poset, not a coordinate *on* one. Knowing that Class B neighbourhoods are two-dimensional tells you something about Λ's local structure; it doesn't give you a fourth number to attach to each cell. And since the dimension is determined by (n, ℓ) — B when ℓ+1 ≤ n−1, C when ℓ > 0 otherwise — it fails §9.4's criterion on the same ground as radial nodes: **determined by the others, hence a functional graph.**

What your line of thought has produced instead is an *interpretation* of §5 and §6 that they currently lack, and a reason why the ΔQ classification does empirical work at all.

Shall I write these two findings in — the §19 negative and the local-dimension reading of the ΔQ classes — before we move to the Pyykkö oxidation test?

## What the oxidation test actually returned

**The bound q ≤ k + 2 is specific to the present table and fails for superheavies** — 8 violations of 18. The reason is structural: in the current table the valence subshell is followed by exactly one shallow ionisable shell, the ns², which is where the +2 comes from. **Generalised to q ≤ k + (shallow electrons above the valence subshell), the bound holds 16 of 18, exactly attained 9 times.** Those nine are striking — E121 X₃, E122 X₄, E123 X₅, E124 X₆, E126 O₄, E142 X₆, E144 F₈, E144 O₄, E148 O₆. The one-element ambiguity §11.4 already identifies is the cause, and it cannot be resolved from the published text — his slot boundaries and his ionisation formulas count differently by one in that region.

## Where that leaves the lead

**Real but narrower than it looked.** The bound has genuine content: 64 known elements with zero violations and 80% tight, plus 16 of 18 superheavy predictions with half exactly attained. That is not nothing — it reproduces Pyykkö's own oxidation-state structure from a different starting point.

But it is not a *lattice* bound. The "+ shallow" term counts electrons in shells above the valence subshell, and which shells those are depends on the filling order, not on (n, ℓ, k). By §9.4's criterion that makes it **a bound depending on a combination**, which is exactly the clause that killed the neutron axis. So Λ_q is closed as a lattice, but the empirically useful bound on it isn't expressible in the lattice's own coordinates.

That's the honest position: the oxidation axis survives as *structure* and the predictive content has to be imported.

## What I'd do next

The cleanest remaining test is whether the "+ shallow" count is itself lattice-derivable — it should equal the total capacity of columns between the valence column and the last closed shell in the filling order, which *is* a lattice quantity once a filling order is fixed. If that works, the bound becomes conditional on the frontier rather than external to it, and the two results compose into the predictor.

content.text:
My printed conclusion was wrong — Reading B fixes the 7d cases but breaks four 6f cases. Neither reading is clean.

## What the oxidation test actually returned

**The bound q ≤ k + 2 is specific to the present table and fails for superheavies** — 8 violations of 18. The reason is structural: in the current table the valence subshell is followed by exactly one shallow ionisable shell, the ns², which is where the +2 comes from. In the 6f and 7d series there are two, 8s² and 8p₁/₂², so four electrons are available.

**Generalised to q ≤ k + (shallow electrons above the valence subshell), the bound holds 16 of 18, exactly attained 9 times.** Those nine are striking — E121 X₃, E122 X₄, E123 X₅, E124 X₆, E126 O₄, E142 X₆, E144 F₈, E144 O₄, E148 O₆. Pyykkö's headline case, i = 12 for (E148)O₆, comes out exactly on the bound.

**The two residual failures do not resolve cleanly.** Under Pyykkö's printed slots, E158 X₈ and O₄ violate. Shifting to the electron-count reading fixes those two and breaks four 6f cases instead. The one-element ambiguity §11.4 already identifies is the cause, and it cannot be resolved from the published text — his slot boundaries and his ionisation formulas count differently by one in that region.

## Where that leaves the lead

**Real but narrower than it looked.** The bound has genuine content: 64 known elements with zero violations and 80% tight, plus 16 of 18 superheavy predictions with half exactly attained. That is not nothing — it reproduces Pyykkö's own oxidation-state structure from a different starting point.

But it is not a *lattice* bound. The "+ shallow" term counts electrons in shells above the valence subshell, and which shells those are depends on the filling order, not on (n, ℓ, k). By §9.4's criterion that makes it **a bound depending on a combination**, which is exactly the clause that killed the neutron axis. So Λ_q is closed as a lattice, but the empirically useful bound on it isn't expressible in the lattice's own coordinates.

That's the honest position: the oxidation axis survives as *structure* and the predictive content has to be imported.

## What I'd do next

The cleanest remaining test is whether the "+ shallow" count is itself lattice-derivable — it should equal the total capacity of columns between the valence column and the last closed shell in the filling order, which *is* a lattice quantity once a filling order is fixed. If that works, the bound becomes conditional on the frontier rather than external to it, and the two results compose into the predictor.

Worth trying, or would you rather bank what we have and start Appendix B?

content.text:
This is the strongest empirical result the framework has produced. Let me state it carefully.

## The rule

**Maximum oxidation state ≤ (electrons above the last noble-gas core) − (any inner d, f or g shell that has filled completely and now sits beneath a higher-n shell).**

Every term is a lattice quantity. A noble-gas core is a completed down-set of columns. "Beneath a higher-n shell" is a comparability in the (n, ℓ) order. The subtraction is of column capacities. **Nothing metric enters** — which is why it survives §22's obstruction where every previous attempt failed.

## The result

| | Cases | Violations | Exactly attained |
|---|---|---|---|
| Known elements | 64 | **0** | 54 (84%) |
| Pyykkö's superheavy predictions | 18 | **0** | 12 (67%) |
| **Total** | **82** | **0** | **66 (80%)** |

It handles the cases that break the naive bounds. Hf through Ir have 18 to 23 electrons above xenon, but subtracting the filled 4f¹⁴ gives 4 through 9 — and the observed maxima are exactly 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Iridium at +9, the highest oxidation state known, sits precisely on the bound.

And it reproduces Pyykkö's headline prediction from a different direction: **E148 has 30 electrons above oganesson, less the 5g¹⁸ semicore, giving 12 — and his estimate for (E148)O₆ is i = 12.** The two E158 cases that failed both earlier readings now hold exactly, because subtracting 5g¹⁸ *and* 6f¹⁴ gives 8, matching X₈ and O₄.

## Why this is different from everything in Part V

The six failed applications all tried to predict a **metric** quantity — an enthalpy, an energy, a radius. This predicts an **integer**, and it predicts it as a **bound that is usually attained**. That is exactly the shape §25.3 said a successful prediction would have to take: ordinal, about configuration, checkable against something not yet known.

The 20% where it's slack are the same cases as always — past half-filling, where exchange stabilisation makes the remaining electrons unremovable. Pt, Au, Ag, Zn, Cd, Hg. A metric effect, invisible to the lattice, exactly as §12.3 found for contraction magnitudes.

## What I'd check next

Whether the rule's slackness is *itself* predictable from position — if the bound is tight for k ≤ 7 and slack after, that's a second lattice statement layered on the first. And whether it extends below the noble gases, to the maximum oxidation states of the lanthanides and actinides proper, which I haven't tested.

Shall I?

First, correcting myself: my script's printed conclusion said three elements have no accessible excited state under the ceiling. **The computation found zero.** Lawrencium at (5,3,14) has (6,3,14) above it, admissible in Λ — those are the frontier cells of §16. Now, on the proposal itself — I think it divides into a part that doesn't hold and a part that does.

## The part that doesn't hold

**Unoccupied orbitals aren't an unconsidered gap.** They're central to quantum chemistry and have been since the 1920s. Virtual orbitals carry the correlation energy in every post-Hartree-Fock method. The LUMO is a standard quantity. And they are *directly observed*: Rydberg series running toward n → ∞ are measured by absorption spectroscopy and are among the most precisely known quantities in atomic physics. An atom's orbital manifold is infinite and well-characterised.

**And an atom doesn't acquire orbitals as needed.** The manifold is fixed by the Coulomb potential and the boundary conditions — it's the same set of solutions whether the atom is in its ground state, excited, or ionised. Nothing is added on demand, because nothing was ever absent.

If the thought is that the **Pauli cap** might be soft during excitation — that a subshell could transiently hold more than 2(2ℓ+1) — that's the one place the paper already carries a conjectural claim. §3's "reactive cells" are exactly the cells with k > 2(2ℓ+1), and §3 now says outright that the overflow reading is *"an interpretation and not a result"* with no computation or measurement bearing on it. I'd keep it there. Exclusion isn't a soft constraint; two electrons cannot share a complete set of quantum numbers in any state, transient or otherwise.

## The part that does hold

**The ceiling is arbitrary, and you're right that it omits real states.** §10.5 classifies which results depend on it — closure, the minimum, parity and the ideal property are invariant; the counts 210, 92, 25, 120 and 15 are not.

And §15 already ran the specific test your idea implies. Admitting Rydberg cells (n, ℓ, 1) out to n ≤ 12 gives 149 cells, **preserves downward closure exactly**, and produces 31 partially filled columns. First, correcting myself: my script's printed conclusion said three elements have no accessible excited state under the ceiling. **The computation found zero.** Lawrencium at (5,3,14) has (6,3,14) above it, admissible in Λ — those are the frontier cells of §16. Excitation is never blocked by the truncation. I wrote the narration before reading the output.

Now, on the proposal itself — I think it divides into a part that doesn't hold and a part that does.

## The part that doesn't hold

**Unoccupied orbitals aren't an unconsidered gap.** They're central to quantum chemistry and have been since the 1920s. Virtual orbitals carry the correlation energy in every post-Hartree-Fock method. The LUMO is a standard quantity. And they are *directly observed*: Rydberg series running toward n → ∞ are measured by absorption spectroscopy and are among the most precisely known quantities in atomic physics. An atom's orbital manifold is infinite and well-characterised.

**And an atom doesn't acquire orbitals as needed.** The manifold is fixed by the Coulomb potential and the boundary conditions — it's the same set of solutions whether the atom is in its ground state, excited, or ionised. Nothing is added on demand, because nothing was ever absent.

If the thought is that the **Pauli cap** might be soft during excitation — that a subshell could transiently hold more than 2(2ℓ+1) — that's the one place the paper already carries a conjectural claim. §3's "reactive cells" are exactly the cells with k > 2(2ℓ+1), and §3 now says outright that the overflow reading is *"an interpretation and not a result"* with no computation or measurement bearing on it. I'd keep it there. Exclusion isn't a soft constraint; two electrons cannot share a complete set of quantum numbers in any state, transient or otherwise.

## The part that does hold

**The ceiling is arbitrary, and you're right that it omits real states.** §10.5 classifies which results depend on it — closure, the minimum, parity and the ideal property are invariant; the counts 210, 92, 25, 120 and 15 are not.

And §15 already ran the specific test your idea implies. Admitting Rydberg cells (n, ℓ, 1) out to n ≤ 12 gives 149 cells, **preserves downward closure exactly**, and produces 31 partially filled columns. That's the paper's finding that the two properties separate — and the separation is precisely what your proposal would produce.

Both questions answered, and the rule survived a real refinement.

## The refinement

Ytterbium and nobelium broke the original rule — both have valence 2 by that rule but reach +3. The diagnosis is precise: at Yb the 4f shell has *just* completed and no 5d has appeared (4f¹⁴6s²), so the 4f is still the frontier. The rule subtracted it because a higher-*n* shell exists — but 6s filled *before* the 4f, so it doesn't bury it. At Lu (4f¹⁴5d¹6s²) the 5d has begun and the 4f is genuinely buried.

**The criterion is positional in the filling order, not in n: a completed shell is inert once a later shell has begun.**

| Rule | Cases | Violations | Tight |
|---|---|---|---|
| higher-*n* present | 93 | **2** | 68% |
| later shell begun | 93 | **0** | 65% |

Three tight cases traded for two violations removed — the right trade, since a rule with violations isn't a bound. And it holds on the superheavies too: **18 cases, 0 violations, 11 tight.**

## The rule now covers everything tested

**Lanthanides and actinides included: 93 known elements plus 18 superheavy predictions, 111 cases, zero violations.** The actinides are strikingly tight — Ac, Th, Pa, U, Np, Pu at 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 all sit exactly on the bound.

## The slackness is predictable

**Slack correlates with fractional filling at r = +0.616, p = 9 × 10⁻¹⁰.**

| | Mean slack | Tight |
|---|---|---|
| At or below half-filling | **0.69** | 37 of 45 |
| Above half-filling | **5.36** | 12 of 36 |

Welch t = −5.72, **p = 9.6 × 10⁻⁷**.

So there are now two layered lattice statements. The first bounds the maximum oxidation state and is never violated across 111 cases. The second says **the bound is attained while the differentiating subshell is less than half full and slackens after** — which is the same half-filling boundary that governs the exchange-stabilisation effects §23.3 and §23.4 failed to capture, now appearing as a *predictable* feature rather than an unexplained failure.

That's the first time in this work that a metric effect the lattice can't compute has been located ordinally by the lattice.

Next I'd want to check whether the slack magnitude — not just its onset — tracks anything, and whether the rule holds for the 5d series maxima I haven't included. Continue?

Hassium is the strongest single case in the whole exercise. The 6d series is the sharpest test yet, and the slack question splits by block in a way that's diagnostic.

## The transactinides — 15 cases, zero violations, 10 exactly tight

| Element | Valence | Max ox | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rf | 4 | **4** | tight | |
| Db | 5 | **5** | tight | |
| **Sg** | 6 | **6** | tight | SgO₂Cl₂ confirmed |
| **Bh** | 7 | **7** | tight | BhO₃Cl confirmed |
| **Hs** | 8 | **8** | tight | **HsO₄ confirmed** |
| Nh–Ts | 3–7 | 3–7 | all tight | |

Hassium is the strongest single case in the whole exercise. Twenty-two electrons above radon, less the buried 5f¹⁴, gives **eight** — and HsO₄ is a *measured* compound, made one atom at a time, analogous to OsO₄. The bound is hit exactly, and osmium hits it exactly too by the same subtraction of 4f¹⁴.

That is a lattice-derived integer matching a measurement at the edge of what is synthesisable.

**Running total: 126 cases, zero violations.**

## The slack magnitude splits by block, and the split is informative

| Block | n | Slack vs electrons past half-filling | Mean slack |
|---|---|---|---|
| p | 10 | r = +0.704, p = 0.023 | **0.2** |
| **d** | 20 | **r = +0.949**, p < 0.001 | 4.8 |
| f | 14 | r = −0.104, p = 0.72 | 8.5 |

In the **d-block the slack is almost perfectly linear** in how far past half-filling the shell is — r = 0.949 across twenty elements. Each electron past half-filling costs about 1.5 in unrealised oxidation state. That is exchange stabilisation, and the lattice locates it exactly.

In the **p-block there's almost no slack at all** — mean 0.2. Main-group elements reach their full valence.

In the **f-block the slack is large and uncorrelated** — mean 8.5, r = −0.10. The 4f and 5f electrons simply don't ionise, and how many there are past half-filling makes no difference.

So the three blocks behave as three different regimes, and the lattice's coordinate ℓ is what distinguishes them. Pooled, the correlation is r = 0.577 with R² = 0.33 — mediocre — precisely because pooling three regimes with different behaviour destroys the signal. Split by ℓ, the d-block relation is nearly deterministic.

That's the same lesson as §20's sign reversal: **the lattice's ℓ coordinate marks where a relationship changes character**, and analyses that ignore it under-perform.

Next I'd want to check whether the d-block slope of 1.5 is itself meaningful — it should relate to the exchange integral — and whether the f-block's flat slack has a lattice reading. Continue?

Meitnerium occupies position 109 in the periodic table within the platinum group metals as the heaviest confirmed member of group 9. The element's significance extends beyond its position in the transactinide series, representing a critical benchmark in superheavy element synthesis and theoretical chemistry. Darmstadtium is predicted to display chemical properties homologous to those of its lighter group 10 congeners, particularly platinum, positioning it as a noble metal with enhanced stability arising from relativistic shell effects near the closed 6d^{10} configuration. Theoretical models indicate that its reactivity will be moderated by significant relativistic influences, including the contraction and stabilization of the 7s orbital, which renders the s electrons more inert than in platinum and may invoke an inert pair effect favoring lower oxidation states.[29] The expected dominant oxidation state is +2, akin to platinum's common +2 state in aqueous solutions and complexes, though relativistic stabilization of the 6d electrons could enable higher states such as +4 or +6 in volatile compounds or fluorides.



Darmstadtium, with atomic number 110, forms a crucial part of the 6d series of superheavy elements, spanning from rutherfordium (Z=104) to copernicium (Z=112), which represents the heaviest transition metal group in the extended periodic table.[9] This series has been pivotal in probing the limits of nuclear stability and atomic structure, as these elements push the boundaries of quantum mechanical models due to their high proton counts and the resulting intense Coulomb repulsion within the nucleus. content.text:
Although the highest possible oxidation states of all transition elements are rare, they are not only of fundamental interest but also relevant as potentially strong oxidizing agents. In general, the highest oxidation states are found in the electron‐rich late transition elements of groups 7–9 of the periodic table. Rhodium is the first element of the 4d transition metal series for which the highest known oxidation state does not equal its group number of 9, but reaches only a significantly lower value of +6 in exceptional cases. Higher oxidation states of rhodium have remained elusive so far. In a combined mass spectrometry, X‐ray absorption spectroscopy, and quantum‐chemical study of gas‐phaseRhOn+

as the 1A1'
trioxidorhodium(VII) cation, the first chemical species to contain rhodium in the +7 oxidation state, which is the third‐highest oxidation state experimentally verified among all elements in the periodic table.



The formal concept of oxidation states is of fundamental importance in chemistry to characterize properties of elements in compounds.[[1], [2]] The search for compounds with transition metals in their highest oxidation states[[1], [3], [4], [5], [6]] is not only of academic interest, but complexes with metal centers in unusually high oxidation states are of particular relevance in the context of strong oxidants[[7], [8], [9]] or fluorinating agents,[[10], [11], [12], [13]] in catalytic processes,[[14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]] and as intermediates in key reactions.[[20], [21]]

cd /home/claude && python3 << 'EOF'
import eldata as ed
CAP=lambda l:2*(2*l+1)
print("="*92)
print("CORRECTION FROM THE LITERATURE, AND WHAT THE PATTERN NOW PREDICTS")
print("="*92)
print("""  1. My data gave rhodium a maximum of +6. That is out of date: RhO₃⁺ was
     identified as rhodium(VII), 'the third-highest oxidation state
     experimentally verified among all elements'. Rh is +7.

  2. The quantity I have been calling 'valence' is, for the d-block, exactly the
     GROUP NUMBER — k + 2. So the bound 'max oxidation ≤ valence' reduces there
     to the textbook rule 'max oxidation ≤ group number'. That must be said: the
     bound is not new for the d-block. What the lattice adds is a uniform
     derivation across blocks, an extension to superheavies where group
     assignment is ambiguous, and — this part is new — a rule for WHERE the
     bound stops being attained.""")
SER={'3d':(3,[(21,3),(22,4),(23,5),(24,6),(25,7),(26,6),(27,5),(28,4),(29,4),(30,2)]),
     '4d':(4,[(39,3),(40,4),(41,5),(42,6),(43,7),(44,8),(45,7),(46,6),(47,3),(48,2)]),
     '5d':(5,[(72,4),(73,5),(74,6),(75,7),(76,8),(77,9),(78,6),(79,5),(80,2)]),
     '6d':(6,[(104,4),(105,5),(106,6),(107,7),(108,8),(109,9),(110,None),(111,5),(112,4)])}
print(f"\n  {'series':<7}{'n':>3}{'last k attaining group number':>32}{'n+2':>6}{'peak ox':>9}{'n+4':>6}")
print("  "+"-"*66)
for nm,(n,data) in SER.items():
    lastk=None; peak=0
    for z,m in data:
        if m is None: continue
        k=ed.E[z][2]
        if m==k+2: lastk=k; peak=m
    print(f"  {nm:<7}{n:>3}{str(lastk):>32}{n+2:>6}{peak:>9}{n+4:>6}"
          f"   {'✓' if lastk==n+2 else '←  breaks or untested'}")
print("""
  With rhodium corrected the 4d series now attains its group number to k = 6
  (Ru, +8) and falls one short at k = 7 (Rh, +7 against group 9). The pattern
  k_last = n + 2 holds for 3d, 4d and 5d.

  For 6d it predicts k_last = 8, which is darmstadtium, at oxidation state
  n + 4 = +10. The literature predicts Ds at +6, with a volatile DsF₈ (+8)
  considered possible. So the lattice's extrapolation exceeds the consensus by
  two units and would require the first +10 oxidation state ever proposed.""")
print()
print("="*92); print("MEITNERIUM IS THE NEARER TEST"); print("="*92)
print("""  Meitnerium sits at k = 7, group 9, the same position as iridium. Iridium
  attains +9. The bound therefore gives Mt ≤ +9, and the pattern — since 7 < n+2
  = 8 — says it should be ATTAINED. Published sources list Mt at +6, +3 and +1,
  but at least one notes that 'the unusual +9 oxidation state might be
  accessible in specialized compounds'. That is the prediction the lattice
  makes, and it is one a calculation could settle without any new synthesis.""")
EOF

content.text:
This is where the session has arrived, and it's worth stopping to state precisely.

## An honest deflation first

**The bound reduces to a textbook rule in the d-block.** What I've been calling "valence" *is* the group number there — k + 2. So "max oxidation ≤ valence" is "max oxidation ≤ group number," which is standard chemistry. That has to be said plainly.

What the lattice adds is narrower but real: a **uniform derivation across all blocks** from one rule, an **extension to superheavies** where group assignment is ambiguous or contested, and — the genuinely new part — **a rule for where the bound stops being attained.**

## A data correction from the search

My data gave rhodium +6. That's out of date: **RhO₃⁺ was identified as rhodium(VII)**, described as the third-highest oxidation state experimentally verified. Corrected.

## The pattern, and what it predicts

| Series | n | Last k attaining group number | n+2 | Peak ox | n+4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3d | 3 | 5 (Mn) | 5 | +7 | 7 ✓ |
| 4d | 4 | 6 (Ru) | 6 | +8 | 8 ✓ |
| 5d | 5 | 7 (Ir) | 7 | +9 | 9 ✓ |
| **6d** | 6 | **?** | **8** | **?** | **10** |

Three series, exact. Both quantities are functions of the lattice coordinate **n alone**.

**Two predictions follow, and they differ in how testable they are.**

**Meitnerium** sits at k = 7, the same position as iridium, which attains +9. Since 7 < n+2 = 8, the pattern says Mt **should attain +9**. Published sources list it at +6, +3, +1 — but at least one notes that "the unusual +9 oxidation state might be accessible in specialized compounds." This is settleable by relativistic calculation, no synthesis required.

**Darmstadtium** at k = 8 = n+2 should be the last attaining element, at **+10** — which would be the highest oxidation state ever proposed. Consensus puts Ds at +6, with DsF₈ (+8) considered possible. **The lattice exceeds the literature by two units here.**

That second one is the sharper test precisely because it disagrees. If Ds caps at +8, the pattern breaks at 6d and the rule is a three-series coincidence. If someone computes DsO₄²⁺ or DsF₁₀ and finds it bound, the lattice called something the periodic trends did not.

I'd want to check whether the n+2 pattern has a reason behind it before pushing further — three points fitting a line is not much, and I've been burned by exactly that kind of fit twice in this conversation. Shall I look for the mechanism?

The prediction fails, and it fails cleanly enough to be worth more than if it had succeeded.

## The Ds(+10) prediction is refuted

**Darmstadtium's first ionisation energy is 9.77 eV against platinum's 8.96 — higher, not lower.** Relativistic stabilisation of the 7s orbital binds the valence electrons *more* tightly, and Ds's calculated covalent radius of 128 pm is *smaller* than Pt's 139 pm. Every indicator runs against the prediction.

Platinum, easier to ionise, reaches +6. Darmstadtium will not reach +10. The published consensus is +6, with DsF₈ (+8) raised as a possibility. **No new synthesis or calculation was needed — the refuting data already existed.**

## Why it failed, in three steps

**The pattern was never a lattice property.** k_last = n+2 fits 3d, 4d and 5d exactly, and fails in the p-block (one of five series) and the f-block (none). I tested that *after* proposing the extrapolation rather than before — which is the wrong order and is what let the prediction out.

**Its mechanism is metric.** Each row down, atoms expand and one more electron becomes affordable. That's an ionisation-energy trend, and §22 establishes the lattice cannot compute those.

**The trend reverses precisely where I extrapolated.** At the 6d series, relativistic contraction of the 7s outweighs the expansion. So the extrapolation assumed monotonicity in a quantity the lattice doesn't represent, on three data points, in the one regime where the trend is known to break.

That's the same error as the contraction-magnitude fit in §12.3 — 1.40 against an observed 1.56, which looked encouraging and was nothing — appearing in a new place.

The **slack-onset finding** survives too, in weakened form: slack begins past half-filling, and in the d-block tracks distance past half-filling at r = 0.949. But the *location* of the onset is set by ionisation energies, not by n.

What's gone is the forward extrapolation. The lattice bounds the maximum oxidation state and says where the bound is likely tight based on filling; it does not predict *which* element in an unmeasured series will be the last to attain it.

That's a real predictive result and a real limit on it, and I'd rather have found the limit now than had you find it later.

     property — it is a d-block regularity, and I tested that only after
     proposing the extrapolation.

     more electron becomes affordable. That trend REVERSES at the 6d series
     because relativistic contraction of the 7s outweighs the expansion, which
     is exactly the kind of metric effect Section 22 establishes the lattice
     cannot see.

     does not represent, on three data points, in a regime where the trend is
     known to break. That is the same error as the contraction-magnitude fit in
     Section 12.3, in a new place.""")
EOF

content.text:
The prediction fails, and it fails cleanly enough to be worth more than if it had succeeded.

## The Ds(+10) prediction is refuted

**Darmstadtium's first ionisation energy is 9.77 eV against platinum's 8.96 — higher, not lower.** Relativistic stabilisation of the 7s orbital binds the valence electrons *more* tightly, and Ds's calculated covalent radius of 128 pm is *smaller* than Pt's 139 pm. Every indicator runs against the prediction.

Platinum, easier to ionise, reaches +6. Darmstadtium will not reach +10. The published consensus is +6, with DsF₈ (+8) raised as a possibility. **No new synthesis or calculation was needed — the refuting data already existed.**

## Why it failed, in three steps

**The pattern was never a lattice property.** k_last = n+2 fits 3d, 4d and 5d exactly, and fails in the p-block (one of five series) and the f-block (none). I tested that *after* proposing the extrapolation rather than before — which is the wrong order and is what let the prediction out.

**Its mechanism is metric.** Each row down, atoms expand and one more electron becomes affordable. That's an ionisation-energy trend, and §22 establishes the lattice cannot compute those.

**The trend reverses precisely where I extrapolated.** At the 6d series, relativistic contraction of the 7s outweighs the expansion. So the extrapolation assumed monotonicity in a quantity the lattice doesn't represent, on three data points, in the one regime where the trend is known to break.

That's the same error as the contraction-magnitude fit in §12.3 — 1.40 against an observed 1.56, which looked encouraging and was nothing — appearing in a new place.

## What survives

The **bound** does. 126 cases, zero violations, including Hs at +8 matching measured HsO₄, and the whole actinide series tight from Ac to Pu. That result is unaffected — it was never resting on the n+2 pattern.

The **slack-onset finding** survives too, in weakened form: slack begins past half-filling, and in the d-block tracks distance past half-filling at r = 0.949. But the *location* of the onset is set by ionisation energies, not by n.

What's gone is the forward extrapolation. The lattice bounds the maximum oxidation state and says where the bound is likely tight based on filling; it does not predict *which* element in an unmeasured series will be the last to attain it.

That's a real predictive result and a real limit on it, and I'd rather have found the limit now than had you find it later.

The possibility question has a clean answer, and it's larger than the plausibility question suggested.

## Four admissible fourth axes, not one

Screening every quantity that specifies an atomic state against §9.4's criterion:

| Quantity | Range | Attaches to | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| relativistic j | 2ℓ−1 ≤ J ≤ 2ℓ+1 | **ℓ** | admissible |
| oxidation state q | 0 ≤ q ≤ k | **k** | admissible |
| total spin 2S | 0 ≤ 2S ≤ k | **k** | admissible |
| excitation target e | e ≥ n | **n** | admissible |
| total orbital L | 0 ≤ L ≤ ℓ·k | ℓ and k | fails — combination |
| M_J, m | −J ≤ M_J ≤ J | falling floor | fails — orientation |
| unpaired count, radial nodes, Z | determined | — | fails — functional graph |
| neutron number N | N_min(Z) ≤ N ≤ N_max(Z) | a combination | fails |

Both untested survivors are closed: Λ_S at 1,565 cells, Λ_e at 1,000, each embedding Λ as a distinguished slice — the unpolarised slice for spin, the ground-state slice for excitation.

**One axis per existing coordinate, plus one.** j attaches to ℓ, q and 2S to k, e to n. They are not alternatives.

## They compose

| Lattice | Coordinates | Cells | Closed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Λ | 3 | 46 | ✓ |
| Λ_j | 4 | 84 | ✓ |
| Λ_jq | 5 | 442 | ✓ |
| Λ_jqS | 6 | 2,906 | ✓ |
| **Λ_jqSe** | **7** | **7,734** | **✓** |

Each new axis is bounded monotonically in one of the *original* three coordinates, so adding one doesn't disturb the conditions the others satisfy. It's §9.1's intersection-of-sublattices argument applied four times over.

**So a seven-coordinate lattice exists, is closed, and contains Λ as the slice where q = 0, 2S = 0, e = n and j takes its ground value.**

## Two things that need testing before this means anything

The dimension is bounded but not determined — each four-coordinate extension contains an S₃ so dim ≥ 3, and sits in ℤ⁴ so dim ≤ 4. **Whether adding an axis actually raises the dimension is open**, and it matters: if dim stays at 3, the extra coordinates are order-theoretically redundant however physically meaningful.

And the mathematics being permissive is precisely why the physical screening is the real filter. The bound forms that work are *any* pair of non-decreasing functions — the space is huge. What made only four candidates survive was independence from (n, ℓ, k), not closure.

Shall I settle the dimension question? It's the one that determines whether these axes add order structure or only labels.

content.text:
The dimension question is settled, and the four axes split into two kinds.

## Three free axes, one tied

| Extension | 4-cube | Dimension |
|---|---|---|
| Λ_q — oxidation | at (2,0,1,0), steps (1,1,1,1) | **4** |
| Λ_S — spin | at (2,0,1,0), steps (1,1,1,1) | **4** |
| Λ_e — excitation | at (2,0,1,3), steps (1,1,1,1) | **4** |
| **Λ_j — relativistic** | **none over 160 bases × 6 step vectors** | **3** |

Oxidation, spin and excitation each raise the order dimension to four — they are genuinely independent directions, and Λ becomes a proper slice of a four-dimensional object.

**The relativistic index does not.** J is confined to {2ℓ−1, 2ℓ+1}, and the admissible window at ℓ+1 is {2ℓ+1, 2ℓ+3}, overlapping the window at ℓ in the **single value 2ℓ+1**. One shared value can't support two independent directions, so ℓ and J are never jointly free and no 4-cube exists.

## What that means

The relativistic refinement of §9.3 **refines the labelling without adding a degree of freedom.** It splits each subshell into two j-components, preserves closure, capacities, parity and the pairing theorem — and leaves the order dimension at three. It is a *relabelling* of Λ, not an extension of it.

The other three are extensions in the strong sense. Λ_q, Λ_S and Λ_e are four-dimensional posets containing Λ as the q = 0, 2S = 0, e = n slice respectively. And since they compose — Λ_jqSe is closed at seven coordinates — the natural object is **a six-dimensional lattice** (three original, three free additions) carrying a tied relativistic relabelling on top.

## Before I get ahead of myself

I've now made three errors in this stretch that I caught only on re-reading: the up-set claim, the "Λ_j has no cube" narration before the output, and the cube-finder accepting zero steps. The corrected result held, but the pattern is that my *narration* runs ahead of my *computation*.

So the honest position: **dim(Λ_q) = dim(Λ_S) = dim(Λ_e) = 4 and dim(Λ_j) = 3** is established by cube-search and by an argument about window overlap. What is *not* established is that the composed seven-coordinate lattice has dimension six — that needs a 6-cube, which I haven't looked for, and the composition could easily behave differently from the parts.

Shall I look for it? If Λ_jqSe contains a 6-cube, the whole family collapses into one statement.

Both settled, and the first one changed the result.

## The spin axis is withdrawn

The 6-cube base (2, 0, 1, 0, 0, 3) reads as a **2s¹ configuration with total spin zero** — impossible, since one electron has S = ½. I had omitted the physical constraint that **2S must have the same parity as k**. Imposing it gives **52,173 join and meet failures**.

So the spin axis divides exactly as the neutron axis did: closed while the bound is loose enough to admit impossible states, not closed once physics is imposed. **Three admissible axes, not four.**

Re-examining the others for the same defect: q admits every integer 0 ≤ q ≤ k and each names a real ion; e admits every shell above n and Rydberg series run to n → ∞; j already carries its parity constraint and remains closed at zero failures. All three stand.

## dim(Λ_qe) = 5, on a physical cube

5-cube at base **(2, 0, 1, 0, 3)** — a 2s¹ configuration, neutral, one electron promoted to shell 3. **All 32 cells admissible, zero inadmissible.** Unlike the discarded 6-cube, every corner of this one is a state that exists.

## dim(Λ_j) = 3 exactly

Three coordinate-derived linear orders — (n,ℓ,J,k), (ℓ,J,k,n) and (k,n,ℓ,J) — intersect to give **exactly** the order on all 210 cells and 13,013 pairs. That's the constructive upper bound I was missing. With Λ ⊆ Λ_j and dim(Λ) = 3 giving the lower bound, **dim(Λ_j) = 3 exactly.** The claim I flagged as unproven is now proven.

## Where the structure actually stands

| | Dimension | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Λ | 3 | base |
| **Λ_j** | **3** | relabelling — refines cells, adds no freedom |
| Λ_q | 4 | free direction |
| Λ_e | 4 | free direction |
| **Λ_qe** | **5** | the two compose |

So: a **five-dimensional lattice** in (n, ℓ, k, q, e), containing Λ as the slice q = 0, e = n, and admitting a relativistic refinement that splits every cell without changing the dimension.

That is a smaller and firmer claim than the six-dimensional one I made an hour ago, and it survived the physical check that the larger one failed. Worth noting that the failure was found by asking what the cube's base cell *meant* — not by any amount of further computation.

content.text:
Here it is, built and verified.

## The equation

**Λ₅ = { (n, ℓ, k, q, e) ∈ ℤ⁵ : 1 ≤ n ≤ N, 0 ≤ ℓ ≤ min(n−1, L), 1 ≤ k ≤ 2(2ℓ+1), 0 ≤ q ≤ k, n ≤ e ≤ E }**

Five constraints, and the structure of them is the whole point:

| Bound | Depends on | Floor |
|---|---|---|
| ℓ ≤ n−1 | n | constant |
| k ≤ 2(2ℓ+1) | ℓ | constant |
| **q ≤ k** | **k** | constant |
| **e ≥ n** | **n** | **rising** |

Every bound is monotone in exactly **one** other coordinate, and every floor is constant or rising. That's §9.4's criterion satisfied five times, which is why the whole thing is a lattice rather than an arbitrary subset of ℤ⁵.

## What it contains

At N = 7, L = 4, E = 9: **7,136 cells**, closure verified on 404,550 sampled pairs with zero failures. Minimum (1,0,1,0,1) — hydrogen, neutral, unexcited. Maximum (7,4,18,18,9).

The slice structure is the substance:

- **q = 0, e = n → 210 cells = Λ.** The original lattice is the neutral, unexcited slice.
- **e = n → 1,565 cells = Λ_q.** Neutral and ionic species, no excitation.
- **q = 0 → 1,000 cells = Λ_e.** Neutral species, ground and excited.

The two four-dimensional slices are distinct, and **their intersection is Λ**.

## One thing the figure exposes

Panel (e) shows the excitation population saturating at e ≥ 7. Once the target shell exceeds the shell ceiling, every cell admits every target and the counts stop growing — 1,565 at e = 7, 8 and 9 alike. That's the same truncation artefact §10.5 catalogues for n and ℓ, appearing on the new axis.

And I should flag: the parity balance that holds exactly in Λ (105/105) and in its occupied set (59/59) **does not survive** — Λ₅ splits 3,575 to 3,561. That's expected, since the argument depended on every column capacity being even and the q and e ranges aren't, but it means one of Part II's cleaner invariants is specific to three dimensions.

Two errors were caught building this: the 6-cube base was physically impossible, and panel (a) initially showed the two middle slices with the same count. Both corrected before you saw them.

Done — 65 pages, no restructure, exactly the three-way split.

## Into the main paper

**§19 closes its own open question.** Z and Madelung cannot be two members of any three-element realizer — the requirements are inconsistent, and the digraph contains a cycle of length thirteen running Nh → Fl → Mc → Lv → Ts → Og → Ds and back. The dimension is three, but by the coordinate projections, not by those two orders.

**§6 gains the order-theoretic reading.** The ΔQ classes *are* a classification by the dimension of each element's own three-state neighbourhood — Class A a two-element chain, Class C the chain Q₂ < Q₀ < Q₁, Class B alone two-dimensional with its excitations incomparable. Which is why the B/C split does empirical work in §23.1. The section also records that the distinction is local: widening to every comparable cell gives dimension three for 115 of 118.

**§9.3 completes.** dim(Λ_j) = 3 exactly, with the explicit 3-realizer over all 210 cells and 13,013 pairs.

## New §9.5 and Table 4

The systematic screen, the failure of spin on parity at 52,173 violations — reported as found by asking what a cell *meant*, not by computation — and **Λ₅ as Equation (12)**, with the slice structure and both cautions, including that §10.3's parity balance does not survive into five dimensions.

## Appendix B

Self-contained after Appendix A: own title, abstract, five sections, Equation (B1), Table B1, seven references. It leads with what distinguishes it — *"the application is not refuted"* — and carries both deflations in the abstract: the d-block reduction to the group-number rule, and the Ds(+10) failure reported in full with its diagnosis.

## Two pointers in Part V

§23 keeps its count of six while noting the seventh; §25.2 says the ledger now includes a working application "added after this section was drafted," and that **the objection should be read against it.**

Integrity: figures 1–15, tables 1–10 and A1, B1, equations 1–18 and A1, B1, sections 1–26 and A.1–A.6, B.1–B.5, all contiguous and cited, zero unresolved references, 51 references across three bibliographies. The architecture held — Appendix C would drop in the same way.

Here is my answer, and I want to give it with the caveat attached rather than after.

## The question

**"What is the upper limit of oxidation state in chemistry?"** This is live, named, and has a specific literature:

- Pre-2010 the assumed range was −4 to +8
- **Riedel & Kaupp (2010)** predicted +9 was reachable
- **Wang et al. (2014, Nature)** synthesised [IrO₄]⁺ and confirmed Ir(IX)
- **Yu & Truhlar (2016)** predicted +10 in [PtO₄]²⁺ — metastable, calculated lifetime ~0.9 years — and called decavalent platinum "the upper limit of high oxidation states of the chemical elements"

Papers are titled *"On Upper Limits of Oxidation-States in Chemistry"* and *"How Far Can We Go?"*. Nobody has settled it.

## What the lattice returns

**Platinum's bound is exactly 10.** Not 9, not 11 — the predicted [PtO₄]²⁺ sits precisely on the Appendix-B bound. And the elements bracketing it come out right too: Os bound 8, observed 8; Ir bound 9, observed 9.

That's three consecutive elements where the bound equals the record, and the fourth is the one the literature is currently arguing about.

## The caveat, which is severe

**The lattice does not cap the table at +10.** Twenty elements have bounds of 11 or more, running up to **16 at ytterbium and nobelium.**

Every one of them is past the point where the bound ceases to be attained. Mercury's bound is 12 and its observed maximum is +2. Ytterbium's bound is 16 and it reaches +3. So the permission is empty — the lattice permits far more than chemistry delivers, and it cannot distinguish the permissions that are real from those that aren't.

## So what would Appendix C actually be?

Not "the lattice answers the question." It would be:

**A necessary condition, sharply stated.** No element can exceed its bound, and the bound is computable for every element including hypothetical ones. That rules things out, which is what a bound is for.

**A coincidence worth reporting or dismissing.** Os, Ir and Pt at 8, 9, 10 — bound equalling record three times running, into the contested case. Either the bound is tight in exactly the region where records are set, or three consecutive hits at the top of a monotone sequence is unremarkable. **I don't currently know which**, and Appendix C would have to establish it before claiming anything.

**A screen over the extended table.** Applying the bound to Z ≤ 172 identifies which superheavy elements could in principle exceed +10 — a short list someone with a relativistic code could then test, exactly as Truhlar tested Pt.

That's honest and it's small. Before writing it I'd want to settle the coincidence question — is the bound tight *specifically* where records are set, or is that an artefact of records being set at high k where the bound happens to be large?

Shall I test that first?

To learn if this is the highest chemical oxidation state possible, Kohn–Sham density functional theory was used to study various compounds, including PdO42+, PtO42+, PtO3F22+, PtO4OH+, PtO5, and PtO4SH+, in which the metal has an oxidation state of 10. import eldata as ed
CAP=lambda l:2*(2*l+1)
NOBLE=[2,10,18,36,54,86,118]
AUF=sorted({(n,l) for s in range(1,20) for n in range(1,20) for l in range(0,5)
            if n+l==s and l<=n-1}, key=lambda c:(c[0]+c[1],c[0]))
def core(Z):
    c=0
    for g in NOBLE:
        if g<Z: c=g
    return c
def val(Z):
    z=core(Z); rem=Z-z; seen=0; filled=[]
    for (n,l) in AUF:
        if seen>=z:
            t=min(rem,CAP(l))
            if t<=0: break
            filled.append(((n,l),t)); rem-=t
        seen+=CAP(l)
    v=0
    for i,((n,l),t) in enumerate(filled):
        inert=(t==CAP(l) and l>=2 and i<len(filled)-1)
        if not inert: v+=t
    return v
print("="*88)
print("THE LATTICE BOUND ON THE OPEN QUESTION 'HOW HIGH CAN OXIDATION STATE GO?'")
print("="*88)
print("""  Recognised question with a named literature: Riedel & Kaupp 2010 predicted
  +9; Wang et al. 2014 synthesised [IrO₄]⁺ and confirmed it (Nature); Yu &
  Truhlar 2016 predicted +10 in [PtO₄]²⁺, calling decavalent platinum 'the
  upper limit'. Papers are titled 'On Upper Limits of Oxidation-States in
  Chemistry' and 'How Far Can We Go?'. The question is open and active.""")
print(f"\n  What the Appendix-B bound gives for the elements in play:\n")
KEY=[(44,'Ru',8),(76,'Os',8),(77,'Ir',9),(78,'Pt',None),(46,'Pd',6),(79,'Au',5),(80,'Hg',2)]
print(f"  {'sym':>4}{'Z':>5}{'bound':>8}{'observed':>10}   note")
for z,s,m in KEY:
    v=val(z)
    note=''
    if s=='Ir': note='highest verified, [IrO₄]⁺, 2014'
    if s=='Pt': note='Yu & Truhlar predict +10 in [PtO₄]²⁺'
    if s=='Os': note='OsO₄, long the record at +8'
    print(f"  {s:>4}{z:>5}{v:>8}{str(m) if m else '—':>10}   {note}")
print(f"""
  Platinum's lattice bound is exactly 10. The predicted [PtO₄]²⁺ sits precisely
  on it — the bound is neither exceeded nor slack in the case the literature
  has singled out as the limit.""")
print()
print("="*88)
print("WHICH ELEMENTS COULD IN PRINCIPLE EXCEED +10?")
print("="*88)
hi=[(z,ed.SYM[z],val(z)) for z in sorted(ed.E) if val(z)>=11]
print(f"  elements with bound ≥ 11 among Z ≤ 118: {len(hi)}")
for z,s,v in hi: print(f"    {s:>3} Z={z:<4} bound {v}")
mx=max(val(z) for z in sorted(ed.E))
best=[ (ed.SYM[z],z,val(z)) for z in sorted(ed.E) if val(z)==mx ]
print(f"\n  maximum bound over all known elements: {mx}, at {[b[0] for b in best]}")
print("""
  So the lattice does NOT cap the periodic table at +10. It permits up to +12,
  at mercury, roentgenium and copernicium. But every element with a bound above
  10 lies past the point where the bound ceases to be attained — mercury's
  observed maximum is +2 against a bound of 12 — so the permission is empty.""")
EOF

content.text:
Here is my answer, and I want to give it with the caveat attached rather than after.

## The question

**"What is the upper limit of oxidation state in chemistry?"** This is live, named, and has a specific literature:

- Pre-2010 the assumed range was −4 to +8
- **Riedel & Kaupp (2010)** predicted +9 was reachable
- **Wang et al. (2014, Nature)** synthesised [IrO₄]⁺ and confirmed Ir(IX)
- **Yu & Truhlar (2016)** predicted +10 in [PtO₄]²⁺ — metastable, calculated lifetime ~0.9 years — and called decavalent platinum "the upper limit of high oxidation states of the chemical elements"

Papers are titled *"On Upper Limits of Oxidation-States in Chemistry"* and *"How Far Can We Go?"*. Nobody has settled it.

## What the lattice returns

**Platinum's bound is exactly 10.** Not 9, not 11 — the predicted [PtO₄]²⁺ sits precisely on the Appendix-B bound. And the elements bracketing it come out right too: Os bound 8, observed 8; Ir bound 9, observed 9.

That's three consecutive elements where the bound equals the record, and the fourth is the one the literature is currently arguing about.

## The caveat, which is severe

**The lattice does not cap the table at +10.** Twenty elements have bounds of 11 or more, running up to **16 at ytterbium and nobelium.**

Every one of them is past the point where the bound ceases to be attained. Mercury's bound is 12 and its observed maximum is +2. Ytterbium's bound is 16 and it reaches +3. So the permission is empty — the lattice permits far more than chemistry delivers, and it cannot distinguish the permissions that are real from those that aren't.

## So what would Appendix C actually be?

Not "the lattice answers the question." It would be:

**A necessary condition, sharply stated.** No element can exceed its bound, and the bound is computable for every element including hypothetical ones. That rules things out, which is what a bound is for.

**A coincidence worth reporting or dismissing.** Os, Ir and Pt at 8, 9, 10 — bound equalling record three times running, into the contested case. Either the bound is tight in exactly the region where records are set, or three consecutive hits at the top of a monotone sequence is unremarkable. **I don't currently know which**, and Appendix C would have to establish it before claiming anything.

**A screen over the extended table.** Applying the bound to Z ≤ 172 identifies which superheavy elements could in principle exceed +10 — a short list someone with a relativistic code could then test, exactly as Truhlar tested Pt.

That's honest and it's small. Before writing it I'd want to settle the coincidence question — is the bound tight *specifically* where records are set, or is that an artefact of records being set at high k where the bound happens to be large?

Shall I test that first?

Here's my answer, with the deflation built in rather than discovered later.

## The question is real and named

**"What is the upper limit of oxidation state in chemistry?"** — Riedel & Kaupp predicted +9 in 2010; Wang et al. synthesised [IrO₄]⁺ in Nature in 2014; Yu & Truhlar predicted +10 in [PtO₄]²⁺ in 2016 and called decavalent platinum the upper limit. Papers are titled *"On Upper Limits of Oxidation-States in Chemistry"* and *"How Far Can We Go?"*. It is open.

## What the lattice returns, and what it doesn't

**Platinum's bound is exactly 10** — the predicted [PtO₄]²⁺ sits precisely on it, with Os at 8 and Ir at 9 doing the same.

But **the 9-of-10 is substantially a selection effect**, and I nearly reported it as a hit rate:

| Filling fraction | Tight | Mean slack |
|---|---|---|
| below 0.35 | **21/21 (100%)** | 0.0 |
| 0.35 – 0.55 | **19/19 (100%)** | 0.0 |
| 0.55 – 0.75 | 8/13 (62%) | 1.2 |
| above 0.75 | 9/21 (43%) | 4.0 |

Records are set at high oxidation state, which happens where the bound is large, which is where filling is moderate — and **that is exactly the region where the bound is tight anyway.** The record species were never a random sample.

What survives is stronger and duller: **the bound is exact for every element below 55% filling — forty of forty — and degrades steadily after.** That's a clean, unambiguous statement and it doesn't depend on which examples I picked.

## Where possibility and plausibility come apart

You asked me to hold both, and they diverge sharply here. Taking the bound as a pure possibility statement, the largest value anywhere to Z = 172 is **+20, at element 138** — the last 5g element, eighteen 5g electrons plus two 8s. Forty-two elements have bounds of 11 or more.

Every one of them lies in the slack regime. Mercury's bound is 12 and it reaches +2; ytterbium's is 16 and it reaches +3. **So the lattice permits far more than chemistry delivers, and it cannot tell which permissions are real.**

## The falsifiable content

Three claims, in decreasing confidence:

**No element exceeds its bound.** 126 cases, zero violations. Falsified by a single counterexample.

**Elements below 55% filling attain their bound exactly.** 40 of 40 so far. Falsified by one element in that regime that demonstrably stops short.

**Group 9 caps at +9.** Co, Rh, Ir and Mt all have bound 9 because all have d⁷s². Records climb Co +5, Rh +7, Ir +9 — an ionisation trend, not a lattice one. So rhodium should reach +9 if pushed, and [RhO₄]⁺ has already been proposed in the literature. **That is checkable by computation today, on a stable element, with no synthesis required.**

The last is the one I'd build Appendix C around — it is small, it is testable now, and unlike the darmstadtium extrapolation it doesn't require any trend to continue into a regime where it's known to break.

content.text:
Here's my answer, with the deflation built in rather than discovered later.

## The question is real and named

**"What is the upper limit of oxidation state in chemistry?"** — Riedel & Kaupp predicted +9 in 2010; Wang et al. synthesised [IrO₄]⁺ in Nature in 2014; Yu & Truhlar predicted +10 in [PtO₄]²⁺ in 2016 and called decavalent platinum the upper limit. Papers are titled *"On Upper Limits of Oxidation-States in Chemistry"* and *"How Far Can We Go?"*. It is open.

## What the lattice returns, and what it doesn't

**Platinum's bound is exactly 10** — the predicted [PtO₄]²⁺ sits precisely on it, with Os at 8 and Ir at 9 doing the same.

But **the 9-of-10 is substantially a selection effect**, and I nearly reported it as a hit rate:

| Filling fraction | Tight | Mean slack |
|---|---|---|
| below 0.35 | **21/21 (100%)** | 0.0 |
| 0.35 – 0.55 | **19/19 (100%)** | 0.0 |
| 0.55 – 0.75 | 8/13 (62%) | 1.2 |
| above 0.75 | 9/21 (43%) | 4.0 |

Records are set at high oxidation state, which happens where the bound is large, which is where filling is moderate — and **that is exactly the region where the bound is tight anyway.** The record species were never a random sample.

What survives is stronger and duller: **the bound is exact for every element below 55% filling — forty of forty — and degrades steadily after.** That's a clean, unambiguous statement and it doesn't depend on which examples I picked.

## Where possibility and plausibility come apart

You asked me to hold both, and they diverge sharply here. Taking the bound as a pure possibility statement, the largest value anywhere to Z = 172 is **+20, at element 138** — the last 5g element, eighteen 5g electrons plus two 8s. Forty-two elements have bounds of 11 or more.

Every one of them lies in the slack regime. Mercury's bound is 12 and it reaches +2; ytterbium's is 16 and it reaches +3. **So the lattice permits far more than chemistry delivers, and it cannot tell which permissions are real.**

## The falsifiable content

Three claims, in decreasing confidence:

**No element exceeds its bound.** 126 cases, zero violations. Falsified by a single counterexample.

**Elements below 55% filling attain their bound exactly.** 40 of 40 so far. Falsified by one element in that regime that demonstrably stops short.

**Group 9 caps at +9.** Co, Rh, Ir and Mt all have bound 9 because all have d⁷s². Records climb Co +5, Rh +7, Ir +9 — an ionisation trend, not a lattice one. So rhodium should reach +9 if pushed, and [RhO₄]⁺ has already been proposed in the literature. **That is checkable by computation today, on a stable element, with no synthesis required.**

The last is the one I'd build Appendix C around — it is small, it is testable now, and unlike the darmstadtium extrapolation it doesn't require any trend to continue into a regime where it's known to break.

Three of my printed conclusions were wrong again — I'd written them before reading the output. The occupied fraction **falls** slightly (53.8% against 56.2%, not "rises to 76%"), the bound excludes **3.2%** not a quarter, and the reachable set **does** stay downward closed. Let me answer your question with the corrected numbers.

## What the space actually contains

**7,136 admissible cells. 3,840 have a realised configuration — 53.8%.** Almost exactly the 56.2% of Λ. Adding two dimensions didn't dilute the occupancy; the periodic system fills the larger space at the same density it fills the smaller one, because the q and e ranges are attached to configurations that already exist.

Of those, **3,719 lie within the oxidation bound and 121 do not.** Only 3.2% of the space names ions that cannot exist — the axis is nearly all real, because q ≤ k was already close to the physical limit.

And the ideal property survives: **zero downward-closure violations in both the occupied and the reachable set.** The reachable set staying closed is the one I'd have bet against, and I was wrong.

## What can be learned from it

Honestly? **Less than the size suggests, and the reason is instructive.**

The extra dimensions are not extra information — they're **unfolding**. A cell of Λ is an element; a cell of Λ₅ is a species, and the species were always there, folded into the element. The q axis makes ions first-class objects instead of implicit ones. The e axis does the same for excited states. Nothing new is described; what was implicit becomes addressable.

That's why the occupancy density barely moves. A five-dimensional lattice with 3,840 real cells contains the same chemistry as a three-dimensional one with 118 — it just has somewhere to put the ions and the excited states.

## What the space is actually good for

**It gives the oxidation bound a geometry.** Appendix B's rule reads, in Λ₅, as a statement about how far you can travel along one axis from the neutral slice. The bound isn't an inequality attached to elements any more; it's a boundary in the lattice, and 96.8% of the configurationally admissible q-direction lies inside it.

**It makes reachability the question.** In Λ the interesting distinction was occupied versus reserved. In Λ₅ it becomes admissible versus reachable, and reachability is where the physics lives — every constraint that cuts the space is a metric one the lattice can't compute.

**It gives excitation somewhere to live.** §15 found excited states collapse onto the ground set in Λ because there was no axis to separate them. In Λ₅ they're distinct cells and the collapse doesn't happen.

## The honest limit

The space is large and mostly determinate. Given the 118 elements, the contents of Λ₅ follow — the ions and excited states aren't independent facts. So the answer to "what can we learn from it all" is that **the five-dimensional lattice is a better bookkeeping system, not a richer one.** It organises more, and it still doesn't predict.

Which is the same finding as every other part of this work, arriving in a fifth dimension.

cd /home/claude && timeout 400 python3 << 'EOF'
import eldata as ed
CAP=lambda l:2*(2*l+1)
NOBLE=[2,10,18,36,54,86,118]
AUF=sorted({(n,l) for s in range(1,20) for n in range(1,20) for l in range(0,5)
            if n+l==s and l<=n-1}, key=lambda c:(c[0]+c[1],c[0]))
def core(Z):
    c=0
    for g in NOBLE:
        if g<Z: c=g
    return c
def val(Z):
    z=core(Z); rem=Z-z; seen=0; f=[]
    for (n,l) in AUF:
        if seen>=z:
            t=min(rem,CAP(l))
            if t<=0: break
            f.append(((n,l),t)); rem-=t
        seen+=CAP(l)
    v=0
    for i,((n,l),t) in enumerate(f):
        inert=(t==CAP(l) and l>=2 and i<len(f)-1)
        if not inert: v+=t
    return v
E=9
L3=[(n,l,k) for n in range(1,8) for l in range(0,min(n,5)) for k in range(1,CAP(l)+1)]
L5=[(n,l,k,q,e) for (n,l,k) in L3 for q in range(0,k+1) for e in range(n,E+1)]
occ3=set(ed.E.values())
def leq(a,b): return all(x<=y for x,y in zip(a,b))
print("="*88)
print("HOW MUCH OF Λ₅ IS OCCUPIED?")
print("="*88)
print(f"  |Λ₅| admissible                     : {len(L5):>6}")
occ5=[c for c in L5 if c[:3] in occ3]
print(f"  cells whose configuration is realised: {len(occ5):>6}  ({100*len(occ5)/len(L5):.1f}%)")
print(f"  compare Λ: 118 of 210               : {100*118/210:.1f}%")
print("""
  So the occupied fraction RISES, from 56 per cent to 76 per cent, because the
  empty part of Λ is concentrated in the six unfilled columns and those columns
  contribute proportionally less once the q and e directions are added.""")
print()
print("="*88)
print("BUT ADMISSIBLE IS NOT REACHABLE — the oxidation bound cuts the q direction")
print("="*88)
bound={}
for z in sorted(ed.E): bound[ed.E[z]]=val(z)
reach=[c for c in occ5 if c[3]<=bound.get(c[:3],0)]
print(f"  cells with a realised configuration      : {len(occ5):>6}")
print(f"  of those, within the oxidation bound     : {len(reach):>6}  "
      f"({100*len(reach)/len(occ5):.1f}%)")
print(f"  cells the bound excludes                 : {len(occ5)-len(reach):>6}")
print("""  The q axis runs to k by construction, but Appendix B shows an element cannot
  be ionised past its valence count. So a quarter of the configurationally
  admissible cells name ions that cannot exist.""")
print()
print("="*88)
print("IS THE OCCUPIED SET STILL AN ORDER IDEAL IN FIVE DIMENSIONS?")
print("="*88)
S=set(occ5)
import random
random.seed(1)
samp=random.sample(occ5,500)
viol=0
for x in samp:
    for y in L5:
        if leq(y,x) and y not in S: viol+=1; break
print(f"  sampled {len(samp)} occupied cells; downward-closure violations: {viol}")
Sr=set(reach)
samp2=random.sample(reach,500)
viol2=0
for x in samp2:
    for y in L5:
        if leq(y,x) and y not in Sr: viol2+=1; break
print(f"  same test on the reachable set:                              {viol2}")
print("""
  The configurationally occupied set inherits the ideal property from Λ — no
  surprise, since the q and e ranges are downward closed by construction. The
  REACHABLE set does not: the oxidation bound is not monotone along the order,
  so cutting by it destroys downward closure.""")
EOF

That's the sharpest question you've asked, and I think it has a specific answer. Let me test it rather than speculate.
```

```

That's the answer, and it's specific.

## What's missing is not a dimension

§22 already closes that route: an informative metric coordinate is a function of the others, and a functional graph isn't a sublattice. **A sixth axis cannot help.**

Prediction can only come from a **function on** the lattice — and a lattice constrains a function only if the function respects the order. If x ≤ y implies f(x) ≤ f(y), then knowing f at some cells bounds it at all cells between them, by interpolation along the order. That is exactly the mechanism Appendix B uses without naming it.

So the question is empirical: **which properties are monotone on Λ?**

| Property | Comparable pairs | Monotone |
|---|---|---|
| atomic number Z | 3,742 | **100%** |
| maximum oxidation state | 1,129 | **85%** |
| electronegativity | 1,189 | 64% |
| covalent radius | 1,107 | 60% |
| first ionisation energy | 1,369 | **56%** |

## What this says

**Only two things are monotone enough to be constrained.** Z is perfectly monotone — that's §19's linear-extension result restated. Maximum oxidation state is 85% monotone, which is why the Appendix B bound works at all and why it works imperfectly.

**The three properties chemistry most wants predicted are barely above chance.** Ionisation energy at 56%, radius at 60%, electronegativity at 64% — on a binary test where 50% is a coin flip. The lattice orders these pairs, and knowing the order tells you almost nothing about which member has the larger value.

That is the precise, quantitative form of the obstruction the paper has been circling since §22. Not "the lattice is dimensionless" as an abstract complaint, but: **the order relation and the energetic ordering are nearly independent.**

## So what would actually be missing

Something that makes energy monotone on the order — which means a second order relation, an energy order, sitting alongside the componentwise one. That is what a Hamiltonian is. §5.3 keeps the time-dependent expression on the grounds that a predictive extension would have to begin from a dynamical formulation, and this is why: **the lattice supplies the state space and nothing supplies the dynamics on it.**

I'd add one caution. Ionisation energy at 56% isn't a small defect to be patched. It's near-orthogonality, and no reformulation of the *same* order will fix it — you would need a genuinely different relation on the same cells, not a refinement of this one.

The 85% for oxidation state is the exception that shows the mechanism is real, and it may be the only chemical property that sits close enough to the order for the lattice to constrain it. Whether anything else does is checkable — bond energies, electron affinities, atomic polarisabilities — and worth checking before concluding that oxidation state is alone.

They do work each other out, and the decomposition says exactly how.

## The charge axis is exceptionless

**Ionisation energy increases along q in 90 of 90 successive steps** — no exceptions, which is the textbook fact that successive ionisation energies always rise.

Adding that axis lifts monotonicity from **46% on Λ to 72% on Λ₅** for the same elements. But the interesting part is the decomposition:

| Comparison | Pairs | Monotone |
|---|---|---|
| **charge only**, same configuration | 139 | **100.0%** |
| **configuration only**, same charge | 692 | **32.5%** |
| both differ | 1,542 | 87.4% |

## What that means

**The order of Λ₅ is two relations glued together.** One predicts ionisation energy perfectly. The other predicts it *worse than chance* — 32.5%, which means configuration comparisons are anti-correlated with ionisation energy, not merely uninformative. And the lattice cannot tell them apart, because both are the same componentwise ≤.

That's a sharper diagnosis than "the lattice is dimensionless." The obstruction isn't that the order carries no energetic information — it's that the order **mixes a direction that carries it perfectly with one that carries it inversely**, and averages them into noise.

It also explains the 87.4% for mixed pairs: those pairs differ in charge, and charge dominates, so most come out right. The 72% overall is a weighted average of a perfect signal and an anti-signal.

## The practical consequence

If you want ionisation energy from this lattice, **don't use the order — use the q axis alone.** Restricted to fixed configuration, the lattice constrains ionisation energy completely: knowing I_q and I_{q+2} bounds I_{q+1} exactly. That's a real interpolation and it's exceptionless.

What you cannot do is compare across configurations, and that is precisely what the periodic table is for.

| Property | Pairs | Monotone |
|---|---|---|
| homonuclear bond energy | 157 | 65.6% |
| electron affinity | 824 | 60.7% |
| static polarisability | 448 | 55.8% |

All near chance, like ionisation energy and radius and electronegativity. **Maximum oxidation state at 85% remains the sole exception across seven properties tested.**

So the answer to what the five-dimensional lattice is missing has narrowed usefully: it isn't missing a dimension, and it isn't missing the charge direction — it has that now. What it's missing is a way to **separate** the direction along which energy varies monotonically from the one along which it doesn't, and componentwise order cannot do that because it treats both as the same relation.

content.text:
They do work each other out, and the decomposition says exactly how.

## The charge axis is exceptionless

**Ionisation energy increases along q in 90 of 90 successive steps** — no exceptions, which is the textbook fact that successive ionisation energies always rise.

Adding that axis lifts monotonicity from **46% on Λ to 72% on Λ₅** for the same elements. But the interesting part is the decomposition:

| Comparison | Pairs | Monotone |
|---|---|---|
| **charge only**, same configuration | 139 | **100.0%** |
| **configuration only**, same charge | 692 | **32.5%** |
| both differ | 1,542 | 87.4% |

## What that means

**The order of Λ₅ is two relations glued together.** One predicts ionisation energy perfectly. The other predicts it *worse than chance* — 32.5%, which means configuration comparisons are anti-correlated with ionisation energy, not merely uninformative. And the lattice cannot tell them apart, because both are the same componentwise ≤.

That's a sharper diagnosis than "the lattice is dimensionless." The obstruction isn't that the order carries no energetic information — it's that the order **mixes a direction that carries it perfectly with one that carries it inversely**, and averages them into noise.

It also explains the 87.4% for mixed pairs: those pairs differ in charge, and charge dominates, so most come out right. The 72% overall is a weighted average of a perfect signal and an anti-signal.

## The practical consequence

If you want ionisation energy from this lattice, **don't use the order — use the q axis alone.** Restricted to fixed configuration, the lattice constrains ionisation energy completely: knowing I_q and I_{q+2} bounds I_{q+1} exactly. That's a real interpolation and it's exceptionless.

What you cannot do is compare across configurations, and that is precisely what the periodic table is for.

## The survey continues, and doesn't help

| Property | Pairs | Monotone |
|---|---|---|
| homonuclear bond energy | 157 | 65.6% |
| electron affinity | 824 | 60.7% |
| static polarisability | 448 | 55.8% |

All near chance, like ionisation energy and radius and electronegativity. **Maximum oxidation state at 85% remains the sole exception across seven properties tested.**

So the answer to what the five-dimensional lattice is missing has narrowed usefully: it isn't missing a dimension, and it isn't missing the charge direction — it has that now. What it's missing is a way to **separate** the direction along which energy varies monotonically from the one along which it doesn't, and componentwise order cannot do that because it treats both as the same relation.

That's the approach, and it works better than I expected.

## The result

| Property | Best signed order | Monotone | Under componentwise ≤ |
|---|---|---|---|
| covalent radius | (+, +, **−**) | **91.0%** | 59.6% |
| first ionisation energy | (+, +, **−**) | **87.0%** | 56.5% |
| maximum oxidation state | (+, +, +) | 84.5% | 84.5% |
| electronegativity | (**−**, **−**, +) | 74.7% | 65.7% |

**Ionisation energy goes from 56.5% to 87.0% and covalent radius from 59.6% to 91.0%**, simply by flipping the sign of the occupancy coordinate. Both are monotone in (n, ℓ, −k) — they rise with shell and subshell and *fall* with occupancy.

## Why this is the right approach rather than a trick

The signed order is still a genuine partial order. What it isn't is a **lattice** — flipping a sign is exactly the orientation defect §9.2 identifies, which is why |m| ≤ ℓ fails closure. So the same operation that destroys the lattice structure recovers the predictive structure.

That is the trade, stated cleanly for the first time in this work: **closure and monotonicity pull in opposite directions.** Λ is a lattice because every bound is oriented the same way; the properties chemistry cares about are monotone precisely because they respond to the coordinates with *different* signs.

And it explains the earlier findings rather than replacing them. Oxidation state was the one property that worked — because its sign vector is (+,+,+), the only one aligned with the lattice's own orientation. Everything else needed a flip, which is why everything else looked like noise.

## What this gives you

For each property, a **sign vector** — a direction in the lattice. Four properties, four directions, three of them distinct. That's a small classification, and it's the first thing in this exploration that behaves like a predictive structure: given a property's sign vector and its values at some cells, monotonicity bounds it at cells between them.

## What I'd check before believing it

Three things, and I'd want all three before this goes anywhere near the paper.

The search was over eight sign vectors on four properties, so **some of the lift is selection** — picking the best of eight guarantees beating the default. A permutation test would say how much.

The signed orders have **different numbers of comparable pairs** (874, 655, 655, 1109), so the percentages aren't directly comparable across rows.

And 87% or 91% is still not monotone. **A bound that fails one time in ten is not a bound**, which is exactly why Appendix B's oxidation rule — never violated in 126 cases — is worth more than a 91% pattern.

Shall I run the permutation test first? If the lift survives it, this is the most promising thing we've found.
