The lift survives comfortably.

## The permutation test

| Property | Observed | Null mean | Null 95th | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first ionisation energy | **87.0%** | 57.9% | 63.9% | **< 0.002** |
| covalent radius | **91.0%** | 59.2% | 66.3% | **< 0.002** |
| maximum oxidation state | **84.5%** | 64.4% | 71.1% | **< 0.002** |

All three observed values sit far outside the null distribution — 87% against a 95th percentile of 64%, 91% against 66%. **Selection over eight sign vectors accounts for about six or seven points of lift; the observed lift is thirty.** None of it is the multiple-comparison artefact I was worried about.

## What this establishes

Ionisation energy and covalent radius are both monotone in **(n, ℓ, −k)** — rising with shell and subshell, falling with occupancy — at 87% and 91%. Under the componentwise order they read as 56% and 60%, which is why every earlier test in this work found them uninformative.

**They were never uninformative. They were mis-oriented.**

That is a genuine finding, and it reframes a result the paper currently reports as a limit. §22 says the lattice cannot reach metric quantities; §12.3 says it fixes position but not magnitude; §23.5 records ionisation energy at 0.28 and electronegativity at 0.09 as failures. Those numbers were all computed against the lattice's own orientation.

## The trade, now stated precisely

**Closure requires every bound oriented the same way. Monotonicity of the chemically interesting properties requires the occupancy coordinate oriented the other way.** You can have Λ as a lattice, or you can have a partial order on which ionisation energy and radius are nearly monotone. Not both, on the same relation.

Oxidation state is the exception because its sign vector is (+,+,+) — the only one aligned with the lattice. That's why it was the only property that worked, and now we know why rather than just that.

## Where I'd stop and be careful

87% and 91% are still not bounds. One pair in ten violates, and Appendix B's value rests on *zero* violations in 126 cases. A 91% pattern is a correlation, not a constraint.

And the signed order is not a lattice, so none of Part II applies to it — no closure, no dimension result, no Sperner property, no ideal. What we'd have is a partial order with good monotonicity and none of the structure the paper spent forty pages establishing.

So the honest position: this is the most promising predictive lead in the whole exploration, and taking it means giving up the object the paper is about. That's a real choice, not a technicality.

Three things worth doing before deciding. Test whether the violating pairs cluster somewhere identifiable — if the 9% failures are all in one region, the pattern may be a bound with a stated exception. Check whether the signed order retains *any* useful structure, or none. And test more properties against their own best sign vectors, since only four have been tried.

content.text:
The lift survives comfortably.

## The permutation test

| Property | Observed | Null mean | Null 95th | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first ionisation energy | **87.0%** | 57.9% | 63.9% | **< 0.002** |
| covalent radius | **91.0%** | 59.2% | 66.3% | **< 0.002** |
| maximum oxidation state | **84.5%** | 64.4% | 71.1% | **< 0.002** |

All three observed values sit far outside the null distribution — 87% against a 95th percentile of 64%, 91% against 66%. **Selection over eight sign vectors accounts for about six or seven points of lift; the observed lift is thirty.** None of it is the multiple-comparison artefact I was worried about.

## What this establishes

Ionisation energy and covalent radius are both monotone in **(n, ℓ, −k)** — rising with shell and subshell, falling with occupancy — at 87% and 91%. Under the componentwise order they read as 56% and 60%, which is why every earlier test in this work found them uninformative.

**They were never uninformative. They were mis-oriented.**

That is a genuine finding, and it reframes a result the paper currently reports as a limit. §22 says the lattice cannot reach metric quantities; §12.3 says it fixes position but not magnitude; §23.5 records ionisation energy at 0.28 and electronegativity at 0.09 as failures. Those numbers were all computed against the lattice's own orientation.

## The trade, now stated precisely

**Closure requires every bound oriented the same way. Monotonicity of the chemically interesting properties requires the occupancy coordinate oriented the other way.** You can have Λ as a lattice, or you can have a partial order on which ionisation energy and radius are nearly monotone. Not both, on the same relation.

Oxidation state is the exception because its sign vector is (+,+,+) — the only one aligned with the lattice. That's why it was the only property that worked, and now we know why rather than just that.

## Where I'd stop and be careful

87% and 91% are still not bounds. One pair in ten violates, and Appendix B's value rests on *zero* violations in 126 cases. A 91% pattern is a correlation, not a constraint.

And the signed order is not a lattice, so none of Part II applies to it — no closure, no dimension result, no Sperner property, no ideal. What we'd have is a partial order with good monotonicity and none of the structure the paper spent forty pages establishing.

So the honest position: this is the most promising predictive lead in the whole exploration, and taking it means giving up the object the paper is about. That's a real choice, not a technicality.

Three things worth doing before deciding. Test whether the violating pairs cluster somewhere identifiable — if the 9% failures are all in one region, the pattern may be a bound with a stated exception. Check whether the signed order retains *any* useful structure, or none. And test more properties against their own best sign vectors, since only four have been tried.

Three results, and one of them is the largest single number this project has produced.

## The signed order is a join-semilattice

**Zero join failures, 8,080 meet failures.** Joins survive because lowering k is always admissible; meets fail because raising k past the capacity of a lower subshell is not. So Λ under σ = (+,+,−) retains least upper bounds and loses greatest lower bounds.

It has **five minimal elements** — (1,0,2), (2,1,6), (3,2,10), (4,3,14) and one more: the *filled* subshells, helium, neon, zinc, ytterbium. And **one maximal element**, (7,4,1): a single electron in 7g. Comparability drops from 54% to 32%.

That's a real object, just a much thinner one. Up-sets and filters survive; Birkhoff representation, Part III's ideal structure and §9.1's closure argument do not.

## The physical reading

σ = (+,+,−) is the componentwise order on (n, ℓ, **h**) where h = 2(2ℓ+1) − k is the number of **holes** in the valence subshell. The order under which these properties are monotone is the order by shell, subshell and **vacancy** — not occupancy.

And electronegativity's best vector (−,−,+) is that same order reversed. **Three properties, one order.**

## Static polarisability at 98.5%

| Property | σ | Pairs | Monotone | Plain ≤ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **static polarisability** | (+,−,−) | 459 | **98.5%** | 55.8% |
| covalent radius | (+,+,−) | 655 | 91.0% | 59.6% |
| first ionisation energy | (+,+,−) | 874 | 87.0% | 56.5% |
| electron affinity | (+,+,−) | 474 | 83.8% | 63.3% |
| melting point | (+,+,−) | 405 | 65.9% | 59.3% |

**Polarisability is monotone in 98.5% of comparable pairs — 452 of 459.** Under the componentwise order it read as 55.8%, indistinguishable from chance. It uses a different sign vector from the others, (+,−,−), meaning ℓ *and* k both oppose n.

That is not a correlation any more. Seven violations in 459 is the kind of number Appendix B's bound has, and it arrived on a property the paper had never tested.

## Where the failures live

The violations aren't uniform. For ionisation energy, **68% of violating pairs involve a d-block element** and 62 of 114 are d–d pairs. For radius, 32 of 59 are s–p pairs. So the failures concentrate where the anomalies and half-filling effects already live — which suggests the residual 9–13% may be the same exchange-stabilisation effect that produces the slack in Appendix B, not random noise.

Worth testing next: whether polarisability's 7 violations cluster too, and whether excluding the d-block lifts ionisation energy toward 98% as well. If the failures are all one mechanism, this stops being a set of correlations and becomes a bound with a stated exception.

content.text:
Three results, and one of them is the largest single number this project has produced.

## The signed order is a join-semilattice

**Zero join failures, 8,080 meet failures.** Joins survive because lowering k is always admissible; meets fail because raising k past the capacity of a lower subshell is not. So Λ under σ = (+,+,−) retains least upper bounds and loses greatest lower bounds.

It has **five minimal elements** — (1,0,2), (2,1,6), (3,2,10), (4,3,14) and one more: the *filled* subshells, helium, neon, zinc, ytterbium. And **one maximal element**, (7,4,1): a single electron in 7g. Comparability drops from 54% to 32%.

That's a real object, just a much thinner one. Up-sets and filters survive; Birkhoff representation, Part III's ideal structure and §9.1's closure argument do not.

## The physical reading

σ = (+,+,−) is the componentwise order on (n, ℓ, **h**) where h = 2(2ℓ+1) − k is the number of **holes** in the valence subshell. The order under which these properties are monotone is the order by shell, subshell and **vacancy** — not occupancy.

And electronegativity's best vector (−,−,+) is that same order reversed. **Three properties, one order.**

## Static polarisability at 98.5%

| Property | σ | Pairs | Monotone | Plain ≤ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **static polarisability** | (+,−,−) | 459 | **98.5%** | 55.8% |
| covalent radius | (+,+,−) | 655 | 91.0% | 59.6% |
| first ionisation energy | (+,+,−) | 874 | 87.0% | 56.5% |
| electron affinity | (+,+,−) | 474 | 83.8% | 63.3% |
| melting point | (+,+,−) | 405 | 65.9% | 59.3% |

**Polarisability is monotone in 98.5% of comparable pairs — 452 of 459.** Under the componentwise order it read as 55.8%, indistinguishable from chance. It uses a different sign vector from the others, (+,−,−), meaning ℓ *and* k both oppose n.

That is not a correlation any more. Seven violations in 459 is the kind of number Appendix B's bound has, and it arrived on a property the paper had never tested.

## Where the failures live

The violations aren't uniform. For ionisation energy, **68% of violating pairs involve a d-block element** and 62 of 114 are d–d pairs. For radius, 32 of 59 are s–p pairs. So the failures concentrate where the anomalies and half-filling effects already live — which suggests the residual 9–13% may be the same exchange-stabilisation effect that produces the slack in Appendix B, not random noise.

Worth testing next: whether polarisability's 7 violations cluster too, and whether excluding the d-block lifts ionisation energy toward 98% as well. If the failures are all one mechanism, this stops being a set of correlations and becomes a bound with a stated exception.

Polarisability at **98.5%** — 452 of 459 — with all seven violations traceable to named contraction effects, stands as the strongest single result. So the honest state: **one property is nearly perfectly ordered by the lattice under a sign flip, three more are strongly but imperfectly ordered, and the residuals do not share a common cause.** That's a real finding and a genuinely different picture from the paper's current position that the lattice reaches no metric quantity at all — but it is not yet a bound, and the difference between 98.5% and 100% is the difference between a pattern and a constraint.

The next thing I'd want is polarisability data for the d-block and f-block, which the current set lacks entirely. If 98.5% holds across all 118 elements rather than 38 main-group ones, that changes what this is. If it collapses, the result was about main groups all along.

The recheck changes two things materially, and one of them undercuts the headline.

## Polarisability's 98.5% does not survive the d-block

**With the d-block added: 89.9%, and the best sign vector changes from (+,−,−) to (+,+,−).** So the 98.5% was a main-group result, and the sign vector that produced it doesn't generalise — the d-block prefers a different orientation entirely, (−,+,−) at 92.3% on its own.

That means what I called "the strongest single result" was a 38-element, main-group-only figure. Adding thirty more elements drops it eleven points into the same 84–91% band as everything else. My caution about needing d-block data was right, and the answer was unfavourable.

One caveat on the caveat: **the d-block polarisabilities are recalled, not read from a source.** They're approximately right in magnitude and ordering but I can't verify them here. If they're wrong the 89.9% is wrong too — though the sign-vector *change* is a structural finding that wouldn't easily reverse.

## The scale-dependence is the more serious problem

| Electronegativity scale | Best σ | Monotone |
|---|---|---|
| Pauling | (−,−,+) | 74.7% |
| **Allen** | **(+,−,−)** | **98.1%** |

**Same property, two scales, and the result moves from 75% to 98% with a different sign vector.**

That is a much bigger warning than the polarisability collapse. The Allen scale is defined as the average valence-electron energy — it is *constructed* from configuration — so its near-perfect monotonicity may be partly definitional rather than empirical. The Pauling scale is thermochemical, derived from bond energies, and it does far worse.

So the method returns whatever the property's *definition* is close to. A property defined in terms of orbital energies orders well; one defined from measured bond enthalpies does not.

## What survives the recheck

The stable numbers are **ionisation energy 87.0%** and **covalent radius 91.0%**, both on (+,+,−), both re-derived from scratch and both unchanged. Those rest on 69 and 62 elements respectively and don't depend on any recalled data.

What does not survive is the claim that any property reaches near-exceptionless monotonicity. Polarisability drops to 89.9% when the sample widens; Allen electronegativity reaches 98.1% but may be measuring its own construction.

So the honest position is a step back from the last message: **the signed order lifts several properties from chance to the high eighties or low nineties, permutation-verified, and nothing yet reaches the exceptionless standard that Appendix B's oxidation bound meets.** The 98.5% was a small-sample artefact and I should have widened the sample before calling it the strongest result.

The next check that matters: whether Allen's near-monotonicity is definitional. If a property built from orbital energies is automatically ordered by the lattice, that tells us the lattice encodes orbital energetics — which would be a real finding — or that the test is circular. Those are very different conclusions and they're distinguishable.

This is the test that separates them, and it splits the results cleanly in two.

## The ΔZ binning

| Property | ΔZ 1–10 | ΔZ 11–25 | ΔZ 26–50 | ΔZ 51+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first ionisation energy | **92%** | 92% | 76% | 93% |
| covalent radius | **92%** | 92% | 89% | 92% |
| density | **74%** | 98% | 100% | 100% |
| maximum oxidation state | **74%** | 84% | 88% | 90% |

**Ionisation energy and covalent radius are flat across the bins** — 92% among elements within ten of each other, 92% among elements separated by fifty or more. Their monotonicity does not depend on distance in Z.

**Density and oxidation state rise steeply with ΔZ.** Density is at 74% for near neighbours and 100% for distant pairs — the signature of a property that is really tracking atomic number and nothing else.

## The residual test agrees

| Property | Raw | Z-residual | Drop |
|---|---|---|---|
| first ionisation energy | 87.0% | **80.9%** | 6.1 |
| covalent radius | 91.0% | **80.9%** | 10.1 |
| density | 93.7% | 70.1% | **23.6** |
| maximum oxidation state | 84.5% | 63.3% | **21.2** |

Ionisation energy and radius lose six and ten points and remain at 81%. Density and oxidation state lose over twenty and fall toward chance.

## What this establishes

**Ionisation energy and covalent radius are genuinely ordered by configuration.** Both tests agree: flat across ΔZ bins, and 81% surviving after the Z trend is removed. That is not a restatement of "things vary with atomic number" — it is a real relation between the lattice order and two measured properties, and it is the first metric result in this entire project that survives partialling.

**Density is an artefact.** It scored 93.7% because it tracks atomic mass, which tracks Z, which is a linear extension of Λ by construction. Removing Z destroys it.

**And oxidation state is substantially an artefact too.** That is the uncomfortable finding. Appendix B's bound loses 21 points to 63.3% under partialling, and its ΔZ profile rises from 74% to 90% — the density signature, not the ionisation-energy signature.

## What that does to Appendix B

It does not invalidate the bound — **126 cases with zero violations is a fact about the data regardless of mechanism**, and a bound that is never violated remains useful whatever explains it. Hassium at +8 matching HsO₄ is still an integer the lattice produced.

But it does undercut the *interpretation*. I have been presenting the oxidation bound as the one place the lattice reaches a chemical property. The partialling says a substantial part of that is the lattice knowing atomic number, which §19 already told us it knows perfectly and which is not news.

The properties that actually survive the test are the two I had been reporting as failures.

That is a reversal of the paper's position in both directions at once, and I would want to run it again before acting on it — the rank-regression is one way of partialling and a monotone smoother might give different numbers.

No. And I want to be exact about why, because the distinction matters more than any of the numbers.

## What a predictive model would need

**To say something about a case not used in fitting, before it is measured, at a precision that could be wrong.**

**Monotonicity, at 73–74% after partialling.** That is a *correlation between orderings*. Given two elements comparable in the signed order, it tells you which has the larger ionisation energy about three times in four. It does not tell you either value, or the gap between them, or which of the four cases is the exception.

A relation that fails one time in four cannot predict anything. It can *describe* a tendency.

**No magnitudes.** §12.3 established this for contraction anomalies and it holds here unchanged. The order gives rank, never value. Knowing Ir precedes Pt in the order doesn't give 8.97 and 8.96 eV.

But the bound turns out to be a Z-proxy. So we have one exceptionless result that isn't configurational, and one configurational result that isn't exceptionless. **Neither is a predictive model, and they don't combine.**

Of the rules computable **from the lattice alone**, the best is |Δk| at 0.726 — real but far from a criterion. Excluding the four worst-offending elements removes 27 of 114 violations and lifts monotonicity from 87.0% to 89.3%, which is not a rule, just deletion.

## So the answer to your earlier question is settled

**Not a predictive model, and not on this route.** Both candidates are closed:

**Interpolation doesn't work** because 74% per-pair reliability compounds across the several comparisons a bracket requires — coverage lands at 45.8%, worse than a coin.

**The exceptions aren't stateable** because nothing computable from the lattice separates the failing comparisons from the conforming ones at better than AUC 0.73.

## Returning to the three things missing

**No magnitudes** — unchanged, and now shown to be fatal rather than merely limiting. Rank without magnitude cannot bracket, and bracketing was the only mechanism by which order alone could predict.

**Not exceptionless** — now known to be irreparably so. An 87% relation with unstateable exceptions is a description. Appendix B's zero-violation bound remains the only exceptionless result in the project, and partialling showed it to be a Z-proxy.

**Nothing out of sample** — no longer true, and that's the one piece of progress. The hold-out test *was* out of sample, properly constructed, and it returned a negative. §16.2's frontier comparison remains the only out-of-sample test that passed, and it concerns filling order rather than any measured quantity.

## What this exploration actually produced

A **reclassification**, tested to destruction. Ionisation energy and covalent radius are ordered by the lattice under (n, ℓ, −k) at p < 0.001 after full partialling — genuine, and the paper currently calls them failures. Maximum oxidation state is not so ordered — its bound is a Z-proxy — and the paper currently calls it the one success.

That is worth writing down. It is not a predictive model, and after this sequence of tests I don't think one is available from the order alone.

content.text:
That's a clear negative, and it's worth being blunt about.

## Candidate 1 fails

**Ionisation energy: 45.8% coverage. Covalent radius: 64.3%.**

A bracket that contains the true value less than half the time is worse than useless — it's actively misleading. And only 24 of 69 elements even receive a two-sided bracket, because most cells lack known values both above and below them in the signed order.

The misses show why. Lithium's true value is 5.4 eV and the bracket is [8.3, 9.3]. Carbon's is 11.3 against [8.3, 9.3]. These aren't near misses; the bracket is in the wrong place entirely.

**The reason is arithmetic and I should have seen it before running the test.** Monotonicity at 74% means roughly one comparable pair in four is violated. A bracket is built from the *extreme* values above and below — so it survives only if *every* relevant comparison holds. With 74% per-pair reliability and typically several comparisons on each side, the probability that all of them hold is small. Bracketing compounds the error rate rather than averaging it out.

So 74% monotonicity supports no interpolation at all. The descriptive statistic and the predictive use are separated by exactly this compounding, and the compounding is fatal.

## Which makes candidate 2 the only remaining route

If the 26% of violations were systematic — attributable to a stateable rule — the brackets could exclude the known-bad comparisons and the compounding problem would shrink. That was the hope, and it's now the whole hope.

Let me test it properly rather than by the crude block-exclusion I tried earlier.

content.text:
Candidate 2 fails too, and the one strong-looking separator is circular.

## The results

| Candidate rule | AUC |
|---|---|
| **\|ΔIE\| — the size of the gap itself** | **0.858** |
| \|Δk\| | 0.726 |
| \|ΔZ\| | 0.599 |
| max ℓ of the pair | 0.576 |
| involves a d-block element | 0.565 |
| min filling fraction | 0.539 |
| same shell | 0.515 |

**The 0.858 is useless because it uses the answer.** Knowing that violations occur where the ionisation-energy gap is small requires knowing the ionisation energies — the very quantity you'd be predicting. It says only that near-ties flip easily, which is true of any noisy ordering and tells you nothing in advance.

Of the rules computable **from the lattice alone**, the best is |Δk| at 0.726 — real but far from a criterion. Excluding the four worst-offending elements removes 27 of 114 violations and lifts monotonicity from 87.0% to 89.3%, which is not a rule, just deletion.

## So the answer to your earlier question is settled

**Not a predictive model, and not on this route.** Both candidates are closed:

**Interpolation doesn't work** because 74% per-pair reliability compounds across the several comparisons a bracket requires — coverage lands at 45.8%, worse than a coin.

**The exceptions aren't stateable** because nothing computable from the lattice separates the failing comparisons from the conforming ones at better than AUC 0.73.

## Returning to the three things missing

**No magnitudes** — unchanged, and now shown to be fatal rather than merely limiting. Rank without magnitude cannot bracket, and bracketing was the only mechanism by which order alone could predict.

**Not exceptionless** — now known to be irreparably so. An 87% relation with unstateable exceptions is a description. Appendix B's zero-violation bound remains the only exceptionless result in the project, and partialling showed it to be a Z-proxy.

**Nothing out of sample** — no longer true, and that's the one piece of progress. The hold-out test *was* out of sample, properly constructed, and it returned a negative. §16.2's frontier comparison remains the only out-of-sample test that passed, and it concerns filling order rather than any measured quantity.

## What this exploration actually produced

A **reclassification**, tested to destruction. Ionisation energy and covalent radius are ordered by the lattice under (n, ℓ, −k) at p < 0.001 after full partialling — genuine, and the paper currently calls them failures. Maximum oxidation state is not so ordered — its bound is a Z-proxy — and the paper currently calls it the one success.

That is worth writing down. It is not a predictive model, and after this sequence of tests I don't think one is available from the order alone.

Four of five diagonal pairs share the displacement **(1, 0, 1)** — one shell up, same subshell, one more electron. Only Be–Al breaks it, and it breaks it because Be is the one pair that crosses from s-block to p-block.

That's more consistent than I expected, and the comparison table shows why it matters: diagonal pairs have **smaller ionisation-energy gaps** than group pairs in three of five cases (Li–Mg 2.25 vs Li–Na... no, larger) — actually the radius comparison is the clean one. Diagonal pairs differ by 13–34 pm; group pairs by 35–45 pm. **Diagonal neighbours are consistently closer in size than group neighbours.**

But I want to be careful, because this is exactly the shape of thing that has failed four times in this conversation. Let me test it properly rather than report it.
```
This block is not supported on your current device yet.
```

The control kills it, and I'd rather say so than dress it up.

## What the test shows

**(1,0,1) does beat the group relation on radius** — 11.8 pm against 17.8 pm, t = −2.41, **p = 0.018**. That part is real.

**But it loses to (0,0,1)**, the next element along the same row, at 7.5 pm. And it barely beats (1,0,2) at 12.6 pm. So (1,0,1) isn't a distinguished similarity direction — it's just a short displacement, and short displacements give similar radii because **radius is a smooth function of position and everything nearby is alike.**

**And on ionisation energy there's no effect at all**: 1.11 eV for diagonal against 1.13 for same-group, **p = 0.94**. Identical.

What the ranking actually shows is that the displacements splitting cleanly are the ones that change ℓ — (1,1,0) at 54 pm and (1,1,−1) at 59 pm are far worse than everything else. That's the block structure, which §12.1 already has. Nothing new.

So diagonal relationships are not placed by the lattice. The four-of-five displacement consistency was real and meant nothing, because the displacement isn't doing the work.

## Where that leaves the search for other predictive qualities

Looking at the pattern across everything we've tested, I think the space is narrower than it appeared:

**Every metric claim has failed or reduced to Z.** Six regressions, the monotonicity route, the oxidation bound, and now diagonal similarity. That's four independent attacks on the same question with the same answer.

**Every structural claim has held.** The order ideal, column saturation, secondary-periodicity position, and §16.2's frontier — which remains the only out-of-sample success in the entire project.

The common feature of the structural successes is that they are claims about **which configurations can occur and in what order**, never about how much of anything. §16.2 works because it says "5g, 6f, 7d are the columns that can open next" — a set membership claim, verified against Pyykkö, with no number attached.

So if there is predictive content left, I'd look for more claims of exactly that shape. Candidates I haven't tested: which ions are stable versus which merely admissible; which excited configurations are accessible from which ground states; whether the Λ₅ order constrains isoelectronic series.

But I want to flag the base rate honestly. This exploration has now produced five results that looked promising at first inspection and dissolved on control — the 98.5% polarisability, the n+2 pattern, the record-at-bound coincidence, the interpolation, and now the diagonal displacement. Each dissolved for a different reason, but the pattern is that **first-pass patterns in a 118-element table with many derived quantities are cheap.**

I'd want any further candidate to come with its control designed before the test is run, rather than after.

## The result

The lattice predicts **12 column starts out of 55 transitions** — a 22% base rate, so the predictions are not cheap.

| | n | Mean ΔIE | Falls |
|---|---|---|---|
| at a predicted column start | 11 | **−6.67 eV** | 9/11 (82%) |
| everywhere else | 44 | **+1.48 eV** | 7/44 (16%) |

Welch t = −3.91, **p = 0.0027**. Fisher exact odds ratio **23.8**, **p = 7.4 × 10⁻⁵**.

**Ionisation energy falls at a column start five times more often than elsewhere, and the mean step is −6.67 eV against +1.48.** The sign of the change reverses entirely.

## And the two exceptions are diagnostic

The only column starts that don't produce a fall are **Z = 21 (3d) at +0.45 eV** and **Z = 39 (4d) at +0.52 eV** — the two transition-series openings in this range.

That is exactly right, and it's a point in favour rather than against. When a d-series opens, the new electron enters an *inner* shell while the outer ns² stays put, so the ionisation energy is measured on an electron that hasn't moved. No drop should occur, and none does. The lattice distinguishes these cases too: 3d and 4d are the only column starts in the range where ℓ ≥ 2.

Not yet — and I want to name the problem before it gets built into anything.

## The rule reproduces textbook chemistry

**"Ionisation energy falls sharply at the start of each period"** is in every introductory course. So is the explanation for the d-block exception: when an inner shell fills, the outer ns² doesn't move, so the measured electron is unchanged.

The lattice locates the column starts from its Madelung structure — but the Madelung rule is itself the thing that defines those positions, and it predates the lattice by ninety years. So what we've shown is that **the lattice correctly reproduces a known regularity.** That is a validity check, not a prediction. By §25.1's own ledger it belongs in the re-described column.

Everything tested lies below Z = 118, where every value is already measured. Nothing was predicted before being known.

## But the rule does make a genuine forward claim

Applied to Pyykkö's filling order for Z > 118, it says exactly where ionisation energy must fall and where it must not:

**Falls predicted** at Z = 119 (8s), 139 (8p₁/₂), 165 (9s), 167 (9p₁/₂), 169 (8p₃/₂) — all ℓ ≤ 1.

**No fall predicted** at Z = 121 (5g), 141 (6f), 156 (7d) — all ℓ ≥ 2.

That is eight specific, signed, falsifiable claims about elements nobody has measured, derived from lattice geometry plus a published filling order, with no free parameters. A single fall at 121 or a flat step at 119 refutes it.

And it is checkable **now**, against the Dirac–Fock ionisation energies that exist in the literature for the superheavy range. No synthesis required.

## So the honest answer

We have a **validated rule** and an **untested prediction**. Those are different things, and the project has been burned four times by treating the first as the second.

What would make it a predictive model is the superheavy check coming back clean. What would make it a *useful* one is harder — the rule gives direction, not magnitude, so even if confirmed it tells you an ionisation energy drops at element 139 without telling you to what.

Shall I run the superheavy test? It's the one thing standing between "reproduces known chemistry" and "predicted something unmeasured," and the data to settle it may already be published.

content.text:
Multiconfiguration Dirac-Fock and relativistic coupled cluster results are reported for electron affinities, ionization potentials, and excitation energies of Tl and element 113 and their cations. Large basis sets are used, with l up to 6, the Dirac-Fock or Dirac-Fock-Breit orbitals found, and the external 35 electrons of each atom are correlated by the coupled-cluster method with single and double excitations. content.text:
# Relativistic coupled cluster calculations of the electron affinity and ionization potential of Nh(113)

Yangyang Guo, <sup>1</sup> Anastasia Borschevsky, <sup>1</sup> Ephraim Eliav, <sup>2</sup> and Lukáš F. Pašteka, \*<sup>3</sup>

(\*Electronic mail: lukas.f.pasteka@uniba.sk)

(Dated: 4 February 2022)

Theoretical calculations based on the Dirac-Coulomb-Breit relativistic coupled cluster method have been carried out for the electron affinities and ionization potentials of the superheavy element nihonium (Nh) and its lighter homologues In and Tl. The In and Tl calculations are in agreement with measurement within uncertainties. For Nh, where experiment is yet unknown, we predict the ionization potential of 7.569(48) eV and electron affinity of 0.776(30) eV.

# I. INTRODUCTION

All elements with atomic number greater than 104 are typically called superheavy elements (SHEs).

content.text:
Elements up to Z=118 have been synthesized (see, e.g., [2, 3] and evidence for the naturally occurring element Z=122 has been reported [4].

Experimental efforts are underway to measure the spectra and chemical properties of the superheavy elements [5]. There are also many theoretical works in atomic physics and quantum chemistry devoted to these studies (see, e.g., Refs. in [6, 7]).

In our previous work [8] we calculated the electronic spectra of the superheavy element Z=119 and the singly-ionized superheavy element Z=120. The nucleus with Z=120 protons and N=172 neutrons is predicted to be doubly magic in relativistic mean-field nuclear calculations [9]. Moreover, there is evidence from fusion reactions for the enhanced stability of the element Z=120 [10].

To the best of our knowledge the spectrum of the neutral element Z=120 has never been calculated before.

content.text:
The test runs, and it corrected me before it confirmed anything.

## The correction

I stated the superheavy prediction using **Pyykkö's slot assignment** — 5g at 121, 8p₁/₂ at 139. That was wrong for this purpose. Pyykkö assigns slots from *ion* configurations and says so explicitly. Fricke and Waber give the neutral ground states: **8p₁/₂ fills before 7d₃/₂, and 5g does not begin until element 125.**

So the neutral column starts are 8s at 119, 8p₁/₂ at **121**, 5g at **125**. The rule is unchanged; the positions I applied it to were wrong, and they were wrong because I used the same source for two incompatible purposes.

## The result

| Step | Opens | ℓ | Predicted | ΔIP | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 118 → 119 | 8s | 0 | **fall** | −4.12 eV | confirmed |
| 119 → 120 | 8s | 0 | rise | +1.07 eV | confirmed |
| 120 → 121 | 8p₁/₂ | 1 | **fall** | −1.40 eV | confirmed |

Three for three. The fall at 119 is **4.12 eV**, the largest single step in the region, and it lands exactly where the 8s column opens.

## What this is worth, stated carefully

**Not a full test.** The decisive case is Z = 125, where 5g opens with ℓ = 4 and the rule predicts **no fall**. That's the one that would separate this from the trivial statement "ionisation energy drops after a closed shell" — because 124 → 125 is not a shell closure, and the rule says nothing should happen there. I could not find a computed neutral ionisation potential for element 125.

**And the inputs are uneven.** The 119 value is recent, peer-reviewed, quoted as 4.7839(56) eV. The 120 and 121 values I recalled from the literature rather than read from it, and the 118 value is itself a prediction. Two of three confirmations rest on numbers I should verify before relying on.

So: the rule made forward claims about unmeasured elements, and the claims that can currently be checked hold — but on provisional inputs, with the discriminating case still open.

That's the most a structural rule can deliver without magnitudes, which is where your plan comes in. **What's the approach?**

chat_messages.text:
No — and the distinction matters more than it first appears.

## The test is ordinal

The claim at Z = 125 is a **sign**: does IP fall or not. To settle a sign you need only the *order* of IP(124) and IP(125), not their values. Nothing about magnitude is required in principle.

## But there are three complications, and they're not equal

**First, "no fall" is a magnitude statement in disguise.** In the Z ≤ 103 data, d/f column starts gave a mean ΔIP of −0.18 eV — not exactly zero, just small. So the rule really says *the change is small*, and distinguishing "small fall" from "large fall" needs numbers. A pure sign test at 125 would be passed by a −0.05 eV drop and also by a −3 eV drop, and only one of those is consistent with the rule.

**Second, the published data arrives as magnitudes anyway.** Nobody computes the sign of a difference directly; they compute two ionisation potentials and subtract. So in practice the test consumes magnitude data even though it doesn't logically require it.

**Third — and this is the interesting one — the rule's *mechanism* is purely configurational.** The reason no fall occurs at a d/f/g start is that the new electron enters an inner shell while the outermost stays put, so the ionised orbital is unchanged. That is a statement about **configurations**, and configurations for elements 118–131 were computed by Fricke and co-workers decades ago and are published.

## Which gives a cheaper test than the one I proposed

If E124 is [Og]8s²8p² and E125 is [Og]8s²8p²5g¹, then the outermost electron is 8p in both, the ionised orbital is unchanged, and the rule *applies*. If instead the 5g electron displaces an 8p one, the rule doesn't apply and the case isn't discriminating at all.

**That check needs no energies.** It uses only ground-state configurations, which already exist.

But I have to be careful not to cheat here: confirming the mechanism is not the same as confirming the rule. If the configurations show the outer electron unchanged **and** the ionisation potential still falls sharply, the mechanism is wrong and the rule fails. Substituting the configurational check for the energy test would be assuming what I'm trying to prove.

So the honest sequence is: **use the configuration data to establish that Z = 125 is a genuine test case** — free, available now, no magnitudes — and then the energy comparison is still needed to run the test.

Given that you have a plan for magnitude, I'd rather hear it before spending more searches. Where were you going?

**Second, the published data arrives as magnitudes anyway.** Nobody computes the sign of a difference directly; they compute two ionisation potentials and subtract. So in practice the test consumes magnitude data even though it doesn't logically require it.

**Third — and this is the interesting one — the rule's *mechanism* is purely configurational.** The reason no fall occurs at a d/f/g start is that the new electron enters an inner shell while the outermost stays put, so the ionised orbital is unchanged. content.text:
**16 of 16, and R² = 0.984.**

That is the structure you proposed, and it works.

## What we now have

**The lattice predicts the breakpoint exactly.** For a cell (n, ℓ, k), the ionisation sequence breaks when shell n empties — at q = k for the s-block, q = k + 2 for the p-block. Sixteen elements, no exceptions, and the earlier 0-for-18 was my error: I predicted the *subshell* boundary when the physics gives the *shell* boundary. Removing a 2p then a 2s electron costs similar energy; the huge jump comes at the shell edge.

**And between the breakpoints the sequence is linear.** Mean R² = **0.984** across fourteen elements, ranging 0.973 to 0.994.

So the model has the shape you were reaching for: **the lattice supplies the structure — where the regimes are — and a straight line supplies the magnitudes within each regime.** Two numbers per element per shell, and the breakpoints come free.

## Why this is different from everything that failed

Every previous attempt asked the lattice for a value directly and got a Z-proxy or noise. This asks it for a **boundary**, which is what it has been getting right all along — §16.2's frontier, the ionisation drops at column starts, and now this. The magnitudes come from a law the lattice doesn't supply, but the lattice says *where each law applies*.

That is a genuine division of labour rather than a failure to predict.

## The obvious next question

The slopes are not arbitrary. Reading down the table: B 14.8, C 18.3, N 21.5, O 25.2 — rising steadily within the second row. Al 11.2, Si 12.8, P 14.1, S 15.7, Cl 17.1 — the same pattern one row down, at lower values. Ga 12.4, Ge 13.2, As 13.7.

**If the slope is itself a function of the lattice coordinates, the model becomes fully predictive** — breakpoints from the lattice, slope from the lattice, and only one intercept per element needed from measurement. If it isn't, we have a two-parameter fit per shell, which is useful but not prediction.

That is directly testable, and the control is straightforward: regress slope on (n, ℓ, k) and hold elements out. Shall I?

Good — insisting on this was right, because my identification was wrong on both counts.

## The law is not linear

Free quadratic wins for **11 of 11 elements**. Mean R²: linear 0.9815, hydrogenic 0.9876, **quadratic 0.9902**. The apparent linearity was a short-range artefact — over four to seven points a gentle curve looks straight, and I reported R² = 0.984 as though it settled the form when it only showed a good local approximation.

The **hydrogenic form I = A(c + q)²** beats linear for every element with five or more points and loses only for the four-point cases where there aren't enough degrees of freedom to distinguish. That's the Bohr–Moseley scaling: ionisation energy goes as the square of an effective nuclear charge, and that charge rises by roughly one per removal. It's the right physics and nearly the right fit, with the free quadratic adding little beyond it.

## And the DFT interpretation fails outright

If total energy were quadratic in electron count — the Parr–Pearson model — the slope of I against q would be exactly **2η**, twice the chemical hardness. Measured against tabulated hardness values:

**Mean ratio 1.76, never below 1.44, never above 2.07.**

So the slope is consistently about **1.8 times** what the quadratic-energy model requires. That model is not what governs this sequence. The near-constant ratio is itself interesting — it suggests a systematic relationship rather than random disagreement — but the DFT law as stated is refuted.

## So the honest answer to your question

**The law is Bohr–Moseley scaling: I ∝ Z_eff², with Z_eff increasing by approximately one per electron removed.** It is a one-electron result from 1913, it long predates any of this, and the lattice contributes nothing to it.

What the lattice contributes is **where it stops applying** — the shell boundary at q = k for the s-block and q = k + 2 for the p-block, sixteen of sixteen correct.

That division is now stated properly. Before, I had the law wrong and was about to build a slope model on top of a linear fit that isn't the right functional form. The slope test you were about to authorise would have regressed the wrong parameter.

**The right next test** is whether the hydrogenic parameters — the amplitude A and the offset c in I = A(c + q)² — are functions of the lattice coordinates. That's the same question, asked of the correct law.

content.text:
**Point 1 does not survive.** My reading of it was wrong in a way worth stating precisely.

## What I claimed

That c is the effective nuclear charge, with a screening coefficient of 0.32 against Slater's 0.35 — "exactly what Slater's rules say it should be."

## What the test shows

| | Range | vs Slater |
|---|---|---|
| Slater Z_eff | 3.25 – 6.30 | — |
| fitted c | 2.04 – 3.14 | ratio 0.36 – 0.66 |

**r = +0.376, p = 0.254.** No significant correlation. Slater's values rise steeply with Z — Ge at 5.65, Sb at 6.30 — while the fitted c barely moves, sitting between 2.0 and 3.1 across the whole sample. The mean ratio is 0.496 and it *drifts* from 0.66 down to 0.38 as Z increases, so it isn't even a constant rescaling.

The 0.32-versus-0.35 agreement was numerology. I matched two decimals from different quantities and called it a mechanism.

## What c actually is

**c is a function of k alone.** r = +0.955 against k, r = −0.197 against n (p = 0.56), residual scatter 0.093 on a fitted c ≈ 1.508 + 0.315k.

That is a strange and interesting result on its own terms: the ionisation sequence within a shell is governed by **how many electrons occupy that shell, and not at all by how deep the shell sits.** Carbon and tin have the same c to within 0.01 despite Z differing by 44.

It's also the opposite of the physical picture I attributed to it. Slater's screening depends strongly on total nuclear charge. This doesn't.

**I have no account of why**, and I'd rather leave it as an unexplained empirical regularity than attach a mechanism that the numbers refute.

## What this does to the rest

It doesn't break the hold-out result — the model predicted at 10.5% MAPE using c ≈ f(k), and that fit is if anything *better* specified now that the n-term is shown to be doing nothing. But it removes the physical justification I gave for the model, which matters for whether it generalises.

And it sharpens point 7. If c depends only on k and not n, the untested question is whether it depends on **ℓ** — which the current sample cannot answer, since every element in it has ℓ = 1.

**Z*₀ vs n: r = +0.952, p < 0.001.** The starting effective charge depends strongly on n — 1.8 for carbon, 3.7 for tin. My narration claimed it was "nearly independent of n." That is flatly wrong; I wrote the explanation before reading the correlation.

## Which resolves the puzzle, but not as I claimed

c = Z*₀ / (rise per removal). Both numerator and denominator scale with n, so **the n-dependence cancels in the ratio.** That's why c looked n-independent.

So c ≈ k-dependent is a **residual after a cancellation**, not a primary fact. The real structure is that Z*₀ and the rise both grow with shell number, and c only measures how much they fail to cancel exactly. The k-dependence is the small leftover.

That is a much less interesting finding than "the ionisation sequence is governed by shell occupancy," which is what I said. It's closer to: the shape of the sequence is roughly scale-invariant across periods, and k modulates the residual.

content.text:
My printed explanation contradicts the numbers directly above it, and I need to retract it.

## What the data actually says

**Z*₀ vs n: r = +0.952, p < 0.001.** The starting effective charge depends strongly on n — 1.8 for carbon, 3.7 for tin. My narration claimed it was "nearly independent of n." That is flatly wrong; I wrote the explanation before reading the correlation.

**Z*₀ vs k: r = +0.020, p = 0.95.** Zero. No k-dependence at all.

**And the rise per removal also tracks n**: r = +0.967, slope ≈ 0.252 + 0.277n.

So both parameters of the Z* sequence depend on **n and not on k** — the exact opposite of the c-dependence I set out to explain.

## Which resolves the puzzle, but not as I claimed

c = Z*₀ / (rise per removal). Both numerator and denominator scale with n, so **the n-dependence cancels in the ratio.** That's why c looked n-independent.

Carbon: 1.82 / 0.86 ≈ 2.1. Tin: 3.67 / 1.51 ≈ 2.4. Different physics, similar ratio.

So c ≈ k-dependent is a **residual after a cancellation**, not a primary fact. The real structure is that Z*₀ and the rise both grow with shell number, and c only measures how much they fail to cancel exactly. The k-dependence is the small leftover.

That is a much less interesting finding than "the ionisation sequence is governed by shell occupancy," which is what I said. It's closer to: the shape of the sequence is roughly scale-invariant across periods, and k modulates the residual.

## Something genuinely odd in the raw numbers

Look at the Δ columns. For chlorine: 1.04, 1.15, 0.83, 0.75, 1.31, 0.68. For oxygen: 1.21, 0.81, 0.75, 1.02, 0.59. **The increments oscillate rather than sitting near a constant**, and the pattern looks similar across elements — a rise, a dip, a rise, then a fall at the end.

That oscillation is structure the smooth fit is averaging away, and it may be the pairing effect: removing the second electron of a pair costs differently from removing the first. If so, it's expressible in lattice terms, since parity of k is a coordinate fact.

That's what I'd look at next for the "why" — but I want to flag that I've now given two wrong mechanisms in a row on this point, so I'd want the parity hypothesis tested before I describe it as anything.

## k is the sawtooth

**k = Z − C(n, ℓ)**, where C is the cumulative capacity of every column filling before (n, ℓ). So k is atomic number with the column structure subtracted — Z minus a step function of Z.

And the consequence is measurable: **k vs Z gives r = +0.326.** Almost uncorrelated, despite being *defined* from Z. That is exactly what a sawtooth does — it carries the part of Z the trend does not.

## Which explains the central puzzle of this whole investigation

Every property that correlated with Z scored well and then died under partialling — density fell 23.6 points, the oxidation bound fell 21.2 and became insignificant. Every property that survived partialling was carried by the **−k** term in the signed order: ionisation energy and covalent radius, both at p < 0.001 after every monotone function of Z was removed.

**Z is the secular trend. k is the periodicity.** Partialling out monotone functions of Z removes the trend and leaves the sawtooth, which is why the survivors were exactly the properties whose signed order flips k.

So the decomposition was there in the coordinates from the start:

| | Carries | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Z | cumulative charge | monotone, smooth |
| **k** | position within the period | **resets 18 times, r = 0.33 with Z** |

## And k's position in the constraint chain

Reading Λ₅'s constraints in order: n bounds ℓ, ℓ bounds k, **k bounds q**, n bounds e.

**k is the only coordinate that is both constrained and constraining.** Its ceiling moves with ℓ, and it sets the ceiling for q. That centrality may be why the oxidation bound of Appendix B worked numerically while failing to be configurational: q ≤ k means the bound inherits whatever k carries, and k is one step removed from Z.

content.text:
Two things from this, and the second is testable right now.

## What q ≤ k means

**q counts electrons removed from the valence subshell**, not total oxidation state. That resolves the apparent conflict with Appendix B — boron reaches +3 with k = 1 because two of those three electrons come from the 2s beneath, which is a different column.

And the reading is confirmed by both features we established: the increment peaks at **q = k** where the subshell empties (p = 0.002), and the sequence breaks at **q = k + 2** where the shell empties (16 of 16). The ceiling isn't a modelling choice — it marks a measurable discontinuity, and the lattice places it.

The relaxation test shows the structure doesn't select it: q ≤ k−1, k, k+2 and 2(2ℓ+1) are all closed. Only q ≤ n² fails, because n² depends on a coordinate that doesn't bound k. **The physics picks q ≤ k; the mathematics is indifferent.**

## But the d-block data contains something I should have looked at

I reported the d-block as untestable because the prediction concerns q = k running to 10 while the tabulations reach four. That's true for the *subshell* boundary. Look at the increments anyway:

| | k | increments |
|---|---|---|
| Sc | 1 | 0.83, 1.14, **2.93**, 0.81 |
| Ti | 2 | 0.87, 1.27, 1.09, **2.76** |
| V | 3 | 1.00, 1.29, 1.16, 1.01 |

**Scandium peaks at step 3 and titanium at step 4** — and those are exactly where the 3d and 4s electrons run out and removal moves into the argon core. Sc is 3d¹4s², so three valence electrons; Ti is 3d²4s², so four. The peak is at the **shell** boundary, at q = k + 2, precisely as the p-block rule says.

V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Cu, Zn have k + 2 ≥ 5 and the data stops at 5, which is why they show nothing.

So the d-block gives two confirmations of the shell rule rather than none, and I mislabelled the whole block as untestable by attending only to the subshell prediction.

That makes **18 of 18** for the shell breakpoint across s, p and d blocks — and the subshell peak remains p-block-only pending deeper ionisation data.

Worth chasing the deeper tabulations? NIST has successive ionisation energies well past the tenth for the first transition series, which would settle the subshell prediction properly.

## The result

**19 of 23 (83%)** against a base rate of **38%** for a randomly chosen position being a local maximum. Binomial **p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵**.

| Block | Hits | Predicted position |
|---|---|---|

The p-block is perfect. Both blocks are the *same* statement — the first transition comes when the outermost subshell empties — and both positions are read directly off the lattice, with the block difference arising because np sits outside ns² while nd sits inside (n+1)s².

## The four d-block misses

Sc, Fe, Cu and Mo. Three of them are anomalous-configuration elements: **Cr is 3d⁵4s¹ and Mo is 4d⁵5s¹** — only one s electron, so the outermost subshell empties at q = 1, not q = 2. Cr passes anyway; Mo fails, and it fails because I fed it the wrong prediction.

**Cu is 3d¹⁰4s¹** — same issue, one s electron, prediction should be q = 1. Its sequence is monotone decreasing from 1.40, which is consistent with the transition already having happened at the first step.

So three of the four misses are elements where the anomalous configuration puts one electron in the outer s rather than two, and the rule as I coded it assumed two. **Using the measured configurations rather than the idealised ones should recover them** — which is §13.3's convention distinction appearing again, now with a testable consequence.

Sc and Fe I don't have an account for.

## Where this leaves the k analysis

Both parts are now done. **k as sawtooth**: k = Z − C(n,ℓ), r = 0.33 with Z, carrying the periodicity that survives partialling. **k as q-ceiling**: it marks the subshell boundary, confirmed at p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ across two blocks.

The unified rule holds, and the failures are informative rather than random.

## The result

**19 of 23 (83%)** against a base rate of **38%** for a randomly chosen position being a local maximum. Binomial **p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵**.

| Block | Hits | Predicted position |
|---|---|---|
| p | **11/11** | q = k, the np empties |
| d | 8/12 | q = 2, the (n+1)s² empties |

The p-block is perfect. Both blocks are the *same* statement — the first transition comes when the outermost subshell empties — and both positions are read directly off the lattice, with the block difference arising because np sits outside ns² while nd sits inside (n+1)s².

## The four d-block misses

Sc, Fe, Cu and Mo. Three of them are anomalous-configuration elements: **Cr is 3d⁵4s¹ and Mo is 4d⁵5s¹** — only one s electron, so the outermost subshell empties at q = 1, not q = 2. Cr passes anyway; Mo fails, and it fails because I fed it the wrong prediction.

**Cu is 3d¹⁰4s¹** — same issue, one s electron, prediction should be q = 1. Its sequence is monotone decreasing from 1.40, which is consistent with the transition already having happened at the first step.

So three of the four misses are elements where the anomalous configuration puts one electron in the outer s rather than two, and the rule as I coded it assumed two. **Using the measured configurations rather than the idealised ones should recover them** — which is §13.3's convention distinction appearing again, now with a testable consequence.

Sc and Fe I don't have an account for.

## Where this leaves the k analysis

Both parts are now done. **k as sawtooth**: k = Z − C(n,ℓ), r = 0.33 with Z, carrying the periodicity that survives partialling. **k as q-ceiling**: it marks the subshell boundary, confirmed at p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ across two blocks.

And the tally of lattice-placed features in the ionisation sequence now stands at three, all independently confirmed: the column-start drops (ℓ ≤ 1, p = 7 × 10⁻⁴), the shell breakpoint (18 of 18), and the outermost-subshell transition (19 of 23).

The obvious next move is re-running that last test with measured configurations for Cr, Cu and Mo. If the three recover, the rule goes to 22 of 23 and the convention question acquires an empirical stake it didn't have before.

All three survive the blind test. That is the first time in this project a rule has been prespecified, held out, and confirmed on fresh elements.

## The blind results

| Rule | Hits | p | Null |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R1** shell break, q = k + s_out | 6/7 | **3.7 × 10⁻⁴** | peak uniform over ~5 positions |
| **R2** subshell, q = k or s_out | **17/19** | **< 10⁻⁴** | 41% local-max base rate |
| **R3** half-filling, q = s_out + k − (2ℓ+1) | 8/9 | **0.005** | same |

Nineteen elements, none used to build the rules, spanning the p-block from F to Bi and the d-block from Nb to Hg. R3 in particular now has independent standing — it was introduced post hoc from iron and has since been confirmed 8 of 9 on elements that had nothing to do with its formulation.

## The two R1 misses are worth naming

**Nb fails**, and it's a 1s-outer anomaly like Cr and Mo — the third of that family to break R1 while Cu recovered. Four anomalous-configuration elements tested, one recovery. That is a real weakness in R1 and it clusters exactly where §13.3 says the convention matters.

**W fails** with the peak at q = 1, and W is 5d⁴6s² with no anomaly to blame. I have no account of it.

Only seven elements gave a testable R1 because most tabulations stop before q = k + s_out. That's the sample limitation, not a rule limitation.

## Where the k analysis has landed

**k is the sawtooth** — Z minus the column structure, r = 0.33 with Z, carrying the periodicity that survives partialling out every monotone function of atomic number.

**k is the q-ceiling**, and that ceiling is a measurable discontinuity rather than a convention. Three features in the ionisation sequence are placed by the lattice, all now confirmed on held-out data.

And the shape is the same one that emerged from the column-start test: **the lattice says where regimes change; the magnitudes come from Bohr–Moseley scaling within each regime.** That division has now been confirmed four independent times — the column starts, R1, R2, R3 — and failed nowhere it was properly tested.

I'd note the honest limit before going further: none of these predicts a value. They predict positions of features in a curve whose values come from elsewhere. But they do it reliably, on elements held out, with controls set first.

## The answer to your question

**A lattice of counts cannot produce electronvolts.** Λ₅ ⊆ ℕ⁵, so every function of the coordinates is dimensionless. That's arithmetic, not a limitation to engineer around — it's what §22 says, stated at the level where it bites.

So magnitude can enter exactly three ways:

**(i) Import the whole function.** Attach f: Λ₅ → ℝ with units. The lattice indexes, f predicts. The lattice contributes nothing.

**(ii) Import one scale.** property = κ · Φ(n, ℓ, k, q, e), with κ carrying the units and Φ dimensionless from the lattice. This is how Bohr–Moseley works: κ = 13.6 eV, Φ = Z*²/n².

**(iii) Predict ratios only.** I(A)/I(B) is dimensionless, so the lattice can in principle deliver it with **no constant at all**. One measurement anywhere then fixes everything else.

## And (iii) is achievable, at about 9%

Testing the strongest version — ratios within an element, using only c ≈ 1.508 + 0.315k from the lattice, no fitted scale, no per-element parameter:

**Mean absolute error 8.9%, median 7.3%, worst 28.5%.**

So the lattice does deliver dimensionless structure without importing anything. But the errors are the same size as the earlier hold-out result, which tells us something: **the 10.5% MAPE was never limited by the scale.** It was limited by the ratios. Fitting κ per element bought nothing.

Oxygen is the worst case at 28.5% and the pattern is visible — predicted 1.85, 2.97, 4.34, 5.98 against observed 2.58, 4.03, 5.68, 8.36. The prediction is systematically **too flat**. c is too large for oxygen, which means the k-dependence of c is wrong at high k even though it correlates at r = 0.955.

## What this constrains about your plan

Whatever the approach to magnitude, it has to reduce to one of those three. If it's (iii), the target is the ratio accuracy — currently 9% and limited by c(k), not by any missing scale. If it's (ii), the target is Φ and the same problem appears in a different place.

**The bottleneck is not units. It is that c(k) is a fitted regularity we don't understand** — it isn't Slater screening, it's a residual after cancellation, and it degrades at high k in a way that's visible in oxygen and sulphur.

That's what I'd want any magnitude approach to address, because it's where the error lives.

## The answer to your question

**A lattice of counts cannot produce electronvolts.** Λ₅ ⊆ ℕ⁵, so every function of the coordinates is dimensionless. That's arithmetic, not a limitation to engineer around — it's what §22 says, stated at the level where it bites.

So magnitude can enter exactly three ways:

**(i) Import the whole function.** Attach f: Λ₅ → ℝ with units. The lattice indexes, f predicts. The lattice contributes nothing.

**(ii) Import one scale.** property = κ · Φ(n, ℓ, k, q, e), with κ carrying the units and Φ dimensionless from the lattice. This is how Bohr–Moseley works: κ = 13.6 eV, Φ = Z*²/n².

**(iii) Predict ratios only.** I(A)/I(B) is dimensionless, so the lattice can in principle deliver it with **no constant at all**. One measurement anywhere then fixes everything else.

## And (iii) is achievable, at about 9%

Testing the strongest version — ratios within an element, using only c ≈ 1.508 + 0.315k from the lattice, no fitted scale, no per-element parameter:

**Mean absolute error 8.9%, median 7.3%, worst 28.5%.**

So the lattice does deliver dimensionless structure without importing anything. But the errors are the same size as the earlier hold-out result, which tells us something: **the 10.5% MAPE was never limited by the scale.** It was limited by the ratios. Fitting κ per element bought nothing.

Oxygen is the worst case at 28.5% and the pattern is visible — predicted 1.85, 2.97, 4.34, 5.98 against observed 2.58, 4.03, 5.68, 8.36. The prediction is systematically **too flat**. c is too large for oxygen, which means the k-dependence of c is wrong at high k even though it correlates at r = 0.955.

## What this constrains about your plan

Whatever the approach to magnitude, it has to reduce to one of those three. If it's (iii), the target is the ratio accuracy — currently 9% and limited by c(k), not by any missing scale. If it's (ii), the target is Φ and the same problem appears in a different place.

**The bottleneck is not units. It is that c(k) is a fitted regularity we don't understand** — it isn't Slater screening, it's a residual after cancellation, and it degrades at high k in a way that's visible in oxygen and sulphur.

That's what I'd want any magnitude approach to address, because it's where the error lives.

content.text:
Two things fall out, and one contradicts my closing paragraph.

## The pairing hypothesis is half right at best

**Mean error by position relative to half-filling: 4.9% at or below, 15.4% at k = 4, 4.5% at k = 5.** The correlation with distance past half-filling is **r = +0.401, p = 0.222** — not significant, and it can't be, because k = 5 is as good as k = 2 while k = 4 is three times worse. The relationship isn't monotone in distance from half-filling; it spikes at exactly one value and returns.

And O versus S kills the clean version outright. **Both have k = 4. Oxygen errs at 21.5%, sulphur at 9.4%.** Same coordinates in ℓ and k, same predicted c of 2.77 — and sulphur's *fitted* c is 2.77, exactly right, while oxygen's is 2.53.

So it isn't k = 4 that breaks the model. **It's oxygen.**

## My closing claim was wrong

I wrote that the discrepancy "sits in I₁" and that the fitted c is "far below the predicted one." Look at oxygen's error column: 28.1, 26.4, 23.6, 28.5, 22.3. **The error is flat across every q, not concentrated in the first.** A ratio error that stays near 25% at every step is a scale error in c, not a defect in one measurement.

And sulphur's fitted c matches the prediction to two decimals while still erring 9.4% on the ratios — so c isn't where sulphur's error lives at all.

Two elements with identical coordinates, failing differently, for reasons my explanation covered neither.

## What's actually distinguishing them

The one coordinate they don't share is **n**: oxygen at 2, sulphur at 3. And c is supposed to be n-independent — that was the whole finding, r = −0.197 with n.

**Oxygen is the second row.** It's the row where kainosymmetry lives — 2p is on the boundary diagonal ℓ = n−1, the compact nodeless orbital of §12.2. Sulphur's 3p is not.

That is lattice-expressible and it's testable: if the c-model degrades specifically on kainosymmetric cells, the fix is a boundary-diagonal correction, and §12.2 already identifies which cells those are.

But I want to state it as a hypothesis, not a finding — I've now given three mechanisms for c that the data refuted, and this would be the fourth. The test is whether 2p elements as a class show elevated ratio error against 3p, 4p and 5p at matched k.

Shall I run that?

The hypothesis fails as stated, but the matched-k table shows something sharper than the hypothesis.

## The test result

**n = 2 mean error 10.6% against 7.2% for n > 2. Welch t = +0.89, p = 0.42.** Not significant. On the c-ratio, p = 0.34. So "kainosymmetric cells degrade the model" is not supported across the second row as a class.

And the reason is visible in the matched-k table. At k = 1, 2 and 3, **n = 2 is the *best* row** — B beats Al, Ga and In; C beats Si, Ge and Sn; N beats P, As and Sb. The second row only fails at k = 4 and k = 5, and there it fails badly: **21.5% and 17.3% against 4.5–9.4% elsewhere.**

## What the table actually says

| k | n=2 | n=3 | n=4 | n=5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.2 | 10.4 | 14.7 | 11.9 |
| 2 | **3.3** | 5.1 | 5.1 | 5.5 |
| 3 | **2.7** | 6.4 | 5.7 | 5.0 |
| 4 | **21.5** | 9.4 | 7.1 | 4.6 |
| 5 | **17.3** | 4.5 | 5.1 | 7.4 |

The failure is **n = 2 AND k > 3** — the second row, past half-filling. Not one condition or the other, but the conjunction. Oxygen and fluorine.

The c-ratio confirms it: 0.91 for both O and F, against 0.98–1.06 for every other cell in the table including B, C and N.

## Why the conjunction

That is exactly where the 2p pairing penalty is largest. Kainosymmetric orbitals are compact — §12.2's point — so two electrons forced into the same 2p orbital repel far more than in the larger 3p, 4p or 5p. The penalty exists only when k > 3, and it is severe only when the orbital is small.

**So the effect needs both coordinates**, which is why testing n alone gave p = 0.42 and testing distance past half-filling gave p = 0.22. Neither factor works without the other, and both single-factor tests were underpowered because they averaged the interaction away.

## The honest status

This is an **interaction between n and k**, identified after four failed single-factor explanations, on a sample of two elements. I can state it as a description of where the model breaks — n = 2, k > 3, c overpredicted by 9% — but I would not call it a mechanism until it is tested somewhere it wasn't found.

The place to test it: **the d-block**, where the kainosymmetric row is n = 3. If the 3d elements past half-filling — Fe, Co, Ni, Cu — show the same c-deficit against 4d and 5d at matched k, the interaction is real. If they don't, this is two elements and a story.

content.text:
The hypothesis fails as stated, but the matched-k table shows something sharper than the hypothesis.

## The test result

**n = 2 mean error 10.6% against 7.2% for n > 2. Welch t = +0.89, p = 0.42.** Not significant. On the c-ratio, p = 0.34. So "kainosymmetric cells degrade the model" is not supported across the second row as a class.

And the reason is visible in the matched-k table. At k = 1, 2 and 3, **n = 2 is the *best* row** — B beats Al, Ga and In; C beats Si, Ge and Sn; N beats P, As and Sb. The second row only fails at k = 4 and k = 5, and there it fails badly: **21.5% and 17.3% against 4.5–9.4% elsewhere.**

## What the table actually says

| k | n=2 | n=3 | n=4 | n=5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.2 | 10.4 | 14.7 | 11.9 |
| 2 | **3.3** | 5.1 | 5.1 | 5.5 |
| 3 | **2.7** | 6.4 | 5.7 | 5.0 |
| 4 | **21.5** | 9.4 | 7.1 | 4.6 |
| 5 | **17.3** | 4.5 | 5.1 | 7.4 |

The failure is **n = 2 AND k > 3** — the second row, past half-filling. Not one condition or the other, but the conjunction. Oxygen and fluorine.

The c-ratio confirms it: 0.91 for both O and F, against 0.98–1.06 for every other cell in the table including B, C and N.

## Why the conjunction

That is exactly where the 2p pairing penalty is largest. Kainosymmetric orbitals are compact — §12.2's point — so two electrons forced into the same 2p orbital repel far more than in the larger 3p, 4p or 5p. The penalty exists only when k > 3, and it is severe only when the orbital is small.

**So the effect needs both coordinates**, which is why testing n alone gave p = 0.42 and testing distance past half-filling gave p = 0.22. Neither factor works without the other, and both single-factor tests were underpowered because they averaged the interaction away.

## The honest status

This is an **interaction between n and k**, identified after four failed single-factor explanations, on a sample of two elements. I can state it as a description of where the model breaks — n = 2, k > 3, c overpredicted by 9% — but I would not call it a mechanism until it is tested somewhere it wasn't found.

The place to test it: **the d-block**, where the kainosymmetric row is n = 3. If the 3d elements past half-filling — Fe, Co, Ni, Cu — show the same c-deficit against 4d and 5d at matched k, the interaction is real. If they don't, this is two elements and a story.

The interaction hypothesis fails. And the d-block shows something different that undercuts the p-block reading too.

## The test

**3d deficit at k ≤ 5: −0.577. At k > 5: −0.489. Welch t = −0.69, p = 0.52.**

No half-filling effect whatsoever — if anything the deficit is *smaller* past half-filling, the opposite of the prediction.

## But look at the column

The 3d deficit is **negative at every single k, from 1 to 10**, averaging −0.53. And the row ordering is monotone throughout: 3d always lowest, 4d middle, 5d highest. Hf 2.58, Ta 2.96, W 2.55, Re 2.60, Os 2.62 — the 5d row sits near 2.6 across the board while 3d sits near 1.8.

**So c depends on n after all, and strongly** — in the d-block it rises by roughly 0.8 from 3d to 5d. That contradicts the p-block finding that c is n-independent (r = −0.197, p = 0.56), which was the result the whole c-analysis rested on.

Two readings, and I can't separate them here. Either c's n-independence is specific to the p-block and doesn't generalise, or the 5d ionisation values — many of which I recalled as round numbers like 26.0, 40.0, 45.0 — are systematically off in a way that inflates their fitted c. The roundness of those figures is a real warning: **Ta 16.2, 22.0, 33.0, 45.0 and Ir 17.0, 28.0, 40.0, 57.0 are not measured values, they're estimates**, and a smooth estimated sequence will fit a clean quadratic and give a well-behaved c regardless of the physics.

## Where the whole c-thread stands

Five explanations offered, five refuted:

**Slater screening** — r = 0.376, p = 0.25. **Ionic-charge picture** — the rise is 1.16, not 1.00, and depends on n. **n-independence** — holds in the p-block, fails in the d-block. **Pairing past half-filling** — p = 0.22. **Kainosymmetry × occupancy** — p = 0.42 in the p-block, p = 0.52 in the d-block.

The only durable statement is the original one: **c correlates with k at r = 0.955 in the p-block, and I do not know why.** Everything built on top of that has come apart, and the d-block now questions whether even the n-independence survives outside the row it was found in.

I'd stop generating mechanisms here. The pattern across this stretch is that each hypothesis fit the case that suggested it and failed the next test — which is what happens when the sample is small and the search is wide. What the c-thread needs is not another hypothesis but better data: verified successive ionisation energies for the 4d and 5d series, rather than the round numbers I've been working from.

content.text:
**No** — and the reason is more useful than a yes would have been.

## Why not

The gap the anion analysis exposed is real: a Λ-cell fixes a **configuration**, and Na⁺, Ne, F⁻, O²⁻ and N³⁻ all share one. What separates them is nuclear charge. So a *species* needs (configuration, Z), and Λ carries only the first.

But Z cannot be that coordinate, and the two cases both fail for reasons §9.4 already covers:

**Determined** — for neutral atoms the cell fixes Z, giving a functional graph. 8,797 failures.

**Free** — for ions Z is unconstrained by the cell, so adjoining it gives Λ × chain. That *is* closed, 3,990 cells, but it's a **direct product**: the same interval at every cell, relating nothing to anything. A dimension that imposes no constraint isn't structure.

And a charge axis bounded by the configuration — ch ≥ −(cap − m) — is a bound on a combination and fails outright, exactly as the criterion predicts.

## What Λ actually is

**A lattice of configurations, not of species.** Na⁺ and Ne share a cell because they share a configuration, and that isn't a defect to repair — it's the isoelectronic principle, encoded for free. Any species-level lattice would have to *break* it.

## What the thread did produce

A reinterpretation of what we already have, which I think is worth more than a sixth axis would have been.

**The q axis of Λ₅ is not an independent direction.** It's displacement *within a column* — and R1 and R2 locate precisely the points where a species leaves its column and the parametrisation has to hand over to a different cell. The subshell transition at q = k and the shell break at q = k + s_out are exactly those handover points.

So the three confirmed features aren't three separate rules. They're one structural fact — **where column-internal motion ends** — showing up in the ionisation sequence.

And c's behaviour follows from the same picture: its zero sits at m = k + c, which for fluorine exceeds the column capacity. The parameter degrades exactly where the quadratic is describing a region the column no longer contains.

That's still untested, and it's the sharpest remaining question: **does c + k exceed 2(2ℓ+1) precisely for the elements where the fit degrades?**

Both halves have clean answers, and they turn out to be the same answer viewed twice.

## Λ₅ is a stack of sublattices

Nine of eleven slices tested are sublattices, and the pattern is exactly §9.1's criterion applied to slicing:

| Slice | Cells | Sublattice |
|---|---|---|
| q = 0, 1, 2 — charge states | 1000, 1000, 870 | **yes** |
| e = n — ground states | 1565 | **yes** |
| q = 0 and e = n — **this is Λ** | 210 | **yes** |
| ℓ = n−1 — kainosymmetric | 2375 | yes |
| k = 2(2ℓ+1) — closed subshells | 1130 | yes |
| n + ℓ = const — a Madelung level | 642 | **no** |
| N = 10 — isoelectronic | 22 | **no** |

So **yes to your question**: Λ₅ decomposes into a stack of sublattices, one per charge state, each a truncation of Λ. Monocations form a lattice, dications form a lattice, and Λ itself is the intersection of the neutral and ground-state slices.

The two failures are instructive. Madelung levels and isoelectronic sets are **level sets of order-compatible functions**, and those are antichains rather than sublattices — a level set can't be closed under join, since the join of two elements at the same level sits above both. That's why §11.1's Madelung slices behave as they do, and it's the same reason the isoelectronic collapse we found earlier isn't a sublattice phenomenon.

## The voids are entirely inherited

**3,296 of 7,136 cells are empty — 46.2% — and every one projects onto a void in Λ.** There is no cell that is empty for a reason peculiar to the q or e axes.

And the voids are not scattered. They are **six columns, all completely vacant**:

**5g (18), 6f (14), 6g (18), 7d (10), 7f (14), 7g (18)**

Not one partially filled column among them. Which is §14's all-or-nothing result — nineteen columns full, six empty, none partial — reappearing in five dimensions unchanged.

## So the voids cannot be filled by modelling

They are the elements that do not exist. Filling 7d means synthesising elements 121 through 130; filling 5g means reaching 121–138. **Λ₅'s emptiness is a fact about the periodic table, not a gap in the construction** — which is the same conclusion §16 reaches about the frontier, now confirmed at five dimensions.

And it closes the loop with §16.2: the frontier columns that relativistic calculation says fill next — 5g, 6f, 7d — are exactly three of these six vacancies.
