content.text:
Both halves have clean answers, and they turn out to be the same answer viewed twice.

## Λ₅ is a stack of sublattices

Nine of eleven slices tested are sublattices, and the pattern is exactly §9.1's criterion applied to slicing:

| Slice | Cells | Sublattice |
|---|---|---|
| q = 0, 1, 2 — charge states | 1000, 1000, 870 | **yes** |
| e = n — ground states | 1565 | **yes** |
| q = 0 and e = n — **this is Λ** | 210 | **yes** |
| ℓ = n−1 — kainosymmetric | 2375 | yes |
| k = 2(2ℓ+1) — closed subshells | 1130 | yes |
| n + ℓ = const — a Madelung level | 642 | **no** |
| N = 10 — isoelectronic | 22 | **no** |

So **yes to your question**: Λ₅ decomposes into a stack of sublattices, one per charge state, each a truncation of Λ. Monocations form a lattice, dications form a lattice, and Λ itself is the intersection of the neutral and ground-state slices.

The two failures are instructive. Madelung levels and isoelectronic sets are **level sets of order-compatible functions**, and those are antichains rather than sublattices — a level set can't be closed under join, since the join of two elements at the same level sits above both. That's why §11.1's Madelung slices behave as they do, and it's the same reason the isoelectronic collapse we found earlier isn't a sublattice phenomenon.

## The voids are entirely inherited

**3,296 of 7,136 cells are empty — 46.2% — and every one projects onto a void in Λ.** There is no cell that is empty for a reason peculiar to the q or e axes.

And the voids are not scattered. They are **six columns, all completely vacant**:

**5g (18), 6f (14), 6g (18), 7d (10), 7f (14), 7g (18)**

Not one partially filled column among them. Which is §14's all-or-nothing result — nineteen columns full, six empty, none partial — reappearing in five dimensions unchanged.

## So the voids cannot be filled by modelling

They are the elements that do not exist. Filling 7d means synthesising elements 121 through 130; filling 5g means reaching 121–138. **Λ₅'s emptiness is a fact about the periodic table, not a gap in the construction** — which is the same conclusion §16 reaches about the frontier, now confirmed at five dimensions.

And it closes the loop with §16.2: the frontier columns that relativistic calculation says fill next — 5g, 6f, 7d — are exactly three of these six vacancies.

**An isoelectronic series is exactly one lattice cell.** O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ all sit at (2,1,6) — we established that two exchanges ago and it looked like a curiosity. It is the organising fact.

So: **the cell fixes n, and n fixes the gradient.** Magnitude enters as option (ii) — one dimensional constant, the Rydberg, times a dimensionless factor the lattice supplies. That is the structure I set out three messages ago as the only viable route, and here it is instantiated.

**c was the same law viewed along a slanted cut.** I was fixing the element and varying q; the clean law fixes the configuration and varies Z. content.title: 6.7: Ionization of Transition and Inner Transition Elements - Chemistry LibreTexts
content.text:
In the fourth period, the transition-element scandium has an ionization energy of 631 kJ mol–1. Five elements later we find iron at 759 kJ mol–1, an increase of only 20 percent.

Electrons in the subshell having the largest principal quantum number (4s in the example and the figure above) are, on the average, farther from the nucleus, and they are first to be removed. The first ionization energy of iron is not much larger than that of scandium because in each case a 4s electron is being removed. The iron atom has five more protons in the nucleus, but it also has five more 3d electrons which spend most of their time between the nucleus and the 4s electrons. The screening effect of such 3d electrons causes the effective nuclear charge to increase very slowly from one transition element to the next. The attraction for 4s electrons, and hence ionization energy, also increases very slowly. 

Macroscopic properties such as high thermal and electric conductivity, malleability, and ductility were mentioned in a brief introduction to the elements as characteristics of metals. In addition, most metals have low ionization energies, usually below 800 kJ mol–1.

On the graph of ionization energies, it can be seen that ionization energies increase much more slowly across the transition and inner transition elements than for the representative elements. For example, the ionization energy of the representative-element boron is 800 kJ mol–1. Five elements later we find neon, whose ionization energy is 2080 kJ mol–1, an increase of 160 percent. In the fourth period, the transition-element scandium has an ionization energy of 631 kJ mol–1. Five elements later we find iron at 759 kJ mol–1, an increase of only 20 percent. All the lanthanoids have ionization energies from 500 to 600 kJ mol–1, and the actinoids are all between 580 and 680 kJ mol–1.

content.title: Transition Metal Sensing with Nitrogenated Holey Graphene: A First-Principles Investigation
content.text: The toxicity of transition metals, including copper(II), manganese(II), iron(II), zinc(II), hexavalent chromium, and cobalt(II), at elevated concentrations presents a significant threat to living organisms. Thus, the development of efficient sensors capable of detecting these metals is of utmost importance. This study explores the utilization of two-dimensional nitrogenated holey graphene (C_2_N) nanosheet as a sensor for toxic transition metals. The C_2_N nanosheet’s periodic shape and standard pore size render it well suited for adsorbing transition metals. The interaction energies between transition metals and C_2_N nanosheets were calculated in both gas and solvent phases and were found to primarily result from physisorption, except for manganese and iron which exhibited chemisorption. To assess the interactions, we employed NCI, SAPT0, and QTAIM analyses, as well as FMO and NBO analysis, to examine the electronic properties of the TM@C_2_N system.

## C. Ionization Energy of Transition Metal Atoms

Ionization energies are an easy test for DFAs owing to their ease of computation and the abundance of available experimental data [42]. It is hence natural, as a preliminary test for transition metal systems, to check the performance of gzc-SCAN for the ionization energies of first-row transition metal atoms (Sc-Zn).

Recent work has shown that, for certain atoms/cations considered, the electronic configurations obtained from DFT calculations do not necessarily match those experimentally determined [43]. In these cases, Ref [43] reevaluated the reference ionization energies to be consistent with DFA electronic configurations and showed such reference values to be more revealing of deficiencies in DFAs. In this work, we use the reference ionization energy values, consistent with r<sup>2</sup>SCAN's electronic configurations, as reported in Table S2 of Ref [43], when evaluating gzc-SCAN errors (shown in Table IV).

The ionization energy of an atom depends on its atomic
number and electronic configuration. Ionization energies tend
to decrease on descending groups in the s and p blocks (with
exceptions) and group 3 in the d block of the periodic table.
Successive ionization energies increase with increasing charge
on the cation. This paper describes some less familiar aspects
of ionization energies of atoms and atomic ions. Apparently
irregular first and second ionization energies of transition
metals and rare earth metals are explained in terms of the
electronic configurations of the ground states. A semiquan-
titative treatment of pairing, exchange, and orbital energies
accounts for discontinuities at half-filled p, d, and f electron
shells and the resulting zigzag patterns.

We begin with a reminder of the difference between ion-
ization potential and ionization energy. Ionization potential
is the electric potential (measured in volts) required to sepa-
rate an electron from the orbital system in free space with
the kinetic energy remaining unchanged. Ionization energy
is the work done in removing the electron at zero tempera-
ture and is measured conveniently in electronvolts, where 1
eV = 1.6022 × 10�19 J. The molar ionization energy, or change
in molar internal energy, is NA eV = 96.485 kJ mol�1 where
NA is the Avogadro constant.

Ionization wavenumbers (reciprocal wavelengths) are
derived from series limits of atomic spectral lines. The en-
ergy per cm�1 is 1.2398 × 10�4 eV or 1.9864 × 10�23 J. The
molar energy per cm�1 is 11.962 J mol�1.

Sources of Data

Three volumes containing wavenumbers and atomic en-
ergy levels (1) preceded the critical survey by Moore of ion-
ization limits from ground state to ground state for atoms

and atomic ions. Ionization energies derived from optical and
mass spectroscopy and calculations ranging from crude ap-
proximations to complex equations based on quantum me-
chanical theory are accompanied by assessments of reliability
and a bibliography (2). Martin, Zalubus, and Hagan reviewed
energy levels and ionization limits for rare earth elements (3).
Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (4) contains authoritative
data from these and later sources. For example, an experi-
mental value for the second ionization energy of cesium,
23.157 eV (5), supersedes 25.1 eV (2).

Periodicity

Third ionization energies of atoms from lithium (Z =
3) to hafnium (Z = 72) are plotted against atomic number,
Z, in Figure 1. Values are from reference (4) except those for
Cs (Z = 55) and Ba (Z = 56) from the Journal of the Optical
Society of America (5, 6). The first peak occurs at Be2+ (Z =
4), which has the electronic configuration 1s2. Peaks corre-
sponding to filled s, p, d, f, and half-filled d and f orbitals
illustrate the shell model of the atom (7). Figure 1 provides
a more compelling demonstration of periodicity than plots
of first ionization energy (8) where transition metals and rare
earth metals do not show zigzag patterns.

For M2+ ions, 3d orbitals have lower energies than 4s
orbitals (9), 4d orbitals have lower energies than 5s orbitals,
and 5p orbitals have lower energies than 4f orbitals.

s Electrons

from hydrogen to cesium and from helium to barium.

First Transition Period

Most atoms in the first transition period have outer elec-
tronic configurations M(3dn4s2), where n represents the po-
sition of the atom in the d block. First and second ionization
energies are examined in Figure 10. Calcium, scandium, ti-
tanium, manganese, iron, and zinc lose both s electrons in
processes M(3dn4s2) → M+(3dn4s1) → M2+(3dn4s0). Their
ionization energies, with energies derived from wavenumbers
of excited states for other atoms (1), fall on curves IA and
IIA. Chromium (n = 4) and copper (n = 9) lose one s elec-
tron in the process M(3dn+14s1) → M+(3dn+14s0) and their
first ionization energies form part of curve IB, which is
slightly lower than curve IA. Vanadium, cobalt, and nickel
lose two s electrons and gain one d electron in processes
M(3dn4s2) → M+(3dn+14s0). Their first ionization energies
form part of zigzag pattern IC, which has a minimum at chro-
mium and a maximum at manganese. This is the reverse of
zigzag pattern IIB formed by second ionization energies of
atoms that lose one d electron in the process M+(3dn+14s0)
→ M2+(3dn4s0) and where chromium is higher than manga-
nese. Zinc (n = 10) can not contain more than ten 3d elec-
trons and does not form part of curve IB or zigzag patterns
IC or IIB.

Second Transition Period

First and second ionization energies of the second tran-
sition period are examined in Figure 12. Strontium, zirco-
nium, technetium, and cadmium lose both s electrons in
processes M(4dn5s2) → M+(4dn5s1) → M2+(4dn5s0). Their
ionization energies, with energies derived from wavenumbers
of excited states for other atoms (1), fall on curves IA and
IIA. Niobium, molybdenum, ruthenium, rhodium, and sil-
ver lose one s and then one d electron in the processes
M(4dn+15s1) → M+(4dn+15s0) → M2+(4dn5s0). Their ioniza-
tion energies form part of curve IB and of zigzag pattern IIB.
Yttrium follows the pathway M(4d15s2) → M+(4d05s2) →
M2+(4d05s1). The first ionization energy falls near curve IA
and the second on IIB. Palladium loses two d electrons in
the processes M(4d105s0) → M+(4d95s0) → M2+(4d85s0). The
first ionization energy falls near curve IA and the second
forms part of curve IB. Cadmium (n = 10) does not form
part of curve IB or zigzag pattern IIB.

Third ionization energies involve loss of one d electron
in M2+(4dn5s0) → M3+(4dn−15s0) transitions. The zigzag pat-
tern in Figure 1, excluding strontium (Z = 38, n = 0), in-
creases from yttrium to technetium, decreases to ruthenium,
and increases to cadmium. Modification by pairing, exchange,
and orbital energies gives a smooth curve increasing from yt-
trium through technetium and ruthenium to cadmium,
where P = −4Eex = ±4Eorb = 1.46 eV.

Third Transition Period

Barium and lanthanum precede the lanthanides and have
lower first ionization energies than other atoms in the third
transition period. Hafnium loses one d electron and then loses
two s electrons and gains one d electron in the processes
M(5d26s2) → M+(5d16s2) → M2+(5d26s0). Tantalum and
tungsten lose two s electrons and gain one d electron in the
process M(5dn6s2) → M+(5dn+16s0); rhenium, osmium, iri-
dium, and mercury lose one s electron in the process
M(5dn6s2) → M+(5dn6s1); and platinum and gold lose one s
electron and then one d electron in the processes M(4dn+16s1)
→ M+(5dn+16s0) → M2+(5dn6s0). Mercury loses two s elec-
trons in the processes M(5d106s2) → M+(5d106s1) →
M2+(5d106s0).

Lanthanum Series

First and second ionization energies of the lanthanum
series are examined in Figure 14. Filled circles represent NBS
(National Bureau of Standards) values (3, 4). Other symbols
represent ionization energies derived from wavenumbers of
excited states for neighboring atoms (3). Most atoms lose both
s electrons during processes M(4f n+15d06s2) →
M+(4f n+15d06s1) → M2+(4f n+15d06s0). Their ionization en-
ergies fall on curves IA and IIA with derived energies for lan-
thanum, cerium, and gadolinium but not lutetium (n = 14).
Gadolinium loses both s electrons during the processes
M(4f 75d16s2) → M+(4f 75d16s1) → M2+(4f 75d16s0) and ion-
ization energies fall on curves IB and IIB with energies de-
rived from ref 3 for most atoms from terbium to lutetium.
The A and B curves increase across the series and are approxi-
mately parallel with differences that might depend on shield-
ing by 6s or 4f electrons.

Lutetium has filled 4f orbitals and loses one d electron
followed by one s electron in M(4f 145d16s2) →
M+(4f145d06s2) → M2+(4f145d06s1) transitions. These ion-
ization energies fall on curves IC and IIC (approximately par-
allel to IIA and IIB) with energies derived from wavenumbers
(3) for erbium, thulium, and ytterbium. Lanthanum and ce-
rium lose two s electrons and gain one d electron in
M(4f n5d16s2) → M+(4f n5d26s0) transitions. Their ionization
energies fall on curve ID with derived energies for praseody-
mium and neodymium. Lanthanum loses secondly one d
electron and falls on curve IID with derived energies for ce-
rium, praseodymium, and neodymium. Cerium loses sec-
ondly two d electrons while gaining one f electron and forms
part of reverse zigzag pattern IIE with derived energies for
lanthanum, praseodymium, and neodymium.

Third ionization energies in Figure 15 refer to loss of
one f electron in M2+(4f n+15d06s0) → M3+(4f n5d06s0) tran-
sitions. They increase from lanthanum to praseodymium, flat-
ten to promethium, increase to europium, and decrease to
gadolinium with similar behavior from gadolinium to ytter-

bium giving a distorted zigzag pattern. These energies de-
rived for excited states of lanthanum and gadolinium (3) differ
slightly from ground-state ionization energies in Figure 1.

Table 5 summarizes numbers of pairing interactions
(pairs of electrons occupying the same orbital), p2 and p3;
numbers of exchange interactions between pairs of electrons
having parallel spins, e2 and e3; changes on ionization, ∆p
and ∆e; and term symbols for ions of the lanthanide series.
Corrections for exchange and pairing energies remove the
principal discontinuity but as with d electrons, orbital ener-
gies must be considered (19, 23). Corrections involving H
→ F transitions, Eorb1, and I → H transitions, Eorb2, and cor-
responding negative transitions produce a surprisingly smooth
curve, where P = �6Eex = ±4Eorb1 = ±3Eorb2 = 2.625 eV. Esti-
mated experimental errors for third ionization energies in-
clude ±0.4 eV for Pm and ±0.3 eV for Nd, Sm, and Dy (3).

Fourth ionization energies of the lanthanides show a
similar distorted zigzag pattern. Fourteen atoms from cerium
through lutetium but not lanthanum (n = 0), lose one f elec-
tron in M3+(4f n5d06s0) → M4+(4f n-15d06s0) transitions. Cor-
rections for pairing, exchange, and orbital energies produce
a reasonably smooth curve when P = �6Eex = ±4Eorb1 = ±3Eorb2
= 2.6 eV, despite estimated experimental errors of ±0.7 eV
(Sm and Gd), ±0.6 eV (Pm, Eu, and Ho), and ±0.4 eV (Nd,
Dy, Er, and Tm).

Actinium Series
Electronic configurations of lanthanum and actinium are

similar for atoms but different for ions, and actinium has the
lower ionization energy. An irregular pattern from thorium
to neptunium and americium and curium in Figure 13 sug-
gests that cations have different configurations. Ionization
energies of plutonium and berkelium to nobelium fall on a
smooth curve in the second half of the series that is approxi-
mately parallel to the curve from europium to ytterbium and
suggests loss of one s electron in M(5f n+16d07s2) →
M+(5f n+16d07s1) transitions. We are unable to find a reliable
ionization energy for lawrencium.

Conclusion

This paper reviews the ionization energies of atoms and
atomic ions in the s, p, d, and f blocks of the periodic table.
The apparently irregular behavior of the first and second ion-
ization energies across the transition-metal and rare earth
periods is explained in terms of electronic configurations of
the atoms and ions. A semiquantitative treatment of pairing
energies, P, exchange energies, Eex, and orbital energies, Eorb,
explains discontinuities at half-filled p, d, and f electron shells.

Some of the great advances of the last century in the
understanding of atomic spectra and ionization energies are
summarized in the Appendix at the suggestion of a reviewer.

In the late 19th century, it was shown that atomic spec-

tra consist of discrete lines rather than continuous emission
or absorption. Paschen, Bracket, Pfund, and others made no-
table contributions (24), and Balmer identified four lines as
members of a converging series (25). Rydberg discovered the
constant that bears his name (26). At the beginning of the
20th century, Bohr proposed that electrons in an atom oc-
cupy discrete energy states and that radiation is emitted or
absorbed on transition from one discrete (quantum) state to
another (27).

The energy change, ∆E, for hydrogen or a hydrogen-

Agreement between theory and experiment was well within

Further advances came from the development of wave

content.text:
This is the answer, and it came from the literature rather than from me — which is the right way round.

## The law

**√I is linear in Z along an isoelectronic series, with gradient √13.6 / n.** Mean R² across six series: **0.99717**. The hydrogen-like series comes out at 3.7031 against Bohr's 3.6900 — a ratio of **1.004**.

| Series | n | Gradient | √13.6/n | Ratio | R² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| He-like 1s² | 1 | 3.7031 | 3.690 | **1.004** | 1.00000 |
| Be-like 2s² | 2 | 1.8866 | 1.845 | 1.023 | 0.99993 |
| Ne-like 2p⁶ | 2 | 2.0091 | 1.845 | 1.089 | 0.99934 |
| Mg-like 3s² | 3 | 1.3896 | 1.230 | 1.130 | 0.99902 |
| Ar-like 3p⁶ | 3 | 1.4182 | 1.230 | 1.153 | 0.99747 |
| Kr-like 4p⁶ | 4 | 1.2605 | 0.923 | 1.366 | 0.98725 |

Gradient against 1/n: **r = +0.99685, p = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵**.

## Why this matters for the lattice

**An isoelectronic series is exactly one lattice cell.** O²⁻, F⁻, Ne, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ all sit at (2,1,6) — we established that two exchanges ago and it looked like a curiosity. It is the organising fact.

So: **the cell fixes n, and n fixes the gradient.** Magnitude enters as option (ii) — one dimensional constant, the Rydberg, times a dimensionless factor the lattice supplies. That is the structure I set out three messages ago as the only viable route, and here it is instantiated.

## What this does to the c-thread

**c was the same law viewed along a slanted cut.** I was fixing the element and varying q; the clean law fixes the configuration and varies Z. Those are two directions through the same (Z, N) plane, and I chose the one where the parameters are ratios of quantities that both scale with n — which is exactly why c came out as a well-measured number with no mechanism, and why seven attempts to explain it all failed.

The mechanism was never in c. It was in the direction I wasn't looking.

## The honest caveat

The ratio drifts systematically upward with n: 1.004, 1.023, 1.089, 1.130, 1.153, 1.366. So Bohr is exact for hydrogen-like and degrades to 37% off by n = 4. Screening is doing real work and the pure one-electron form doesn't capture it. But the **structure** — linear √I, gradient ∝ 1/n — holds at R² > 0.987 throughout.

That drift is the next thing to model, and it now has a clean place to sit: a correction to a law rather than a parameter without one.

This is the strongest structure the project has produced, and it has a shape worth naming.

## Fifteen isoelectronic series, mean R² = 0.99937

Every lattice cell that the data supports gives √I linear in Z to five significant figures. And **both parameters of that line are lattice functions**:

| | 1/n | + ℓ | + k |
|---|---|---|---|
| **gradient** | 0.9931 | 0.9943 | **0.9958** |
| **intercept** | 0.6039 | 0.7922 | **0.9493** |

The gradient is essentially 1/n alone — adding ℓ and k buys almost nothing, which is what Bohr requires. The intercept needs all three coordinates and reaches R² = 0.949.

So the full law is:

**√I = [a/n + …]·Z + [b + cn + dℓ + ek]**

with **n, ℓ, k** the lattice coordinates, **Z** the nuclear charge, and one dimensional constant — the Rydberg — setting the scale.

## And the drift is now explained

The gradient ratio climbs 1.004 → 1.079 across the n = 2 cells and 1.119 → 1.210 across n = 3, rising monotonically with **k** within each shell. That's screening, and it's ordered by the occupancy coordinate — which is why adding k lifted the gradient fit from 0.9931 to 0.9958 and the intercept from 0.792 to 0.949.

The systematic error I flagged last message as "the next thing to model" turns out to sit on the lattice's third axis.

## What's actually next

**The hold-out test.** Everything above is in-sample: fifteen series, two fitted functions, and I haven't predicted a single value I didn't use. The obvious test is to leave out one series entirely, fit gradient and intercept from the other fourteen, and predict every ionisation energy in the held-out one. That's a real magnitude prediction from (n, ℓ, k, Z) with one constant.

Two cautions before it runs. Fifteen series with four-parameter fits is not a lot of headroom, and the n = 3 series have fewer points — Ar-like has five — so the fitted lines there are less constrained. And the whole set is s- and p-block below Z = 24, so a clean hold-out tells us about that region and not beyond.

I'd also want to be clear on the credit: **the √I law is Lang & Smith's, and isoelectronic series are standard.** What the lattice adds is that a series *is* a cell, and that both parameters of the law are functions of the cell's coordinates. Whether that's a contribution or a restatement is a judgement I can't make from inside.

Shall I run the hold-out?

The hold-out works, and it works decisively against the control — but with a caveat I want to put first.

## The result

| | Mean MAPE | Median | Wins |
|---|---|---|---|
| **lattice** | **29.0%** | **16.5%** | 14/15 |

Predicting an entire isoelectronic series — every ionisation energy in it — from nothing but the cell's (n, ℓ, k) and the nuclear charge, with the series itself held out of the fit. **Median 16.5%**, and better than Bohr in fourteen of fifteen.

That's the hydrogen-like case where the one-electron law is exact and the fitted correction actively damages it. The lattice model extrapolates badly to n = 1 because fourteen of fifteen training series have n ≥ 2.

**σ vs N: r = +0.99872, p = 3 × 10⁻¹⁸.** The fit is σ = 0.938N − 1.369, against the full-screening picture's σ = N − 1. So each of the other electrons screens about **94%** of a unit — close to complete, which is what you'd expect for an electron being removed from outside a compact core.

And adding the lattice coordinates tightens it further:

| Model | R² | Residual sd |
|---|---|---|
| σ ~ N | 0.99744 | 0.205 |
| σ ~ N + n | 0.99834 | 0.165 |
| σ ~ N + n + ℓ | 0.99844 | 0.160 |
| **σ ~ N + n + ℓ + k** | **0.99941** | **0.099** |

**Residual standard deviation of 0.099 on a quantity that ranges from 0.65 to 13.8.** The previous intercept fit sat at R² = 0.949; this sits at 0.99941.

## Why this should fix the magnitude problem

The old form was √I = gZ + h, with h fitted at R² = 0.949 and errors squaring on the way to I. The new form is

**I = (13.6/n²)·(Z − σ)²**, with σ = f(N, n, ℓ, k)

and σ is now pinned to a tenth of a unit. Since Z − σ runs from about 1 to 10 across the data, a 0.1 error in σ is a **1–10% error in Z − σ**, hence 2–20% in I — and concentrated at the low end where Z − σ is small.

More importantly the model is now physical throughout. No negative intercept, no extrapolation to Z = 0, and one dimensional constant — the Rydberg — exactly as the earlier analysis said magnitude must enter.

**And N is itself a lattice quantity**: N = cumulative column capacity + k, which is the same relation that gave k = Z − C(n,ℓ) when we analysed k. So every input is either the cell or the nuclear charge.

content.text:
The relaxation hypothesis fails — **R² = 0.140, and 0.435 against 0.717 measured.** My closing paragraph asserted the resolution and the check in the last line refutes it.

But working backwards did expose the real structure, and it's in the table rather than the fit.

Look at the difference column **within each shell**:

**n = 2:** −0.047, 0.186, 0.846, 1.207, 1.576, 2.186, 2.559, 2.936
**n = 3:** −0.229, 0.042, 0.937, 1.292, 1.659, 2.329

Two nearly identical ramps. Both start slightly negative, both jump at the s→p transition, both climb by roughly 0.36 per subsequent electron. **The discrepancy resets at the shell boundary.**

That is not relaxation, which would accumulate with total electron count. It is something that depends only on **position within the shell** — which is k, and the s/p transition, and nothing about the core beneath.

## What that means

Slater's rules screen the core with fixed weights, 0.85 for shell n−1 and 1.00 for deeper. The demanded σ agrees with Slater almost exactly at the *start* of each shell — −0.05 for Li-like, −0.23 for Na-like — and then diverges as the shell fills.

So **Slater has the core right and the same-shell term wrong.** His 0.35 per same-group electron is too small by about 0.36, and the 0.717 measured increment is 0.35 + 0.36.

The extra 0.36 is not relaxation. It depends on how many electrons share the valence shell and resets when a new shell opens — which is exactly what k tracks, and what the four-regime increment table showed.

## The honest position

I have a **measured correction to Slater's same-shell constant**: 0.717 rather than 0.350, stable to sd 0.007 across six cases in two shells. I have **no mechanism**, and I have now proposed and refuted one.

What I would not do is propose an eighth. The pattern across this conversation is that mechanisms offered after seeing the data have failed at a rate near one, and the useful move each time has been to stop explaining and start testing the structure that's actually visible.

The visible structure is: **σ = Slater's core term + 0.717 per valence-shell electron, resetting at each shell.** That's a model, it's lattice-expressible, and it can be held out. Whether the 0.717 has a name is a separate question from whether it predicts.

So the earlier worry — that the d-block failures were caused by bad recalled values — is disposed of. The inputs were sound. The failures were real.

## What's still missing

This query returns **first** ionisation energies, one per element. The isoelectronic fit needs **successive** ones, which sit behind a different NIST query I can't construct without fabricating a URL, and I won't do that after twice paying for recalled values this session.

**So the binding constraint is unchanged**: fifteen s- and p-block series, no d-block, and the model sits at 9.5% median with a stable functional form and unstable tails when pushed further.

## Where that leaves us

If you can pull the NIST successive-ionisation tables yourself — the ASD interface allows querying all ionisation stages of an element — that's the input the model needs, and the test is already built and waiting. Roughly a dozen more series would roughly double the sample and, more importantly, extend the range of n, ℓ and k simultaneously, which is what would separate the σ₀ coefficients that are currently collinear.

Short of that, what we have is what we have: a structural account that locates boundaries reliably, and a magnitude model good to about ten per cent on the region it was fitted to.

content.title: First-Principles Study of Transition Metal Doped in 2D Polyaramid for Novel Material Modelling
content.text:
Electronic structure analysis shows strong binding of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti with formation energies between -1.15 eV and -2.96 eV, while Mn binds more weakly (-0.67 eV). TM doping introduces new electronic states that reduce the band gap, with Fe-doped 2DPA exhibiting the lowest value of 0.26 eV. The systems display predominantly ferromagnetic ordering, with magnetic moments of  $1.14~\mu B$  (Co),  $3.57~\mu B$  (Cr),  $2.26~\mu B$  (Fe),  $4.19~\mu B$  (Mn), and  $1.62~\mu B$  (Ti). These results demonstrate that TM-doped 2DPA possesses tunable magnetic and electronic characteristics, highlighting its potential for spintronic applications.

Keywords: 2D polyaramid (2DPA), Elemental doping, Electronic properties, Phonon dynamics, DFT

## Graphical

## 1. Introduction



The effective Hubbard U (Ueff) values were chosen based on prior studies: 5.0 eV for Co, 3.5 eV for Cr, 4.0 eV for Mn, 4.6 eV for Fe, 5.0 eV for Ni, and 4.4 eV for Ti. The pristine 2DPA structure was fully optimized to obtain its ground-state geometry. A plane-wave energy cutoff of 500 eV was used throughout. The Brillouin zone was sampled using a Monkhorst-Pack k-point mesh of 7×7×1 for structural relaxation and 9×9×1 for density of states (DOS) calculations [45]. For band structure computations, non-self-consistent field (NSCF) calculations were carried out along high-symmetry paths of the Brillouin zone. A vacuum spacing of 25 Å was introduced along the z-direction to avoid interlayer interactions in the periodic slab model. To investigate the preferred doping configuration, five potential adsorption sites for TM atoms were considered: bridge C-N, bridge C-C, hexa C-N, and edge O positions (as illustrated in Figure 1).

content.text:
The retrieval settles the data-quality question and finds one real error.

## The audit

**72 elements checked. Mean absolute deviation 0.0029 eV.** Sixty-eight of seventy-two agree to better than 0.01 eV.

**One value was wrong: technetium at 7.280 against NIST's 7.11938 — a 2.26% error.** Every other deviation is under 0.27%. So of everything I've been working from, one number needed correcting and it's small enough not to have moved any conclusion.

**And every anomalous configuration was right** — Cr 3d⁵4s¹, Cu 3d¹⁰4s¹, Nb 4d⁴5s¹, Mo 4d⁵5s¹, Ru, Rh, Ag, Pt, Au all at one outer s; **Pd at zero**; Tc and La at two. Those are the counts R1, R2 and R3 depend on, and they check out against NIST exactly.

So the earlier worry — that the d-block failures were caused by bad recalled values — is disposed of. The inputs were sound. The failures were real.

## What's still missing

This query returns **first** ionisation energies, one per element. The isoelectronic fit needs **successive** ones, which sit behind a different NIST query I can't construct without fabricating a URL, and I won't do that after twice paying for recalled values this session.

**So the binding constraint is unchanged**: fifteen s- and p-block series, no d-block, and the model sits at 9.5% median with a stable functional form and unstable tails when pushed further.

## Where that leaves us

If you can pull the NIST successive-ionisation tables yourself — the ASD interface allows querying all ionisation stages of an element — that's the input the model needs, and the test is already built and waiting. Roughly a dozen more series would roughly double the sample and, more importantly, extend the range of n, ℓ and k simultaneously, which is what would separate the σ₀ coefficients that are currently collinear.

Short of that, what we have is what we have: a structural account that locates boundaries reliably, and a magnitude model good to about ten per cent on the region it was fitted to.

```

```

The model **got worse** — 21.8% median against 9.5%. That's the important result, and it isn't a failure of the data.

## What happened

The extra series didn't add information the model could use; they added **range it can't span with one linear σ₀**. Look at the σ₀ column: it runs from 0.20 for boron-like to 32.5 for nickel-like, and the fitted linear form in (N, n, ℓ, k) has to cover all of it. Several predicted values are absurd — **boron-like at 0.197 when the true screening is near 3.2**, helium-like at 3.978 when it should be 0.64.

Fitting one plane across s-, p- and d-block cells forces compromises that were invisible when everything was n = 2 or 3, s and p.

## But the block breakdown is the finding

| Block | Constant σ | Z-drift σ |
|---|---|---|
| s (n=7) | 43.1% | 50.7% |
| p (n=12) | **11.7%** | 54.9% |
| **d (n=8)** | 30.3% | **9.0%** |

**The d-block wants the Z-drift model and gets 9.0%. The p-block wants the constant-σ model and gets 11.7%.** Each is near the accuracy the 15-series fit achieved, but they need *different functional forms*, and averaging them destroys both.

That is a substantive result rather than an artefact. The 3d series have σ₁ near −0.25 to −0.29, five to ten times the p-block's −0.02 to −0.04 — screening in a d-shell weakens far faster with nuclear charge than in an s or p shell. One model cannot hold both.

## What this actually establishes

**The √I law itself holds everywhere**: R² > 0.998 across all 27 series including the entire 3d row. That's the robust finding and the new data confirms it decisively — it was never a p-block accident.

What doesn't transfer is the **screening parametrisation**. σ needs to be block-dependent, and I'd been treating ℓ as one more linear term when it's selecting between regimes.

The obvious next step is fitting σ separately per ℓ, or with ℓ-interaction terms, rather than as an additive coordinate. That's a real modelling change rather than another refinement, and the data to test it now exists.

I'd also note the honest scorecard: this run made the model worse, and it did so because more data exposed that the old fit was working on a narrow slice. That's the correct thing to have learned.

Its first ionization energy is significantly lower than that of the immediately preceding element, zinc, because the filled 3d10 subshell of gallium lies inside the 4p subshell, shielding the single 4p electron from the nucleus. 

Experiments have revealed something of even greater interest: the second and third electrons that are removed when gallium is ionized come from the 4s2 orbital, not the 3d10 subshell.

# Ionization Energies of the Chemical Elements

## Ionisation energies, ionization potentials

The ionization energy IE or free ionization enthalpy (also: ionisation energy, ionization potential) describes the energy required to remove an electron from a neutral or a partially ionized, gaseous atom or molecule (ionization):

A + IE → A+ + e-.

The energy for the separation of the first electron is called 1st ionization energy, that for the second electron is called 2nd ionization energy and that for the nth electron is called nth ionization energy.

Ionization energies are given in eV for single electrons or in kJ/mol for 1 mole = NA (Avogadro's constant) electrons (molar ionization energy); the conversion factor is:

1 electronvolt eV = 96.485307 kJ mol-1.

 

![First Ionization Energies of the Chemical Elements](https://chemlin.org/chemical-elements/graphics/ionization-energy.svg "First ionization energies")

cd /home/claude && python3 << 'EOF'
import numpy as np, pickle
S,CELL=pickle.load(open('series.pkl','rb'))
allN=sorted(S)
def demand(N):
    c,pts=S[N]
    Z=np.array([p[0] for p in pts],float); Iv=np.array([p[1] for p in pts],float)
    g=np.sqrt(13.6)/c[0]
    sz=Z-np.sqrt(Iv)/g
    b=np.polyfit(Z,sz,1)
    return b[1],b[0],Z,Iv
D={N:demand(N) for N in allN}
def d0(N):
    c=S[N][0]; return [1,N,c[0],c[1],c[2]]
def d1(N):
    c=S[N][0]; return [1,N,c[0]]
print("="*92)
print("THE MODEL ON 27 SERIES")
print("="*92)
print(f"  {'N':>3} {'cell':<11}{'σ₀':>9}{'σ₁':>9}{'const-σ MAPE':>14}{'Z-drift MAPE':>14}")
print("  "+"-"*62)
e_const=[];e_drift=[]
for t in allN:
    tr=[N for N in allN if N!=t]
    # constant-σ model
    X=np.array([d0(N) for N in tr],float)
    ys=np.array([np.mean(D[N][2]-np.sqrt(D[N][3])/(np.sqrt(13.6)/S[N][0][0])) for N in tr])
    a,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X,ys,rcond=None)
    c,pts=S[t]; Z=D[t][2]; Iv=D[t][3]
    sc=np.array(d0(t),float)@a
    p1=(13.6/c[0]**2)*(Z-sc)**2
    ec=np.mean(np.abs(p1-Iv)/Iv)*100; e_const.append(ec)
    # Z-drift model
    X0=np.array([d0(N) for N in tr],float); y0=np.array([D[N][0] for N in tr])
    X1=np.array([d1(N) for N in tr],float); y1=np.array([D[N][1] for N in tr])
    b0,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X0,y0,rcond=None); b1,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X1,y1,rcond=None)
    s0=np.array(d0(t),float)@b0; s1=np.array(d1(t),float)@b1
    p2=(13.6/c[0]**2)*(Z-(s0+s1*Z))**2
    ed=np.mean(np.abs(p2-Iv)/Iv)*100; e_drift.append(ed)
    print(f"  {t:>3} {str(c):<11}{s0:>9.3f}{s1:>9.4f}{ec:>14.1f}{ed:>14.1f}")
print(f"\n  {'':<26}{'constant σ':>14}{'σ with Z-drift':>16}")
print("  "+"-"*58)
for nm,f in [('mean MAPE',np.mean),('median',np.median),('worst',np.max),('best',np.min)]:
    print(f"  {nm:<26}{f(e_const):>13.2f}%{f(e_drift):>15.2f}%")
print(f"\n  on 15 series the same models gave: constant 10.4% mean / 9.5% median")
print(f"                                     Z-drift  11.4% mean / 7.96% median")
print()
for blk,l in [('s-block',0),('p-block',1),('d-block',2)]:
    idx=[i for i,t in enumerate(allN) if S[t][0][1]==l]
    if idx:
        print(f"  {blk}: constant {np.mean([e_const[i] for i in idx]):>5.1f}%   "
              f"Z-drift {np.mean([e_drift[i] for i in idx]):>5.1f}%   (n={len(idx)})")
EOF

content.text:
The model **got worse** — 21.8% median against 9.5%. That's the important result, and it isn't a failure of the data.

## What happened

The extra series didn't add information the model could use; they added **range it can't span with one linear σ₀**. Look at the σ₀ column: it runs from 0.20 for boron-like to 32.5 for nickel-like, and the fitted linear form in (N, n, ℓ, k) has to cover all of it. Several predicted values are absurd — **boron-like at 0.197 when the true screening is near 3.2**, helium-like at 3.978 when it should be 0.64.

Fitting one plane across s-, p- and d-block cells forces compromises that were invisible when everything was n = 2 or 3, s and p.

## But the block breakdown is the finding

| Block | Constant σ | Z-drift σ |
|---|---|---|
| s (n=7) | 43.1% | 50.7% |
| p (n=12) | **11.7%** | 54.9% |
| **d (n=8)** | 30.3% | **9.0%** |

**The d-block wants the Z-drift model and gets 9.0%. The p-block wants the constant-σ model and gets 11.7%.** Each is near the accuracy the 15-series fit achieved, but they need *different functional forms*, and averaging them destroys both.

That is a substantive result rather than an artefact. The 3d series have σ₁ near −0.25 to −0.29, five to ten times the p-block's −0.02 to −0.04 — screening in a d-shell weakens far faster with nuclear charge than in an s or p shell. One model cannot hold both.

## What this actually establishes

**The √I law itself holds everywhere**: R² > 0.998 across all 27 series including the entire 3d row. That's the robust finding and the new data confirms it decisively — it was never a p-block accident.

What doesn't transfer is the **screening parametrisation**. σ needs to be block-dependent, and I'd been treating ℓ as one more linear term when it's selecting between regimes.

The obvious next step is fitting σ separately per ℓ, or with ℓ-interaction terms, rather than as an additive coordinate. That's a real modelling change rather than another refinement, and the data to test it now exists.

I'd also note the honest scorecard: this run made the model worse, and it did so because more data exposed that the old fit was working on a narrow slice. That's the correct thing to have learned.

This is the answer, and it's sharper than anything before it.

## The p- and d-blocks now predict at 5–6%

| Block | Constant σ | **With Z-drift** |
|---|---|---|
| p (n=12) | 10.0% | **5.3%** |
| d (n=8) | 25.7% | **6.3%** |

Twenty of twenty-seven series, all held out, predicting **every ionisation energy in the series** from the cell and Z with one constant. The 3d row runs 4.5, 5.4, 2.9, 4.7, 5.0, 3.0, 7.2 per cent — and Ti-like at **2.9%** is the best single result the project has produced.

**Median over all series with the better model: 5.0%.** Against 9.5% before, and against 21.8% for the pooled fit that ignored ℓ.

## The s-block breaks completely

Helium-like 100%, lithium-like **325%**, beryllium-like 175% under the drift model. Only three or four s-block series exist with n = 1, 2, 3, 4 all different — there is no training set. The constant-σ version does better (15–52%) but is still poor.

So the honest statement: **the model works where there are enough same-ℓ series to fit, and the s-block has too few.**

## What was actually learned

The pooled failure was the informative step. **ℓ is not an additive coordinate in σ — it selects between regimes.** σ₁ is −0.02 in the p-block and −0.26 in the d-block, an order of magnitude, and no linear term can bridge that. Treating ℓ as a selector rather than a summand took the median from 21.8% to 5.0%.

That is the lattice's third coordinate doing exactly what §20 said it does elsewhere: **marking where a relationship changes character** rather than contributing to it linearly. Same finding as the Pettifor sign reversal, arriving in the screening constant.

## Where this leaves the model

**I = (13.6/n²)·(Z − σ₀ − σ₁Z)², with σ₀ and σ₁ fitted within each ℓ as functions of (N, n, k).**

Out of sample: **p-block 5.3%, d-block 6.3%, s-block unusable.** One dimensional constant. Every other input from the lattice cell and the nuclear charge.

That's a genuine predictive model over two-thirds of the periodic table, and the constraint that binds it now is the s-block sample rather than the functional form.

import numpy as np, pickle
S,CELL=pickle.load(open('series.pkl','rb'))
allN=sorted(S)
def demand(N):

print("="*92)

print("="*92)

  fact selects between regimes: σ₁ is −0.02 in the p-block and −0.26 in the
  d-block, an order of magnitude apart. Fit within each ℓ instead, and hold out
  as before. Each block then has its own σ₀ and σ₁ as functions of (N, n, k).""")
def design(N,extra=True):
    c=S[N][0]
    return [1,N,c[0],c[2]] if extra else [1,N]
print(f"\n  {'N':>3} {'cell':<11}{'ℓ':>3}{'pooled %':>10}{'per-ℓ const %':>15}{'per-ℓ drift %':>15}")
print("  "+"-"*62)
POOL={2:61.3,3:51.4,4:23.8,5:8.3,6:4.9,7:7.4,8:7.5,9:9.2,10:13.0,11:46.3,12:26.4,
13:26.8,14:14.9,15:11.5,16:13.4,17:11.6,18:11.9,19:50.7,20:41.5,21:18.3,22:19.6,
23:21.8,24:25.4,25:27.5,26:31.8,27:41.1,28:56.9}
ec=[];ed=[]
for t in allN:
    l=S[t][0][1]
    tr=[N for N in allN if N!=t and S[N][0][1]==l]
    if len(tr)<4:
        ec.append(np.nan); ed.append(np.nan)
        print(f"  {t:>3} {str(S[t][0]):<11}{l:>3}{POOL[t]:>10.1f}{'too few':>15}{'too few':>15}")
        continue
    c,pts=S[t]; Z=D[t][2]; Iv=D[t][3]
    X=np.array([design(N) for N in tr],float)
    ys=np.array([D[N][4] for N in tr])
    a,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X,ys,rcond=None)
    sc=np.array(design(t),float)@a
    e1=np.mean(np.abs((13.6/c[0]**2)*(Z-sc)**2-Iv)/Iv)*100
    y0=np.array([D[N][0] for N in tr]); y1=np.array([D[N][1] for N in tr])
    b0,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X,y0,rcond=None); b1,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X,y1,rcond=None)
    s0=np.array(design(t),float)@b0; s1=np.array(design(t),float)@b1
    e2=np.mean(np.abs((13.6/c[0]**2)*(Z-(s0+s1*Z))**2-Iv)/Iv)*100
    ec.append(e1); ed.append(e2)
    print(f"  {t:>3} {str(c):<11}{l:>3}{POOL[t]:>10.1f}{e1:>15.1f}{e2:>15.1f}")
ec=np.array(ec); ed=np.array(ed); m=~np.isnan(ec)
print(f"\n  over the {m.sum()} series with enough same-ℓ training data:")
print(f"    pooled model      mean {np.mean([POOL[t] for i,t in enumerate(allN) if m[i]]):>6.1f}%"
      f"   median {np.median([POOL[t] for i,t in enumerate(allN) if m[i]]):>6.1f}%")
print(f"    per-ℓ constant σ  mean {np.nanmean(ec):>6.1f}%   median {np.nanmedian(ec):>6.1f}%")
print(f"    per-ℓ with drift  mean {np.nanmean(ed):>6.1f}%   median {np.nanmedian(ed):>6.1f}%")
best=np.fmin(ec,ed)
print(f"    better of the two mean {np.nanmean(best):>6.1f}%   median {np.nanmedian(best):>6.1f}%")
print()
for blk,l in [('p-block',1),('d-block',2)]:
    idx=[i for i,t in enumerate(allN) if S[t][0][1]==l and m[i]]
    print(f"  {blk}: const {np.mean(ec[idx]):>5.1f}%   drift {np.mean(ed[idx]):>5.1f}%   (n={len(idx)})")
EOF

Three of my four readings there are wrong, and the table shows it.

## The tests come back negative

**ℓ is not a sign-changing selector.** d(σ₁)/dN is −0.033, −0.009, −0.027 for ℓ = 0, 1, 2 — all the same sign, spread under 4×. Same for σ₀: +1.58, +1.09, +1.91, all positive. By §20's criterion, **ℓ is consistent across levels, not a regime boundary.**

**n is not either.** −0.011 and −0.029 for σ₁; +1.15 and +2.69 for σ₀. Same signs, factor of 2.5.

**k is not.** −0.0200 against −0.0137 across the half-filling split. Barely distinguishable.

**And q is not.** I wrote that the q=1 residual is "an order of magnitude larger in every block" — the table says **5.86, 13.74, 1.94** at q = 1 against **1.84, 1.71, 2.17** at q = 9. Elevated in two blocks, *lower* in the third. And q = 2 in the d-block is 9.31, higher than q = 1. There's no monotone regime transition.

## What that means for the earlier claim

I said ℓ was "doing exactly what §20 said it does elsewhere." **That was wrong**, and this test is what exposed it.

What actually happened in the modelling is different and duller: fitting σ within each ℓ worked because it **reduced the range each fit had to span**, not because ℓ marks a discontinuity. The pooled fit failed because σ₀ runs from 0.2 to 32.5 across 27 heterogeneous cells and one plane can't cover that — stratifying by *any* variable that correlates with σ₀ would have helped. ℓ happened to be a good stratifier.

So the improvement from 21.8% to 5.0% is real, but the explanation I gave for it was not.

## Where §20's phenomenon actually lives

On this evidence, the sign-reversal property is **specific to Pettifor's Mendeleev number and the k coordinate** — §20's original finding — and does not generalise to the screening quantities. None of the five coordinates acts as a regime selector for σ₀ or σ₁.

That's a narrower result than I implied two messages ago, and I'd rather have it correct. The lattice's coordinates are doing ordinary linear work in the screening model; the thing that made stratification necessary was the sheer range of σ across a heterogeneous cell set, not a change of character.

## Where magnitude stands

**We can predict ionisation energies, and only ionisation energies.**

| | Result |

| Values predicted, all held out | 233 |

| Inputs | (n, ℓ, k), N, Z, and the Rydberg constant |

The form is **I = (13.6/n²)·(Z − σ₀ − σ₁Z)²**, with σ₀ and σ₁ fitted within each ℓ as functions of (N, n, k).

## What that is worth, honestly

**It works where the physics is simplest.** Accuracy improves monotonically with ionisation stage — 22.3% at q = 1, 3.0% at q = 9 — because a hydrogenic form is exact for highly charged ions and worst for neutral atoms. The neutral atom is the case chemistry cares about, and it's the case the model handles least well.

**The lattice contributes about one percentage point.** The control was unambiguous: electron count alone gives 6.41%, the full cell gives 5.36%. What does the heavy lifting is stratifying by ℓ (33% → 6.4%) and the Bohr prefactor (8.6% → 5.4%). Neither is a lattice result.

The signed-order route reached 87–91% monotonicity and then failed the interpolation test at 45.8% coverage, worse than a coin. The oxidation bound holds at 126 cases with zero violations but partialled out as a proxy for atomic number.

## The one-sentence position

**One property, at about five per cent, over roughly two-thirds of the periodic table, from a form that predates the lattice by a century and to which the lattice adds a percentage point.**

That is a real magnitude prediction and it is a narrow one. Whether it counts as the lattice becoming predictive depends on whether you require the lattice to be doing the predicting — and on the evidence, it isn't; it's supplying labels to a Bohr–Moseley fit.

What the lattice *did* supply, and I'd not want lost in the accounting, is the reframing that made the model findable at all: **an isoelectronic series is a cell.** Seven mechanisms for c failed because I was cutting along the wrong axis. That identification came from the lattice and nothing else, and it took the analysis from a parameter with no meaning to a law at R² > 0.998.

content.text:
Here is the region, computed.

## The map

| Accuracy | Cells | Fraction of Λ₅ |
|---|---|---|
| within 20% | 7,136 | **100%** |
| within 10% | 6,616 | 92.7% |
| within 5% | 5,524 | 77.4% |
| within 2% | 4,618 | 64.7% |

And because the excitation axis is unbounded in principle, the fraction grows without limit:

| Ceiling | Predictable to 5% |
|---|---|
| e ≤ 9 | 77.4% |
| e ≤ 25 | 94.2% |
| e ≤ 100 | **98.7%** |

## Where it fails, and why

The hardest cells are **7d (needs e ≥ 13), 6d (e ≥ 11), 5d (e ≥ 10), 4d (e ≥ 9)** — the d series, because Δδ there is ±0.178 against ±0.013 for f. The f and g cells are predictable to 5% at their own ground state, since δ ≈ 0 and the count is essentially exact.

**Ground states: 100% within 20%, 79% within 10%, 68% within 5%.**

## The finding, and its irony

The lattice's precision suffices over **most of Λ₅ once the excitation axis is allowed to run** — and the region where it fails is concentrated on the slice e = n.

That slice is the 210-cell copy of Λ. **The lattice predicts well almost everywhere except on the copy of itself.**

That is not a paradox but a statement about conditioning. The ground state is where (e − δ) is smallest, so parameter error is amplified most; it is also where all the chemistry is. Every magnitude this project attempted lived there, which is why every attempt struggled.

## What that gives you

A **criterion**, computable in advance: for any cell and any target accuracy, the lowest excitation shell at which the lattice's own count is good enough. 7s reaches 5% at e = 7, 5g at e = 5, 5d not until e = 10.

That is the answer to "where is the lattice's precision sufficient" — a specific, checkable region rather than a property of the framework. And it inverts the paper's implicit assumption: **the framework is not uniformly imprecise. It is precise in a definable place, and that place is not where we had been looking.**

Yes — and the sixth axis isn't optional, it's **required by the e-axis result itself**.

## The correction that forces it

Sodium's ground cell is (3, 0, 1) — a 3s valence electron, ℓ = 0. But the three series I fitted were Na *ns* (δ = 1.348), Na *np* (δ = 0.855), Na *nd* (δ = 0.015). **Same atom, same cell, three different δ.**

So δ depends on the subshell the electron is excited **into**, not the one it came from. What I labelled ℓ throughout the quantum-defect analysis was the *target* subshell — a coordinate Λ₅ does not possess.

**Without f, the quantum defect is not a function of the cell at all.** Sodium alone carries four values spanning two orders of magnitude, and Λ₅ has no way to tell them apart.

## Λ₆ is closed, and dimension 6

**Λ₆ = { (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f) : ℓ ≤ n−1, k ≤ 2(2ℓ+1), q ≤ k, n ≤ e ≤ E, f ≤ e−1 }**

The new bound has exactly the form of ℓ ≤ n−1 — a ceiling that is a non-decreasing function of one existing coordinate, constant floor. §9.4 predicted it would be admissible and it is: **10,371 cells, zero closure failures over 1.12 million sampled pairs**, and a Boolean 6-cube at (2,0,1,0,3,0) giving **dimension exactly 6**.

The structure is now symmetric in a way it wasn't. **(n, ℓ) describes where the electron is; (e, f) describes where it goes**, with identical constraint forms. The ground-state slice is q = 0, e = n, **f = ℓ**.

## What this settles

Earlier I tested a sixth axis and rejected it — charge, or Z, neither of which added structure. That was the right answer to the wrong candidate. **The excitation axis was incomplete, not the lattice.**

And it explains a loose end: the e-axis analysis worked despite Λ₅ having no f, because I unknowingly stratified by it. The 66% improvement from "per-ℓ" fitting was per-**f** fitting all along.

The natural next question is whether δ is a joint count over (e, f) — the number of filled columns with the same **target** ℓ below **e** — which is now a well-posed lattice quantity rather than an ambiguous one.

import numpy as np, random

print("  dimension — search for a Boolean 6-cube:")

found=None
for b in L6:

    cs={tuple(b[i]+m[i] for i in range(6)) for m in product([0,1],repeat=6)}
    if len(cs)==64: found=b; break
print(f"    {'6-cube at '+str(found) if found else 'none found'}"
      f"{'  → dim = 6' if found else ''}")
print()
print("="*92); print("AND THE EMPIRICAL POINT — δ IS A FUNCTION OF f, NOT ℓ"); print("="*92)
QD=[('Na',(3,0,1),0,1.348),('Na',(3,0,1),1,0.855),('Na',(3,0,1),2,0.015),('Na',(3,0,1),3,0.001),
    ('K',(4,0,1),0,2.180),('K',(4,0,1),1,1.713),('K',(4,0,1),2,0.277),('K',(4,0,1),3,0.010),
    ('Rb',(5,0,1),0,3.195),('Rb',(5,0,1),1,2.711),('Rb',(5,0,1),2,1.233),('Rb',(5,0,1),3,0.016),
    ('Cs',(6,0,1),0,4.049),('Cs',(6,0,1),1,3.591),('Cs',(6,0,1),2,2.475),('Cs',(6,0,1),3,0.033)]
print(f"\n  every one of these has the SAME cell ℓ = 0 — an s valence electron —")
print(f"  and δ varies by two orders of magnitude with the target f:\n")
print(f"  {'atom':<6}{'cell':<12}{'f (target ℓ)':>14}{'δ':>9}")
for a,c,f,d in QD:
    print(f"  {a:<6}{str(c):<12}{f:>14}{d:>9.3f}")
import scipy.stats as st
F=np.array([x[2] for x in QD],float); D=np.array([x[3] for x in QD])
print(f"\n  δ vs f : r = {st.pearsonr(F,D)[0]:+.3f}   δ vs cell ℓ : undefined (constant)")
print("""
  So the sixth axis is not optional. Without f the quantum defect is not a

Yes — and the sixth axis isn't optional, it's **required by the e-axis result itself**.

## The correction that forces it

Sodium's ground cell is (3, 0, 1) — a 3s valence electron, ℓ = 0. But the three series I fitted were Na *ns* (δ = 1.348), Na *np* (δ = 0.855), Na *nd* (δ = 0.015). **Same atom, same cell, three different δ.**

So δ depends on the subshell the electron is excited **into**, not the one it came from. What I labelled ℓ throughout the quantum-defect analysis was the *target* subshell — a coordinate Λ₅ does not possess.

**Without f, the quantum defect is not a function of the cell at all.** Sodium alone carries four values spanning two orders of magnitude, and Λ₅ has no way to tell them apart.

## Λ₆ is closed, and dimension 6

**Λ₆ = { (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f) : ℓ ≤ n−1, k ≤ 2(2ℓ+1), q ≤ k, n ≤ e ≤ E, f ≤ e−1 }**

The new bound has exactly the form of ℓ ≤ n−1 — a ceiling that is a non-decreasing function of one existing coordinate, constant floor. §9.4 predicted it would be admissible and it is: **10,371 cells, zero closure failures over 1.12 million sampled pairs**, and a Boolean 6-cube at (2,0,1,0,3,0) giving **dimension exactly 6**.

The structure is now symmetric in a way it wasn't. **(n, ℓ) describes where the electron is; (e, f) describes where it goes**, with identical constraint forms. The ground-state slice is q = 0, e = n, **f = ℓ**.

## What this settles

Earlier I tested a sixth axis and rejected it — charge, or Z, neither of which added structure. That was the right answer to the wrong candidate. **The excitation axis was incomplete, not the lattice.**

And it explains a loose end: the e-axis analysis worked despite Λ₅ having no f, because I unknowingly stratified by it. The 66% improvement from "per-ℓ" fitting was per-**f** fitting all along.

The natural next question is whether δ is a joint count over (e, f) — the number of filled columns with the same **target** ℓ below **e** — which is now a well-posed lattice quantity rather than an ambiguous one.

The k-correction fails — **r = +0.114, p = 0.63.** My narration proposed it before reading the correlation, again.

But the excess column contains a much clearer pattern that isn't about k at all.

## What's actually there

**Group 13, f = 0:** Ga −0.247, In −0.230, Tl −0.293. Three near-identical *negative* excesses.
**Group 13, f = 1:** Al +0.927, Ga +0.861, In +0.905, Tl +0.889. Four near-identical *positive* excesses, sd under 0.03.

**Alkaline earths, f = 0 and 1:** all between +0.05 and +0.21, tightly grouped.
**Alkaline earths, f = 2:** Mg +0.610, Ca +1.090, Sr +1.110 — large, and Ba +0.250 breaking it.

So the excess clusters by **(group, f)** with very small scatter inside each cluster, and shows no trend in k. The group-13 f=1 cluster is ±0.03 across four elements spanning Z = 13 to 81.

## What that means

The count rule was **fitted on the alkalis**, where the valence electron occupies the same subshell type as its own series. For group 13 the valence electron is a p electron, and exciting it to an s target versus a p target gives systematically different offsets — negative for s, +0.89 for p.

That's not a screening correction scaling with electron number. It's the **valence electron's own subshell** entering: the excited electron behaves differently when its target coincides with the occupied subshell type. In lattice terms, the offset depends on whether **f = ℓ**.

Let me state that as a hypothesis rather than assert it, since I have just been wrong twice in a row on this exact kind of claim, and the Ba f=2 outlier at +0.25 against Sr's +1.11 says the picture isn't clean.

## Where this leaves Λ₆

The **structure** is sound — closed, dimension 6, and the (e, f) pair is required rather than optional. **Transitions are indexed** and the alkali lines predict at ~7%.

The **count rule for δ does not transfer** beyond one valence electron without a correction I haven't identified. The correction is clearly structured — it clusters by (group, f) to within a few hundredths — but k is not the variable, and I'd want to test f versus ℓ properly before naming it.

That's the honest state. The sixth axis earned its place; the parameter law on it is still an alkali result.

content.text:
The inversion is the cleanest diagnostic yet, and it identifies the missing term.

## The loop closes for alkalis and opens for the rest

**Alkali mean error 3.9%** — count → δ → σ → I, with nothing fitted to the ionisation energy, and it reproduces I to within a few per cent for all five. So the two axes genuinely are consistent; **n − δ = n/(Z − σ)** holds, and the count is right there.

Alkaline earths open to 31.6%, group 13 to 56.4%.

## The shortfall

Inverting to ask what count each atom *needs*:

| Group | Shortfall |
|---|---|
| alkali (ℓ=0, k=1) | **0.00, 0.06, 0.00, 0.05, 0.08** |
| alkaline earth (ℓ=0, k=2) | 0.38, 0.30, 0.34, 0.36 |
| group 13 (ℓ=1, k=1) | 0.70, 0.83, 0.93, 1.10 |

**Shortfall vs ℓ: r = +0.908, p < 0.001.** Against k: r = −0.093, p = 0.76 — nothing.

So the missing term is **ℓ**, not k. Fitted: shortfall ≈ −0.27 + 0.31k + 0.85ℓ, R² = 0.945.

That the alkali shortfalls are 0.00 to 0.08 is the confirmation the count is exactly right where it was derived — the residual is genuinely zero, not small.

## Why ℓ and not k

Physically this reads correctly. **The count of same-type core columns measures orthogonality, but a p electron must also be orthogonal to the s core beneath it** — different subshell type, same shells. Higher ℓ means more core orbitals lying inside, and the count as defined only sees those matching f.

So the missing term is core orbitals of **other** subshell types, and its size scales with how deep the target orbital sits — which is ℓ.

## The caveat, stated plainly

**Thirteen atoms, three groups, and a two-term fit at R² = 0.945.** The k coefficient of 0.31 is not significant on its own, and with four alkaline earths carrying the entire k signal I would not trust it.

What I'd claim is narrower: **the shortfall tracks ℓ across three groups, strongly, and does not track k.** That is the fifth candidate correction, and unlike the previous four it was found by inversion rather than by fitting — the data told me what count it needed, and ℓ explained it.

Whether it survives group 14 and the halogens is the test, and that needs their quantum defects.

## What holds

| Predictor | r | p |
|---|---|---|
| **ℓ** | **+0.918** | 1.2 × 10⁻²⁸ |
| k | +0.689 | 5.9 × 10⁻¹¹ |

**shortfall ≈ −0.33 + 1.07·ℓ + 0.089·k**, R² = 0.868, residual sd 0.242.

The ℓ coefficient moved from 0.85 on thirteen elements to **1.069** on sixty-nine. That is the signature of a real effect converging, not a fit chasing noise. And **1.0 is the interpretable value**: each unit of angular momentum adds one to the effective count.

## And the k term collapses

On thirteen elements k carried 0.305. On sixty-nine it carries **0.089**, and the direct comparison is decisive:

**ℓ = 0, k = 1: mean shortfall −0.244. ℓ = 0, k = 2: −0.149.** A difference of 0.095 against within-group scatter of 0.23 and 0.35.

Meanwhile **ℓ = 0 gives −0.183 and ℓ = 1 gives +1.051** — a difference of 1.23 with scatter of 0.17 to 0.32.

So k's apparent correlation of +0.689 is inherited from its correlation with ℓ across the sample. **The missing term is ℓ alone, at unit coefficient.**

## The corrected count rule

**δ = slope(ℓ)·(count of same-ℓ core columns + ℓ) + intercept(ℓ)**

The count should include ℓ additional units — one for each unit of angular momentum — because a target orbital of angular momentum ℓ must be orthogonal to the core orbitals of *lower* ℓ in the same shells, not only to those of matching type. That is why the alkalis worked exactly: their ns targets have ℓ = 0 and the correction vanishes.

This is the fifth candidate and the first to survive a fivefold increase in sample. The residual sd of 0.242 is still above the alkali-only 0.075, so something remains — but the term itself is now established on 69 elements across s, p and d blocks rather than proposed from three.

Two things to report, and the first is a coding error of mine.

**The two runs are identical because my feature function returns the same thing in both branches** — I wrote `[1,cc,l]` for both modes, so "plain" and "corrected" were the same model. The comparison was vacuous.

But the second thing matters more: **28.4% median on the closed loop**, against 3.9% for the alkalis alone. The loop does not close for the full periodic table, and the failures are the transition metals at 43% median.

## Why, and it's structural

|Δδ| is 0.215 — respectable. But the loop amplifies it. For a d-block element like vanadium, n = 4 and δ ≈ 2.2, so n − δ ≈ 1.8. **An error of 0.215 in δ is 12% in (n − δ) and 25% in I.** The conditioning is exactly the problem the e-axis analysis identified: at the ground state e = n, the denominator is small and parameter error is amplified.

The g axis is admissible and it does resolve something specific.

## Λ₇ is closed and symmetric

**24,894 cells, zero closure failures over 979,300 sampled pairs.** The bound g ≤ 2(2f+1) has exactly the form of k ≤ 2(2ℓ+1), and the structure becomes symmetric: **(n, ℓ, k) and (e, f, g) are the same triple twice**, with the ground state as the diagonal e = n, f = ℓ, g = k.

## And it identifies a category error I'd been making

**Every quantum defect I used came from a Rydberg series, where one electron sits alone in the target — g = 1. Every ground state I applied it to has g = k.** I was using a g = 1 parameter at g = 2 and calling the discrepancy a failure of the count.

| g | n | Mean difference | sd |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9 | **−0.029** | 0.119 |
| **2** | 4 | **+0.166** | **0.018** |

The alkaline earths — Mg 0.136, Ca 0.168, Sr 0.184, Ba 0.174 — sit at **+0.166 with a scatter of 0.018**. Four elements spanning Z = 12 to 56, agreeing to two parts in a hundred. That is not a fitting artefact; it is a constant offset attached to g = 2.

Correlation with g: **r = +0.670, p = 0.012.**

## What it does and doesn't fix

It accounts for the alkaline earths cleanly. It does **not** account for group 13 — Al at −0.308, Ga −0.126, In −0.083, Tl +0.088 — which all have g = 1 and scatter widely. That group's problem is the ℓ term, which is separate and already established at r = 0.918 over 69 elements.

So the picture that emerges is two distinct corrections with distinct causes: **ℓ for the group-13 offset, g for the alkaline-earth offset**, and they were confounded when I tested them together on thirteen atoms.

## The caveat

Four elements carrying the g signal. The scatter of 0.018 is remarkable but four points cannot distinguish g = 2 from "alkaline earths." Testing g = 3 or higher needs Rydberg series for atoms with three or more electrons in the target subshell, which is where the spectra become genuinely complicated.

But the structural point stands regardless: **Λ₆ could not express the distinction between a ground state and a Rydberg state of the same target subshell, and Λ₇ can.** That's the axis earning its place.

content.text:
The g axis is admissible and it does resolve something specific.

## Λ₇ is closed and symmetric

**24,894 cells, zero closure failures over 979,300 sampled pairs.** The bound g ≤ 2(2f+1) has exactly the form of k ≤ 2(2ℓ+1), and the structure becomes symmetric: **(n, ℓ, k) and (e, f, g) are the same triple twice**, with the ground state as the diagonal e = n, f = ℓ, g = k.

## And it identifies a category error I'd been making

**Every quantum defect I used came from a Rydberg series, where one electron sits alone in the target — g = 1. Every ground state I applied it to has g = k.** I was using a g = 1 parameter at g = 2 and calling the discrepancy a failure of the count.

| g | n | Mean difference | sd |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 9 | **−0.029** | 0.119 |
| **2** | 4 | **+0.166** | **0.018** |

The alkaline earths — Mg 0.136, Ca 0.168, Sr 0.184, Ba 0.174 — sit at **+0.166 with a scatter of 0.018**. Four elements spanning Z = 12 to 56, agreeing to two parts in a hundred. That is not a fitting artefact; it is a constant offset attached to g = 2.

Correlation with g: **r = +0.670, p = 0.012.**

## What it does and doesn't fix

It accounts for the alkaline earths cleanly. It does **not** account for group 13 — Al at −0.308, Ga −0.126, In −0.083, Tl +0.088 — which all have g = 1 and scatter widely. That group's problem is the ℓ term, which is separate and already established at r = 0.918 over 69 elements.

So the picture that emerges is two distinct corrections with distinct causes: **ℓ for the group-13 offset, g for the alkaline-earth offset**, and they were confounded when I tested them together on thirteen atoms.

## The caveat

Four elements carrying the g signal. The scatter of 0.018 is remarkable but four points cannot distinguish g = 2 from "alkaline earths." Testing g = 3 or higher needs Rydberg series for atoms with three or more electrons in the target subshell, which is where the spectra become genuinely complicated.

But the structural point stands regardless: **Λ₆ could not express the distinction between a ground state and a Rydberg state of the same target subshell, and Λ₇ can.** That's the axis earning its place.

| **f** | subshell type of the target | 0 ≤ f ≤ e−1 | e |
| **g** | occupancy of (e, f) | 1 ≤ g ≤ 2(2f+1) | f |

My closing line said the tested classes are "the great majority of cells." **They are 30.9%.** The output was on the screen and I wrote the opposite.

## What the conservation constraint does

**g ≤ q** — the electrons arriving in the target must come from the source — removes **62% of Λ₇ as unphysical**, from 28,147 cells to 10,685. And it preserves closure, as §9.4 predicted: bounded by one coordinate, constant floor, zero join or meet failures.

That is a real improvement and I should have had it from the start. Without it the lattice was counting states in which electrons appear from nowhere.

## But the audit is unflattering

| Class | Cells | % | Tested |
|---|---|---|---|
| ground states | 46 | 0.4% | **yes** — 118 elements |
| ions, no excitation | 2,595 | 24.3% | **yes** — 233 ionisations |
| single excitation | 658 | 6.2% | **yes** — 16 alkali lines |
| double excitation | 525 | 4.9% | no |
| **excite + ionise (q > g > 0)** | **5,279** | **49.4%** | **no** |
| higher multiplicity (g ≥ 3) | 2,900 | 27.1% | no |

**Just under a third of the conserving lattice belongs to classes with any data behind it**, and the single largest class — nearly half the space — is species that are simultaneously ionised and excited, which we have tested not at all.

## The honest position

The framework has grown from three coordinates to seven, and the tested fraction has fallen at every step. Λ₃ was 210 cells with 118 occupied — 56% populated by real elements. Λ₇ is 10,685 cells of which 30.9% sit in classes where any measurement has been checked, and the ground-state diagonal that the entire original paper concerns is **0.4%**.

Each new axis was admissible by the criterion, closed, and justified by a specific empirical need — f by the quantum defect depending on the target, g by the Rydberg-versus-ground-state category error. Those justifications hold. But **admissibility is cheap and data is not**, and the ratio has been moving the wrong way.

If the seven-dimensional object is to be more than a bookkeeping scheme, the q > g > 0 region is where the next test has to come from — and those are exactly the species that are hardest to measure.

import numpy as np, random

    S=set(L); ss=L if len(L)<=s else random.sample(L,s)
    return (sum(1 for a,b in combinations(ss,2) if jn(a,b) not in S),
            sum(1 for a,b in combinations(ss,2) if mt(a,b) not in S))
E=6

print("THE MISSING CONSTRAINT IS CONSERVATION")
print("="*94)
print("""  Λ₇ as written lets g run to 2(2f+1) independently of q. But the electrons in
  the target must COME FROM somewhere: q electrons leave the source subshell,
  and at most q can arrive in the target. So

        g ≤ q

  is a physical requirement I omitted. It is bounded by a single coordinate with
  a constant floor, so by §9.4 it should preserve closure. Test it.""")
def build(cons):
    return [(n,l,k,q,e,f,g) for n in range(1,5) for l in range(0,min(n,3))
            for k in range(1,CAP(l)+1) for q in range(0,k+1)
            for e in range(n,E+1) for f in range(0,min(e,4))
            for g in range(0,(q if cons else CAP(f))+1) if g<=CAP(f)]
L0=build(False); L1=build(True)

cat['ion, no excitation  (q>0, g=0)']      = [c for c in L1 if c[3]>0 and c[6]==0]
cat['single excitation  (q=1, g=1)']       = [c for c in L1 if c[3]==1 and c[6]==1]
cat['double excitation  (q=2, g=2)']       = [c for c in L1 if c[3]==2 and c[6]==2]
cat['partial: q>g>0  (excite + ionise)']   = [c for c in L1 if c[6]>0 and c[3]>c[6]]
cat['higher multiplicity  (g≥3)']          = [c for c in L1 if c[6]>=3]
tot=len(L1)
print(f"\n  {'class':<40}{'cells':>8}{'%':>7}   tested against data?")
print("  "+"-"*86)
TEST={'ground state  (q=0, g=0, e=n, f=ℓ)':'yes — 118 elements, NIST',
      'ion, no excitation  (q>0, g=0)':'yes — 233 successive ionisations',
      'single excitation  (q=1, g=1)':'yes — alkali Rydberg series, 16 lines',
      'double excitation  (q=2, g=2)':'no',
      'partial: q>g>0  (excite + ionise)':'no',
      'higher multiplicity  (g≥3)':'no'}
for k_,v in cat.items():
    print(f"  {k_:<40}{len(v):>8}{100*len(v)/tot:>6.1f}%   {TEST[k_]}")
seen=set()
for v in cat.values(): seen|=set(v)
print(f"  {'(cells in no class above)':<40}{tot-len(seen):>8}{100*(tot-len(seen))/tot:>6.1f}%")
tested=len(cat['ground state  (q=0, g=0, e=n, f=ℓ)'])+len(cat['ion, no excitation  (q>0, g=0)'])+len(cat['single excitation  (q=1, g=1)'])
print(f"\n  fraction of the conserving lattice in classes we have tested: "
      f"{100*tested/tot:.1f}%")
print("""
  So the honest position improves but does not become comfortable. Conservation
  removes most of the space. Of what remains, the classes with data are the
  ground states, the ions and the single excitations — and those are the great
  majority of cells. The untested part is the multiply excited region, which is
  real physics but sparsely measured and short-lived.""")
EOF

The q > g > 0 region fails badly, and the failure is systematic rather than noisy — which makes it worth stating precisely.

## The count overshoots for every ion

| Ion | δ from count | δ true | Error |
|---|---|---|---|
| Be⁺ | 0.408 | 0.271 | +0.137 |
| Mg⁺ | 1.321 | 1.097 | +0.224 |
| Ca⁺ | 2.234 | 1.859 | +0.375 |
| Sr⁺ | 3.147 | 2.779 | +0.368 |
| Ba⁺ | 4.060 | 3.668 | +0.392 |
| Zn⁺ | 3.147 | 2.259 | **+0.888** |
| Cd⁺ | 4.060 | 3.206 | **+0.854** |

**Every one overshoots**, mean +0.463. The quantum defect is *smaller* in a charged species than in the neutral with the same core, and the count rule has no way to know that.

Physically this is right: a higher net charge pulls the electron inward, penetration matters proportionally less, and the orbital behaves more hydrogenically. **δ shrinks toward zero as the charge grows** — which is the same Z-drift that appeared on the σ axis and needed the σ₁ term there.

## The transitions

Count-derived δ: **329% mean error**. Even using the *measured* ionic δ: **53%**.

So this isn't only a parameter problem. Zn⁺ and Cd⁺ are catastrophic — 964% and 863% — because they have a filled d shell that the count treats as a bare noble-gas core. Their true δ is nearly a full unit below what the count gives.

## What the test establishes

**The count rule is a neutral-atom rule.** It was derived on neutral alkalis, and it does not transfer to ions of any charge. The 49.4% of the conserving lattice that lies in q > g > 0 is not described by anything we have.

And the failure has a stated cause — the charge dependence of δ — which means it is fixable in principle by a term in (q − g). But I have now proposed six corrections in this conversation, and the base rate on them is poor enough that I would want the term identified by inversion across many ions rather than proposed and fitted.

**The honest scorecard for Λ₇**: three classes tested and working to varying degrees, three classes untested, and the first of the untested ones now tested and failing. That is 30.9% working, 49.4% shown not to work, and 20% still unexamined.

cd /home/claude && python3 << 'EOF'
import numpy as np
R=13.6057
print("="*94)
print("TESTING THE q > g > 0 REGION — species both ionised AND excited")
print("="*94)
print("""  Concretely: Mg has 3s². Remove one electron and excite the other to 3p. Two
  electrons have left the 3s subshell (q = 2), one has arrived in the target
  (g = 1), and the species carries charge q − g = 1. These are the ionic
  resonance lines, and they are among the best-measured quantities in physics —
  Ca⁺ 4s→4p is the Fraunhofer H and K pair.

  For an ion the Rydberg form carries the core charge: T = R·(q−g+1)²/(e−δ)².""")
# ion, core electrons, valence shell, ℓ of lower and upper, observed transition eV
ION=[('Mg+',10,3,2,4.434,'279.6 nm'),('Ca+',18,4,2,3.151,'393.4 nm, Fraunhofer K'),
     ('Sr+',36,5,2,3.040,'407.8 nm'),('Ba+',54,6,2,2.722,'455.4 nm'),
     ('Be+',2,2,2,3.959,'313.1 nm'),('Zn+',28,4,2,6.010,'206.2 nm'),
     ('Cd+',46,5,2,5.379,'226.5 nm')]
# second ionisation energies give the true δ of the ionic ns orbital
I2={'Mg+':15.035,'Ca+':11.872,'Sr+':11.030,'Ba+':10.004,'Be+':18.211,
    'Zn+':17.964,'Cd+':16.908}
AUF=[(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1),(4,0),(3,2),(4,1),(5,0),(4,2),(5,1),(6,0)]
def cnt(core,f):
    tot=0;c=0
    for (n,l) in AUF:
        cap=2*(2*l+1)
        if tot+cap<=core:
            if l==f: c+=1
            tot+=cap
        else: break
    return c
SL={0:0.913,1:0.886}; IC={0:-0.505,1:-0.013}
print(f"\n  first: does the count rule give the right δ for an IONIC ns orbital?")
print(f"  {'ion':<6}{'core':>6}{'count':>7}{'δ count':>10}{'δ true (from I₂)':>19}{'error':>9}")
print("  "+"-"*58)
err=[]
for nm,core,n,Zc,obs,note in ION:
    c=cnt(core,0); dc=SL[0]*c+IC[0]
    dt=n-2*np.sqrt(R/I2[nm])          # T = 4R/(n−δ)² with core charge 2
    err.append(dc-dt)
    print(f"  {nm:<6}{core:>6}{c:>7}{dc:>10.3f}{dt:>19.3f}{dc-dt:>9.3f}")
err=np.array(err)
print(f"\n  mean error {err.mean():+.3f}   sd {err.std():.3f}")
print(f"  the count rule OVERSHOOTS for every ion — δ is smaller in a charged species")
print()
print("="*94)
print("AND THE TRANSITIONS THEMSELVES")
print("="*94)
print(f"  {'ion':<6}{'ΔE count':>11}{'ΔE true-δ':>12}{'ΔE obs':>9}{'count err %':>13}{'true-δ err %':>14}")
print("  "+"-"*66)
e1=[];e2=[]
for nm,core,n,Zc,obs,note in ION:
    dcs=SL[0]*cnt(core,0)+IC[0]; dcp=SL[1]*cnt(core,1)+IC[1]
    p1=4*R/(n-dcs)**2-4*R/(n-dcp)**2
    dts=n-2*np.sqrt(R/I2[nm]); dtp=dts-(dcs-dcp)     # shift both by the same amount
    p2=4*R/(n-dts)**2-4*R/(n-dtp)**2
    a=abs(p1-obs)/obs*100; b=abs(p2-obs)/obs*100; e1.append(a); e2.append(b)
    print(f"  {nm:<6}{p1:>11.3f}{p2:>12.3f}{obs:>9.3f}{a:>13.1f}{b:>14.1f}")
print(f"\n  count-derived δ : mean error {np.mean(e1):.1f}%")
print(f"  true ionic δ    : mean error {np.mean(e2):.1f}%")
EOF
