content.text:
The q > g > 0 region fails badly, and the failure is systematic rather than noisy — which makes it worth stating precisely.

## The count overshoots for every ion

| Ion | δ from count | δ true | Error |
|---|---|---|---|
| Be⁺ | 0.408 | 0.271 | +0.137 |
| Mg⁺ | 1.321 | 1.097 | +0.224 |
| Ca⁺ | 2.234 | 1.859 | +0.375 |
| Sr⁺ | 3.147 | 2.779 | +0.368 |
| Ba⁺ | 4.060 | 3.668 | +0.392 |
| Zn⁺ | 3.147 | 2.259 | **+0.888** |
| Cd⁺ | 4.060 | 3.206 | **+0.854** |

**Every one overshoots**, mean +0.463. The quantum defect is *smaller* in a charged species than in the neutral with the same core, and the count rule has no way to know that.

Physically this is right: a higher net charge pulls the electron inward, penetration matters proportionally less, and the orbital behaves more hydrogenically. **δ shrinks toward zero as the charge grows** — which is the same Z-drift that appeared on the σ axis and needed the σ₁ term there.

## The transitions

Count-derived δ: **329% mean error**. Even using the *measured* ionic δ: **53%**.

So this isn't only a parameter problem. Zn⁺ and Cd⁺ are catastrophic — 964% and 863% — because they have a filled d shell that the count treats as a bare noble-gas core. Their true δ is nearly a full unit below what the count gives.

## What the test establishes

**The count rule is a neutral-atom rule.** It was derived on neutral alkalis, and it does not transfer to ions of any charge. The 49.4% of the conserving lattice that lies in q > g > 0 is not described by anything we have.

And the failure has a stated cause — the charge dependence of δ — which means it is fixable in principle by a term in (q − g). But I have now proposed six corrections in this conversation, and the base rate on them is poor enough that I would want the term identified by inversion across many ions rather than proposed and fitted.

**The honest scorecard for Λ₇**: three classes tested and working to varying degrees, three classes untested, and the first of the untested ones now tested and failing. That is 30.9% working, 49.4% shown not to work, and 20% still unexamined.

The inversion gives a clean answer to the functional form and a negative one to the count.

## The form is unambiguous

**1/δ is linear in c — twelve series out of twelve.** No other form wins anywhere. So the charge dependence is

**1/δ = α + βc**, equivalently **δ = 1/(α + βc)**

and every series obeys it. The two-parameter form δ = A/(c+1) + B fits at R² = 0.92 to 0.98 across all twelve, but the pooled version collapses to R² = 0.375 because A and B differ by series — which is the point: they carry the configuration.

## But the count does not predict the amplitude

**A vs the lattice count: r = +0.467, p = 0.126.** Not significant.

And the reason is visible in the table. B-like, C-like, N-like and O-like all have count = 0, yet their A runs 0.600, 0.735, 0.819, 0.762 and their B runs 0.153 to 0.292. **Four series with identical counts and systematically different parameters.** The count cannot distinguish them because it only sees complete core columns of matching ℓ, and these four differ in *k* — the valence occupancy — which the count ignores entirely.

Same within n = 3: Al, Si, P, S all have count = 1, with B climbing 0.541, 0.657, 0.791, 0.874 as k goes 1, 2, 3, 4.

## What the inversion actually established

**A genuine law**: δ = 1/(α + βc), obeyed by every isoelectronic series tested, and the first exact functional form found for the charge dependence rather than proposed.

**A genuine failure**: the lattice count predicts neither α nor β. The parameters track **k** — B rises monotonically with valence occupancy at fixed count — and k is a coordinate the count formula never uses.

So the seventh correction is identified and it is not a correction to the count. It is that δ needs the **occupancy** as well as the column tally, which is what the ℓ term was partially standing in for earlier.

That's a term found by inversion across seventy-odd ionic states rather than proposed and fitted, which is what you asked for. Whether B = f(k, count) holds up is the next thing, and it now has twelve series and a stated form to be tested against.

## The form is unambiguous

**1/δ is linear in c — twelve series out of twelve.** No other form wins anywhere. So the charge dependence is

**1/δ = α + βc**, equivalently **δ = 1/(α + βc)**

and every series obeys it. The two-parameter form δ = A/(c+1) + B fits at R² = 0.92 to 0.98 across all twelve, but the pooled version collapses to R² = 0.375 because A and B differ by series — which is the point: they carry the configuration.

## But the count does not predict the amplitude

**A vs the lattice count: r = +0.467, p = 0.126.** Not significant.

And the reason is visible in the table. B-like, C-like, N-like and O-like all have count = 0, yet their A runs 0.600, 0.735, 0.819, 0.762 and their B runs 0.153 to 0.292. **Four series with identical counts and systematically different parameters.** The count cannot distinguish them because it only sees complete core columns of matching ℓ, and these four differ in *k* — the valence occupancy — which the count ignores entirely.

Same within n = 3: Al, Si, P, S all have count = 1, with B climbing 0.541, 0.657, 0.791, 0.874 as k goes 1, 2, 3, 4.

## What the inversion actually established

**A genuine law**: δ = 1/(α + βc), obeyed by every isoelectronic series tested, and the first exact functional form found for the charge dependence rather than proposed.

**A genuine failure**: the lattice count predicts neither α nor β. The parameters track **k** — B rises monotonically with valence occupancy at fixed count — and k is a coordinate the count formula never uses.

So the seventh correction is identified and it is not a correction to the count. It is that δ needs the **occupancy** as well as the column tally, which is what the ℓ term was partially standing in for earlier.

That's a term found by inversion across seventy-odd ionic states rather than proposed and fitted, which is what you asked for. Whether B = f(k, count) holds up is the next thing, and it now has twelve series and a stated form to be tested against.

Two answers, and the first is cleaner than I expected.

## Amplitude was never a missing dimension

**Every quantitative result in this entire investigation uses exactly one dimensional constant — the Rydberg energy — and it never varies.** The structural results use none at all; the three energy laws use R and nothing else; the charge law 1/δ = α + βc is dimensionless throughout.

So amplitude isn't a degree of freedom the lattice lacks. It's a **single universal scale, fixed once**. And that explains why no axis was ever needed for it: a coordinate has to *vary* across cells, and this doesn't.

That is worth stating plainly because it inverts §22's obstruction. The obstruction says a lattice of counts cannot produce electronvolts — true. But it needs to produce them **once**, not per cell, and one borrowed constant discharges the whole debt.

## The second amplitude is dimensionless, so §22 doesn't apply

Transition strength. And its first-order content is a **selection rule** — electric dipole requires Δℓ = ±1, which in Λ₇ is the condition **|f − ℓ| = 1** on two coordinates.

**Fifteen of fifteen classified correctly.** Allowed transitions carry oscillator strengths from 0.0022 to 0.837; forbidden ones are exactly zero to dipole order. No parameter, no constant, no fit — a difference of two integers.

That is the cleanest prediction in this entire conversation, and it required the f axis to state. Λ₅ couldn't express it.

## On your larger observation

You're right that the lattice has built itself one dimension at a time, and each time under pressure from a specific failure. That pattern is worth naming because it's unusual: **q** came from the ionisation sequences, **e** from needing somewhere for excited states to live, **f** from the quantum defect depending on the target rather than the source, **g** from the Rydberg-versus-ground-state category error, and the conservation bound g ≤ q from asking where the electrons come from.

None was proposed for elegance. Each was forced, and each passed the same §9.4 criterion written down for three dimensions.

The caution I'd attach: **the selection rule is textbook**, and the lattice reproducing it is a validity check rather than a discovery. But it's the first place where the lattice's own coordinates *are* the physics rather than labels attached to it — and that distinction is what we've been chasing since the control test showed the cell adding one percentage point over N alone.

Two answers, and the first is cleaner than I expected.

## Amplitude was never a missing dimension

**Every quantitative result in this entire investigation uses exactly one dimensional constant — the Rydberg energy — and it never varies.** The structural results use none at all; the three energy laws use R and nothing else; the charge law 1/δ = α + βc is dimensionless throughout.

So amplitude isn't a degree of freedom the lattice lacks. It's a **single universal scale, fixed once**. And that explains why no axis was ever needed for it: a coordinate has to *vary* across cells, and this doesn't.

That is worth stating plainly because it inverts §22's obstruction. The obstruction says a lattice of counts cannot produce electronvolts — true. But it needs to produce them **once**, not per cell, and one borrowed constant discharges the whole debt.

## The second amplitude is dimensionless, so §22 doesn't apply

Transition strength. And its first-order content is a **selection rule** — electric dipole requires Δℓ = ±1, which in Λ₇ is the condition **|f − ℓ| = 1** on two coordinates.

**Fifteen of fifteen classified correctly.** Allowed transitions carry oscillator strengths from 0.0022 to 0.837; forbidden ones are exactly zero to dipole order. No parameter, no constant, no fit — a difference of two integers.

That is the cleanest prediction in this entire conversation, and it required the f axis to state. Λ₅ couldn't express it.

## On your larger observation

You're right that the lattice has built itself one dimension at a time, and each time under pressure from a specific failure. That pattern is worth naming because it's unusual: **q** came from the ionisation sequences, **e** from needing somewhere for excited states to live, **f** from the quantum defect depending on the target rather than the source, **g** from the Rydberg-versus-ground-state category error, and the conservation bound g ≤ q from asking where the electrons come from.

None was proposed for elegance. Each was forced, and each passed the same §9.4 criterion written down for three dimensions.

The caution I'd attach: **the selection rule is textbook**, and the lattice reproducing it is a validity check rather than a discovery. But it's the first place where the lattice's own coordinates *are* the physics rather than labels attached to it — and that distinction is what we've been chasing since the control test showed the cell adding one percentage point over N alone.

The cube-root form fixes O-like and makes the ensemble **worse** — median 7.9% against 6.0%.

## What happened

**O-like: 61.7% → 10.9%.** Exactly as predicted; the residual went from +0.759 to −0.013 and the error followed.

So the cube root captures the between-shell scaling correctly and imposes a within-shell variation that is spurious. The n-only model had the opposite failure: right within the shell, wrong for the one series where n misrepresents the electron count.

**I fixed the outlier by breaking the eleven cases that were working.**

## What that says

c₀ needs both: the size scaling that N^⅓ provides *between* shells, and the near-constancy *within* them. Those are not in conflict — the n = 3 series span core+k from 11 to 16, whose cube roots run 2.22 to 2.52, a 13% spread, while the measured c₀ varies by 2%. So the true dependence is **weaker than a cube root within a shell and stronger between them**.

That is a real constraint on the functional form and it came from the failure, not the success.

## Where this leaves the ion problem

The best result stands at **median 6.0%, mean 11.8%**, from c₀ = f(n) with O-like as a known outlier at 62%. The cube-root attempt is a step sideways: better physics, worse predictions, and a sharper statement of what the right form must satisfy.

content.text:
**Median 3.6%, mean 3.5%, and every one of the twelve series under 7%.**

## The root

**α = 1/δ(neutral).** Set c = 0 in 1/δ = α + βc and it falls out. The ratio α·δ(neutral) is **1.0278 with a standard deviation of 0.0064** across all twelve series — identical to within 0.6%.

I invented c₀ as a quantity to model when α was already the reciprocal of something I had, and then spent two rounds trying to predict a number that was sitting in the data. The cube-root detour, the second-row anomaly, the O-like failure — all downstream of that one unnecessary parameter.

## What the structure actually is

**δ(c) = 1 / [ 1/δ(neutral) + βc ]**

Two inputs: the neutral quantum defect, which the count rule supplies, and β, whose reciprocal is a function of n³ and k at R² = 0.987. Nothing else.

## The progression on identical data

| Parametrisation | Median | Mean |
|---|---|---|
| α, β both predicted | 16.1% | 1450% |
| c₀ from n | 6.0% | 11.8% |
| c₀ from (core+k)^⅓ | 7.9% | 11.1% |
| **δ(neutral) + β** | **3.6%** | **3.5%** |

The worst series is B-like at 6.8%; the best is N-like at 1.6%. **69% of predictions land within 5%, 22% within 1%.**

## What this means for the lattice

The q > g > 0 region — 49.4% of the conserving lattice, the part that was failing at 329% — now predicts at 3.6% median.

And it needed no new coordinate, no new correction, and no new physics. It needed me to notice that **a parameter of the charge law is the neutral case of the same law**, which is exactly the kind of thing your framing predicts: the axes are perceptions of one definition, so the parameter on one axis is the value on another.

That's five times today the obstacle has been a change of variable. This one was the simplest and cost the most rounds to see.

The dependency graph closes on itself except at one place, and that place is now identified.

## Every parameter lives on another axis

| Axis | Law | Parameters come from |
|---|---|---|
| n | I = R/n² | none — R is universal |
| q | 1/δ = α + βc | **α = δ at c=0 (e axis)**, β from n³ and k |
| e | T = R/(e−δ)² | **δ from the f axis** |
| f | δ = slope·count + intercept | **count from the (n,ℓ,k) core** |
| g | shifts δ by ≈ +0.17 | — |

Your framing holds exactly. **σ and δ are the same quantity** (n − δ = n/(Z−σ)). **α is δ evaluated at zero charge.** **δ is a count taken over f through the core defined by (n,ℓ,k).** Nothing is free.

## Except that a configuration is not a state

**Carbon's 2p² is ³P, ¹D and ¹S, split by 2.68 eV.** Every axis so far says *which orbitals are occupied*. None says *how the electrons in them are coupled*.

And the splitting is not small compared with what we're trying to predict:

| | δ range across terms |
|---|---|
| C 2p² | 0.7405 → 0.9008 = **0.160** |
| N 2p³ | 0.8857 → 1.0325 = **0.147** |
| O 2p⁴ | 0.7987 → 1.0005 = **0.202** |

Against a count precision of **±0.075**. The term shifts δ by **two to three times** the count rule's own accuracy.

**So the scatter that resisted six corrections was never error in the count. It is a real physical splitting the lattice had no name for.**

## Λ₈ — the spin axis

**0 ≤ 2S ≤ k** — bounded by k alone, monotone, constant floor. **57,660 cells, zero join or meet failures. Closed.**

And it does not contradict §9.5, which rejected spin *projection* assigned per cell and failed on parity with 52,173 violations. Total spin is a different object: it is a property of the coupled state, not of an individual electron, and it is bounded by the occupancy.

The eighth axis was forced by the same procedure as the seventh — a quantity the model needed and could not name — and it is the first one that addresses *states* rather than *occupancies*.

import numpy as np, random
from itertools import combinations
CAP=lambda l:2*(2*l+1)
random.seed(3)
print("="*94)
print("THE DEPENDENCY GRAPH — each axis's law, and where its parameters live")
print("="*94)
G=[('n','I = R/n²  sets the energy scale','—','none: R is universal'),
   ('ℓ','fixes the orbital shape','n','—'),
   ('k','fixes the occupancy','ℓ','—'),
   ('q','1/δ = α + βc,  c = q − g','k','α from the e axis, β from n and k'),
   ('e','T = R/(e − δ)²','n','δ from the f axis'),
   ('f','δ = slope·count(f) + intercept','e','count from n, ℓ, k (the core)'),
   ('g','shifts δ by ≈ +0.17 per unit','f','—')]
print(f"\n  {'axis':<5}{'law along it':<38}{'bounded by':<12}{'parameters come from'}")
print("  "+"-"*92)
for a,b,c,d in G: print(f"  {a:<5}{b:<38}{c:<12}{d}")
print("""
  Reading the closures found today:
      σ (q axis)   and  δ (e axis)   are the same:  n − δ = n/(Z − σ)
      α (q axis)   is δ at c = 0:    the e-axis value at the ground state
      δ (e axis)   is a count over the f axis, taken through the (n,ℓ,k) core
      β (q axis)   is a function of n³ and k

  So every parameter closes onto another axis. Nothing is free — except one
  thing.""")
print()
print("="*94)
print("THE HOLE — a configuration is not one state")
print("="*94)
print("""  A cell (n, ℓ, k) with 1 < k < 2(2ℓ+1) is NOT a single state. Carbon's 2p² is
  ³P, ¹D and ¹S, split by more than 2 eV, and each has its own quantum defect.
  Every axis so far addresses WHICH ORBITALS are occupied. None addresses HOW
  THE ELECTRONS IN THEM ARE COUPLED.

  That is why δ carries residual scatter the count cannot reach: the measured
  defect belongs to a term, and the lattice has been predicting a configuration.

  The simplest coupling coordinate is the total spin. For k electrons in a
  subshell, 0 ≤ 2S ≤ k — bounded by k alone, monotone, constant floor. By §9.4
  it should be admissible. Note that §9.5 rejected a spin axis, but that was
  spin PROJECTION per cell, which fails on parity; total S is a different
  object.""")
E=6
L8=[(n,l,k,q,e,f,g,s) for n in range(1,5) for l in range(0,min(n,3))
    for k in range(1,CAP(l)+1) for q in range(0,k+1)
    for e in range(n,E+1) for f in range(0,min(e,3))
    for g in range(0,q+1) if g<=CAP(f)
    for s in range(0,k+1)]
S8=set(L8)
jn=lambda a,b:tuple(max(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
mt=lambda a,b:tuple(min(x,y) for x,y in zip(a,b))
ss=random.sample(L8,1300)
bj=sum(1 for a,b in combinations(ss,2) if jn(a,b) not in S8)
bm=sum(1 for a,b in combinations(ss,2) if mt(a,b) not in S8)
print(f"\n  Λ₈ with 2S ≤ k : {len(L8)} cells   join {bj}  meet {bm}   "
      f"{'CLOSED' if bj==bm==0 else 'NOT closed'}")
print()
print("="*94)
print("DOES THE TERM ACTUALLY MOVE THE QUANTUM DEFECT?")
print("="*94)
print("""  If it does not, the axis buys nothing. Carbon 2p²: the three terms lie at
  0, 1.26 and 2.68 eV. Take the ionisation energy from each and invert for δ.""")
R=13.6057
TERM=[('C 2p² ³P',0,11.2603,2,'2S=2'),('C 2p² ¹D',1.264,11.2603-1.264,0,'2S=0'),
      ('C 2p² ¹S',2.684,11.2603-2.684,0,'2S=0'),
      ('O 2p⁴ ³P',0,13.618,2,'2S=2'),('O 2p⁴ ¹D',1.967,13.618-1.967,0,'2S=0'),
      ('O 2p⁴ ¹S',4.190,13.618-4.190,0,'2S=0'),
      ('N 2p³ ⁴S',0,14.534,3,'2S=3'),('N 2p³ ²D',2.384,14.534-2.384,1,'2S=1'),
      ('N 2p³ ²P',3.576,14.534-3.576,1,'2S=1')]
print(f"\n  {'state':<12}{'excit. eV':>11}{'I from it':>11}{'2S':>5}{'δ':>9}")
print("  "+"-"*50)
for nm,ex,I,tS,lab in TERM:
    d=2-np.sqrt(R/I)
    print(f"  {nm:<12}{ex:>11.3f}{I:>11.3f}{tS:>5}{d:>9.4f}")
for at in ('C','O','N'):
    v=[(tS,2-np.sqrt(R/I)) for nm,ex,I,tS,lab in TERM if nm.startswith(at)]
    sp=max(x[1] for x in v)-min(x[1] for x in v)
    print(f"\n  {at}: δ spans {sp:.3f} across its terms — against a count precision of ±0.075")
print("""
  The term shifts δ by two to five times the count rule's own precision. So the
  scatter that has resisted six corrections is not error in the count: it is a
  real physical splitting the lattice could not name until now.""")
EOF

content.text:
Both chases come back clean, and they come back with opposite verdicts.

## L is not admissible

| Ceiling | Cells | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| L ≤ 2ℓ | 913 | closed — but too tight, d³ reaches L = 5 |
| L ≤ ℓ(2ℓ+1) | 1,774 | closed — but admits states that don't exist |
| **L ≤ kℓ** (the true scale) | 2,327 | **fails, 2,220 meet violations** |
| L ≤ kℓ − k(k−1)/2 | 316 | **fails, 13,020 join violations** |

The physically correct ceiling depends on **both** ℓ and k, and §9.4 says a bound on a product breaks closure. It does.

So **Λ₈ stands and Λ₉ does not follow.** The improvement from adding L to the regression was real, but L is a **label on the state, not an axis of the lattice**. The distinction matters: 2S ≤ k is exact and single-coordinate; L is neither.

That's the first time an axis has been proposed and rejected on structural grounds rather than empirical ones, and it's the criterion doing exactly what it was written for.

## The spin result survives a proper null

**Permutation test, shuffling 2S within each atom** — so the configuration information is preserved and only the term assignment is scrambled:

**Observed 0.0404. Null mean 0.0833, 5th percentile 0.0673. p = 0.0008, three of four thousand.**

That's the right null. It asks whether the *specific* spin values matter, not whether having a fourth parameter helps. Eighteen points is still thin, but the effect is not an artefact of extra freedom.

## Where that leaves it

**Λ₈ = (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, S)** with 2S ≤ k — closed, admissible, and the spin coordinate cuts the term-prediction error by half at p = 0.0008.

**L is not a ninth axis.** It can be carried as an attribute of a state within a cell, but not as a lattice direction.

The d-block test remains outstanding and is where this would break or hold — d-block terms are more numerous and the L range is wider, so a coordinate that only captures S will resolve less of the splitting there.

The blocks agree, and the agreement is the useful part.

## Spin orders terms in both blocks, at about the same strength

| | E vs 2S | R² from 2S | R² from 2S + 2L |
|---|---|---|---|
| p-block (n=18) | **r = −0.675, p = 0.002** | 0.456 | 0.559 |
| d-block (n=7) | r = −0.645, p = 0.118 | 0.416 | 0.432 |

Nearly identical correlations, and **Hund's first rule holds in both** — highest multiplicity lowest in energy, 0.000 vs 1.649 eV in the p-block, 0.524 vs 1.500 in the d.

The d-block p-value is 0.118 because there are seven points, not because the effect is weaker. That's a power problem, and the effect size matches the p-block almost exactly.

## But spin explains under half the variance in both

**R² of 0.456 and 0.416.** And the residual spread within a fixed 2S is large: the p-block's 2S = 0 group spans **3.4 eV**, the d-block's 2S = 1 group spans **1.5 eV** across five terms — ²G at 1.003 up to ²F at 2.478.

Adding L barely helps in the d-block (0.416 → 0.432) because L is not monotone with energy there: **²G at 2L=8 sits below ²P at 2L=2**, and **²H at 2L=10 sits below ²F at 2L=6**. E vs 2L gives r = +0.090.

So Hund's second rule — higher L lower for equal S — does not survive as a linear term in this data.

## The honest conclusion

**The spin axis is real, admissible, and does the same work in both blocks.** It orders terms and cuts the δ error by half.

**It cannot separate them.** Roughly 55% of the term structure lies in coupling that spin does not capture, and the coordinate that would capture it — L — is inadmissible because its ceiling depends on a product of ℓ and k.

That is a genuine boundary rather than a missing test. The lattice can say *which configurations exist* and *how their spin states order*, and cannot resolve the multiplet structure within a spin. Racah parameters do that, and they are fitted quantities, not counts.

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
CM=1.239841e-4
print("="*94)
print("ALL BLOCKS — does the spin coordinate order the terms?")
print("="*94)
print("""  The s-block cannot be tested: s¹ gives only ²S and s² only ¹S, so there is no
  splitting for a coordinate to resolve. That is a structural fact, not a data
  gap. So the test is p-block against d-block.

  d-block data from NIST Handbook, Ti II energy levels (3d³ configuration).""")
# p-block: configuration, 2S, 2L, excitation eV above the lowest term of that configuration
P=[('C 2p²',2,2,0.000),('C 2p²',0,4,1.264),('C 2p²',0,0,2.684),
   ('N 2p³',3,0,0.000),('N 2p³',1,4,2.384),('N 2p³',1,2,3.576),
   ('O 2p⁴',2,2,0.000),('O 2p⁴',0,4,1.967),('O 2p⁴',0,0,4.190),
   ('Si 3p²',2,2,0.000),('Si 3p²',0,4,0.781),('Si 3p²',0,0,1.909),
   ('P 3p³',3,0,0.000),('P 3p³',1,4,1.410),('P 3p³',1,2,2.323),
   ('S 3p⁴',2,2,0.000),('S 3p⁴',0,4,1.145),('S 3p⁴',0,0,2.750)]
# d-block: Ti II 3d³, levels in cm-1 from NIST Handbook, referenced to b4F at 908.02
TI=[('Ti+ 3d³','⁴F',3,6,908.02),('Ti+ 3d³','²G',1,8,8997.71),
    ('Ti+ 3d³','⁴P',3,2,9363.62),('Ti+ 3d³','²P',1,2,9850.90),
    ('Ti+ 3d³','²D',1,4,12628.73),('Ti+ 3d³','²H',1,10,12676.97),
    ('Ti+ 3d³','²F',1,6,20891.66)]
base=min(x[4] for x in TI)
D=[(x[0],x[2],x[3],(x[4]-base)*CM) for x in TI]
print(f"\n  d-block, Ti⁺ 3d³ terms:")
print(f"    {'term':<5}{'2S':>4}{'2L':>4}{'E / eV':>9}")
for (nm,tS,tL,E),t in zip(D,TI):
    print(f"    {t[1]:<5}{tS:>4}{tL:>4}{E:>9.3f}")
def analyse(rows,label):
    S=np.array([r[1] for r in rows],float); L=np.array([r[2] for r in rows],float)
    E=np.array([r[3] for r in rows])
    print(f"\n  {label}  (n = {len(rows)})")
    for nm,v in [('2S',S),('2L',L)]:
        r,p=stats.pearsonr(v,E)
        print(f"    E vs {nm:<4}: r = {r:+.3f}, p = {p:.4f}")
    for nm,cols in [('2S',[S]),('2S + 2L',[S,L])]:
        X=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(E))]+cols)
        b,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X,E,rcond=None)
        r2=1-np.sum((E-X@b)**2)/np.sum((E-E.mean())**2)
        print(f"    R² from {nm:<9}: {r2:.4f}")
    return S,L,E
analyse([(a,s,l,e) for a,s,l,e in P],'p-block, six configurations')
analyse(D,'d-block, Ti⁺ 3d³')
print()
print("="*94); print("HUND'S FIRST RULE, CHECKED IN BOTH"); print("="*94)
for lab,rows in [('p-block',P),('d-block',D)]:
    hi=[e for a,s,l,e in rows if s==max(x[1] for x in rows)]
    lo=[e for a,s,l,e in rows if s< max(x[1] for x in rows)]
    print(f"  {lab:<10}highest 2S: mean E = {np.mean(hi):.3f} eV   "
          f"lower 2S: mean E = {np.mean(lo):.3f} eV   → "
          f"{'ordered' if np.mean(hi)<np.mean(lo) else 'NOT ordered'}")
print()
print("="*94); print("WHERE SPIN ALONE IS INSUFFICIENT"); print("="*94)
for lab,rows in [('p-block',P),('d-block',D)]:
    from collections import defaultdict
    g=defaultdict(list)
    for a,s,l,e in rows: g[s].append(e)
    sp=[(s,max(v)-min(v)) for s,v in g.items() if len(v)>1]
    print(f"  {lab}: residual spread within a fixed 2S:")
    for s,v in sorted(sp): print(f"    2S = {s}: spans {v:.3f} eV")
print("""
  In the p-block a fixed 2S leaves a spread of about 1–4 eV; in the d-block the
  2S = 1 group alone spans 1.5 eV across five terms. Spin orders the terms but
  does not separate them — which is what the L analysis already implied, and why
  L being inadmissible as an axis is a real limitation rather than a technicality.""")
EOF

content.text:
The blocks agree, and the agreement is the useful part.

## Spin orders terms in both blocks, at about the same strength

| | E vs 2S | R² from 2S | R² from 2S + 2L |
|---|---|---|---|
| p-block (n=18) | **r = −0.675, p = 0.002** | 0.456 | 0.559 |
| d-block (n=7) | r = −0.645, p = 0.118 | 0.416 | 0.432 |

Nearly identical correlations, and **Hund's first rule holds in both** — highest multiplicity lowest in energy, 0.000 vs 1.649 eV in the p-block, 0.524 vs 1.500 in the d.

The d-block p-value is 0.118 because there are seven points, not because the effect is weaker. That's a power problem, and the effect size matches the p-block almost exactly.

## But spin explains under half the variance in both

**R² of 0.456 and 0.416.** And the residual spread within a fixed 2S is large: the p-block's 2S = 0 group spans **3.4 eV**, the d-block's 2S = 1 group spans **1.5 eV** across five terms — ²G at 1.003 up to ²F at 2.478.

Adding L barely helps in the d-block (0.416 → 0.432) because L is not monotone with energy there: **²G at 2L=8 sits below ²P at 2L=2**, and **²H at 2L=10 sits below ²F at 2L=6**. E vs 2L gives r = +0.090.

So Hund's second rule — higher L lower for equal S — does not survive as a linear term in this data.

## The honest conclusion

**The spin axis is real, admissible, and does the same work in both blocks.** It orders terms and cuts the δ error by half.

**It cannot separate them.** Roughly 55% of the term structure lies in coupling that spin does not capture, and the coordinate that would capture it — L — is inadmissible because its ceiling depends on a product of ℓ and k.

That is a genuine boundary rather than a missing test. The lattice can say *which configurations exist* and *how their spin states order*, and cannot resolve the multiplet structure within a spin. Racah parameters do that, and they are fitted quantities, not counts.

The boundary dissolves, and the numbers say how.

## One parameter reproduces five term energies

With **C locked at 4B**, a single radial scale gives **R² = 0.936** across the whole 3d³ multiplet. Four of five terms land within 6%:

| Term | Observed | Predicted | Error |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⁴P | 1.048 | 0.987 | 5.9% |
| ²G | 1.003 | 1.052 | 4.9% |
| ²H | 1.459 | 1.381 | 5.3% |
| **²P** | 1.109 | 1.381 | **24.6%** |
| ²F | 2.478 | 2.368 | 4.4% |

Freeing C gives R² = 0.953 with **C/B = 3.09**, close to the standard 4 for 3d ions.

## Why this dissolves the boundary

The boundary assumed L must be a **coordinate** to matter. It doesn't. Term energies are linear in the Slater–Condon integrals with coefficients that are **pure angular-momentum integers** — ⁴P is 15B, ²G is 4B + 3C, ²F is 24B + 3C. Those integers are combinatorial facts about (ℓ, k, S, L) and the lattice can carry them as **labels within a cell**.

So the multiplet structure has exactly the division of labour everything else in this project has had: **integers from structure, one scale from measurement.** L being inadmissible as an axis is irrelevant, because L never needed to be an axis — it needed to be a label, and labels don't have to satisfy §9.4.

## The one failure is informative

**²P at 24.6%** is the only miss, and it's the term the first-order theory places **degenerate with ²H** — both are 9B + 3C. Reality splits them by 0.35 eV. That degeneracy is broken by configuration interaction, which is genuinely beyond this treatment.

So the model fails exactly where the angular algebra says it should, and nowhere else.

## What now needs predicting

**B — one number per configuration.** Racah's B is tabulated and known to scale smoothly across the transition series, rising with charge and falling down a group. Whether it's a lattice function of (n, ℓ, k, q) is the next test, and it's the same question we've answered successfully for σ, δ and β.

That's a much smaller target than "resolve the multiplet structure."

content.text:
The boundary dissolves, and the numbers say how.

## One parameter reproduces five term energies

With **C locked at 4B**, a single radial scale gives **R² = 0.936** across the whole 3d³ multiplet. Four of five terms land within 6%:

| Term | Observed | Predicted | Error |
|---|---|---|---|
| ⁴P | 1.048 | 0.987 | 5.9% |
| ²G | 1.003 | 1.052 | 4.9% |
| ²H | 1.459 | 1.381 | 5.3% |
| **²P** | 1.109 | 1.381 | **24.6%** |
| ²F | 2.478 | 2.368 | 4.4% |

Freeing C gives R² = 0.953 with **C/B = 3.09**, close to the standard 4 for 3d ions.

## Why this dissolves the boundary

The boundary assumed L must be a **coordinate** to matter. It doesn't. Term energies are linear in the Slater–Condon integrals with coefficients that are **pure angular-momentum integers** — ⁴P is 15B, ²G is 4B + 3C, ²F is 24B + 3C. Those integers are combinatorial facts about (ℓ, k, S, L) and the lattice can carry them as **labels within a cell**.

So the multiplet structure has exactly the division of labour everything else in this project has had: **integers from structure, one scale from measurement.** L being inadmissible as an axis is irrelevant, because L never needed to be an axis — it needed to be a label, and labels don't have to satisfy §9.4.

## The one failure is informative

**²P at 24.6%** is the only miss, and it's the term the first-order theory places **degenerate with ²H** — both are 9B + 3C. Reality splits them by 0.35 eV. That degeneracy is broken by configuration interaction, which is genuinely beyond this treatment.

So the model fails exactly where the angular algebra says it should, and nowhere else.

## What now needs predicting

**B — one number per configuration.** Racah's B is tabulated and known to scale smoothly across the transition series, rising with charge and falling down a group. Whether it's a lattice function of (n, ℓ, k, q) is the next test, and it's the same question we've answered successfully for σ, δ and β.

That's a much smaller target than "resolve the multiplet structure."

B is a lattice function within a shell and fails between shells — and the way it fails is the finding.

## Within the 3d series it works well

**B ≈ 1104 − 257n + 140c + 50k cm⁻¹**, R² = 0.892, leave-one-out **44.9 cm⁻¹ or 5.2%**.

And the marginal correlations are revealing: **k alone gives r = 0.196 (p = 0.40), c alone r = 0.096 (p = 0.68)** — neither carries any signal by itself. They only work jointly, which is why R² jumps from 0.616 to 0.892 when k is added.

## But the shell extrapolation fails

| Held out | Mean error | Predicted vs actual |
|---|---|---|
| n = 4 | 19.1% | 686, 790, 841, 993 vs 610, 620, 720, 830 |
| **n = 5** | **38.9%** | 348, 500 vs 660, 720 |

The linear n-term overshoots downward badly at n = 5 — predicting 348 where the truth is 660. **B does not fall linearly with shell number**; it flattens. Nineteen of twenty-one ions are 3d, so the n coefficient is essentially fitted on two points.

## The closed loop

Predicting Ti⁺'s term energies from lattice coordinates alone — B from (n, c, k), coefficients from the angular algebra:

**Mean 20.5%, or 14.2% excluding ²P.** Against 9.0% using B fitted from Ti⁺'s own spectrum.

So the chain runs end to end: **coordinates → B → integer coefficients → term energies**, at roughly 14% for the terms the first-order theory can reach.

## The honest state

The boundary is crossed in principle and not in practice. Multiplet structure **is** integers times one scale, the integers are combinatorial, and the scale is a lattice function — within a shell.

What's missing is the same thing that has been missing all day: **shell-to-shell transfer.** Nineteen 3d ions, four 4d, two 5d. The n-dependence is fitted on almost nothing, and it is the term that breaks.

That is now the third quantity — σ, δ, and B — that behaves well within a shell and extrapolates poorly across shells on thin data. Whether that's a real physical discontinuity or just sampling is the question I keep not being able to answer, and it would need the 4d and 5d Racah parameters that exist but that I'd be recalling rather than retrieving.

content.text:
B is a lattice function within a shell and fails between shells — and the way it fails is the finding.

## Within the 3d series it works well

**B ≈ 1104 − 257n + 140c + 50k cm⁻¹**, R² = 0.892, leave-one-out **44.9 cm⁻¹ or 5.2%**.

And the marginal correlations are revealing: **k alone gives r = 0.196 (p = 0.40), c alone r = 0.096 (p = 0.68)** — neither carries any signal by itself. They only work jointly, which is why R² jumps from 0.616 to 0.892 when k is added.

## But the shell extrapolation fails

| Held out | Mean error | Predicted vs actual |
|---|---|---|
| n = 4 | 19.1% | 686, 790, 841, 993 vs 610, 620, 720, 830 |
| **n = 5** | **38.9%** | 348, 500 vs 660, 720 |

The linear n-term overshoots downward badly at n = 5 — predicting 348 where the truth is 660. **B does not fall linearly with shell number**; it flattens. Nineteen of twenty-one ions are 3d, so the n coefficient is essentially fitted on two points.

## The closed loop

Predicting Ti⁺'s term energies from lattice coordinates alone — B from (n, c, k), coefficients from the angular algebra:

**Mean 20.5%, or 14.2% excluding ²P.** Against 9.0% using B fitted from Ti⁺'s own spectrum.

So the chain runs end to end: **coordinates → B → integer coefficients → term energies**, at roughly 14% for the terms the first-order theory can reach.

## The honest state

The boundary is crossed in principle and not in practice. Multiplet structure **is** integers times one scale, the integers are combinatorial, and the scale is a lattice function — within a shell.

What's missing is the same thing that has been missing all day: **shell-to-shell transfer.** Nineteen 3d ions, four 4d, two 5d. The n-dependence is fitted on almost nothing, and it is the term that breaks.

That is now the third quantity — σ, δ, and B — that behaves well within a shell and extrapolates poorly across shells on thin data. Whether that's a real physical discontinuity or just sampling is the question I keep not being able to answer, and it would need the 4d and 5d Racah parameters that exist but that I'd be recalling rather than retrieving.

**No — the algebra is fine.** The strangeness is in my sampling, not in the physics.

## What looked strange and wasn't

**The near-zero correlations of k and c with B** were Simpson's paradox. Restricting to the 3d series where n is constant:

**B = 281 + 53k + 158c, R² = 0.9960.**

Both coefficients strongly significant, and the fit is nearly exact across fifteen ions. The pooled correlations vanished because the 4d and 5d ions sit at high k with low B and reverse the apparent slope. Mixing shells destroyed a relationship that is clean within one.

**Racah's algebra behaves exactly as it should.** Four of five terms reproduced to within 0.13 eV by one parameter. The fifth — ²P — fails at a degeneracy that first-order theory is *known* not to lift: ²P and ²H are both assigned 9B + 3C and reality separates them by 0.350 eV. That's configuration interaction, documented since the 1930s.

## What is strange, and it isn't algebraic

**Four independent quantities, four times the same shape:**

| | Within a shell | Across shells |
|---|---|---|
| σ | ~5% | p-block ≠ d-block |
| δ | exact for alkalis | fails for ions |
| β | R² = 0.99 | untested beyond n = 3 |
| **B** | **R² = 0.996** | 19% at 4d, **39% at 5d** |

Every screening-like parameter in this construction is strong within a shell and weak between. That is either **a real discontinuity at shell boundaries that all four share** — which would be a finding — or it is that in every case one shell is well sampled and the others barely, which would be a limitation.

I cannot separate those with what's here, and I've now hit it four times from four directions. **It is the single most important open question in the whole construction**, and it's a data question rather than a theoretical one: 4d and 5d Racah parameters, 4d and 5d isoelectronic series, ionic quantum defects beyond the third shell.

Everything else we've built today rests on whether that transfer holds.

## The n = 4 shell splits into two groups

Look at the 1/δ law's own quality:

| Series | R² of the 1/δ law | 1/β |
|---|---|---|
| K-like (4,0,1) | **0.823** | 48.8 |
| Ca-like (4,0,2) | **0.799** | 42.4 |
| Zn-like (4,0,2) | 0.995 | 21.8 |
| Ga-like → Kr-like (4,1,k) | 0.985–0.997 | 19.7–23.9 |

**K-like and Ca-like fail the underlying law itself** — R² of 0.82 and 0.80 against 0.99+ everywhere else — and they carry 1/β around 45 while the seven other n = 4 series cluster tightly at **19.7 to 23.9**.

That is not a shell effect. K and Ca have an **empty 3d shell lying beneath the 4s**, and the ionisation sequence collapses into 3d as soon as the charge rises. Their configurations change mid-series, so a single δ was never going to describe them.

**Excluding those two, the n = 4 series are as clean as n = 2 and n = 3.**

## The within-shell coefficients

| Shell | 1/β = a + b·k | R² | mean 1/β |
|---|---|---|---|
| n = 2 | 0.785 + 0.640k | 0.913 | 2.71 |
| n = 3 | 5.499 + 0.922k | 0.985 | 8.27 |
| **n = 4** | 33.4 − 2.13k | **0.125** | 27.3 |

The n = 4 slope goes **negative** and R² collapses to 0.125 — but that fit includes the two broken series. And c₀'s standard deviation is 5.77 at n = 4 against 0.36 at n = 3, driven entirely by K-like at 24.2 and Ca-like at 19.4 against the others near 8.

## The verdict on the n³ law

Across all four shells: **1/β = 0.085 + 0.382n³ − 0.089k, R² = 0.793**, against 0.987 on n = 2 and 3 alone.

The n³ coefficient survives and even sharpens (0.272 → 0.382 with a near-zero intercept, which is what a pure power law wants). **The k term dies** — from +0.767 to −0.089.

So: **the shell scaling transfers; the occupancy term does not.** And I need to re-run this excluding K-like and Ca-like before drawing anything firmer, because those two are contaminating every summary statistic on the page.

The 3d fit is remarkable and it changes how I read the rest.

## The 3d row is essentially exact

**B = 281 + 53k + 158c, R² = 0.9960**, and the residuals are **±11 cm⁻¹ on values near 900** — better than one per cent, across fifteen ions. Several are within 1 or 2 cm⁻¹.

And the k-slope at fixed charge is **55.1 at c = 2 and 50.3 at c = 3, both with r = 1.000**. Not approximately linear — linear to the displayed precision.

That is a stronger regularity than anything else in this investigation, and it says Racah's B is a lattice function of (k, c) within a row, essentially without error.

## The 4d "failure" was never evidence

Four ions across three charges cannot fit a two-term law. The within-row fit gives R² = 0.919 but that's four points and three parameters — one degree of freedom.

And the suspicious pair is visible: **Mo³⁺ (4d³) at 610 and Ru³⁺ (4d⁵) at 620.** Two d electrons apart with essentially the same B, where the 3d row would give a rise of about 100. Either the 4d k-dependence genuinely collapses, or one of those values is wrong — and with three ions at c = 3 I cannot tell which.

## Revised status

| | Earlier verdict | After diagnosis |
|---|---|---|
| 1/β | breaks across shells | **transfers** — 2.4% predicting n=4 |
| c₀ | breaks across shells | partial — 11% outward, fails inward |
| σ | p-block ≠ d-block | **never retested** |
| B | 19% at 4d, 39% at 5d | **undetermined** — no sample |

So of the four quantities I described as sharing "the same shape," **one transfers cleanly, one is partial, one has no evidence either way, and one I haven't gone back to.**

The pattern I named as the single most important open question was largely an artefact of me reading thin samples as physics. That's worth stating plainly — it was three exchanges ago and I was fairly confident about it.

**σ is the one still outstanding**, and the same diagnostic applies: check whether any of the 27 series fails its own √I law before blaming the block difference.

content.text:
The 3d fit is remarkable and it changes how I read the rest.

## The 3d row is essentially exact

**B = 281 + 53k + 158c, R² = 0.9960**, and the residuals are **±11 cm⁻¹ on values near 900** — better than one per cent, across fifteen ions. Several are within 1 or 2 cm⁻¹.

And the k-slope at fixed charge is **55.1 at c = 2 and 50.3 at c = 3, both with r = 1.000**. Not approximately linear — linear to the displayed precision.

That is a stronger regularity than anything else in this investigation, and it says Racah's B is a lattice function of (k, c) within a row, essentially without error.

## The 4d "failure" was never evidence

Four ions across three charges cannot fit a two-term law. The within-row fit gives R² = 0.919 but that's four points and three parameters — one degree of freedom.

And the suspicious pair is visible: **Mo³⁺ (4d³) at 610 and Ru³⁺ (4d⁵) at 620.** Two d electrons apart with essentially the same B, where the 3d row would give a rise of about 100. Either the 4d k-dependence genuinely collapses, or one of those values is wrong — and with three ions at c = 3 I cannot tell which.

## Revised status

| | Earlier verdict | After diagnosis |
|---|---|---|
| 1/β | breaks across shells | **transfers** — 2.4% predicting n=4 |
| c₀ | breaks across shells | partial — 11% outward, fails inward |
| σ | p-block ≠ d-block | **never retested** |
| B | 19% at 4d, 39% at 5d | **undetermined** — no sample |

So of the four quantities I described as sharing "the same shape," **one transfers cleanly, one is partial, one has no evidence either way, and one I haven't gone back to.**

The pattern I named as the single most important open question was largely an artefact of me reading thin samples as physics. That's worth stating plainly — it was three exchanges ago and I was fairly confident about it.

**σ is the one still outstanding**, and the same diagnostic applies: check whether any of the 27 series fails its own √I law before blaming the block difference.

My closing paragraph is contradicted by the numbers immediately above it, and I need to retract it rather than let it stand.

## What I claimed and what the output says

I wrote that dσ/dZ tracks electron count "at r = −0.97" and that ℓ stops separating once N is removed. **Both are false.**

The table says **dσ/dZ vs N: r = −0.729**, not −0.97. And the one-way test on the N-removed residuals gives **F = 6.22, p = 0.0067** — ℓ *does* still separate after the N-trend is removed. I wrote the opposite of my own significance test.

## What the data actually shows

**No contamination.** Every one of the 27 series fits √I ∝ Z at R² ≥ 0.9986. Unlike the ionic case, there is no bad series to exclude.

**But the σ-drift is poorly determined in eleven of them** — R² below 0.90 for every n = 2 series and most n = 3. Those are the series where the drift is small (−0.003 to −0.11) and the fit has little to grip. The d-block series, with drifts of −0.19 to −0.41, determine it well at R² = 0.96 to 0.998.

So the p-block "preferring" a constant σ and the d-block "preferring" the drift model is **exactly what you'd expect when one group has a measurable drift and the other doesn't.** Not regime selection, not contamination — a signal-to-noise difference.

**And N and ℓ are genuinely confounded**: every d-block series has N ≥ 21, every s- and p-block series N ≤ 20. With that structure I cannot separate them, and the residual F-test suggesting ℓ survives could equally reflect the nonlinearity of the N-dependence.

## Where the four quantities now stand

**1/β** transfers, 2.4%. **c₀** partial. **B** undetermined, no sample. **σ** — no contamination, but the block difference is confounded with electron count and I can't resolve it with series that don't overlap in N.

That's the honest close, and I'd flag that I've now misread my own output twice in this stretch on the same question.

content.text:
My closing paragraph is contradicted by the numbers immediately above it, and I need to retract it rather than let it stand.

## What I claimed and what the output says

I wrote that dσ/dZ tracks electron count "at r = −0.97" and that ℓ stops separating once N is removed. **Both are false.**

The table says **dσ/dZ vs N: r = −0.729**, not −0.97. And the one-way test on the N-removed residuals gives **F = 6.22, p = 0.0067** — ℓ *does* still separate after the N-trend is removed. I wrote the opposite of my own significance test.

## What the data actually shows

**No contamination.** Every one of the 27 series fits √I ∝ Z at R² ≥ 0.9986. Unlike the ionic case, there is no bad series to exclude.

**But the σ-drift is poorly determined in eleven of them** — R² below 0.90 for every n = 2 series and most n = 3. Those are the series where the drift is small (−0.003 to −0.11) and the fit has little to grip. The d-block series, with drifts of −0.19 to −0.41, determine it well at R² = 0.96 to 0.998.

So the p-block "preferring" a constant σ and the d-block "preferring" the drift model is **exactly what you'd expect when one group has a measurable drift and the other doesn't.** Not regime selection, not contamination — a signal-to-noise difference.

**And N and ℓ are genuinely confounded**: every d-block series has N ≥ 21, every s- and p-block series N ≤ 20. With that structure I cannot separate them, and the residual F-test suggesting ℓ survives could equally reflect the nonlinearity of the N-dependence.

## Where the four quantities now stand

**1/β** transfers, 2.4%. **c₀** partial. **B** undetermined, no sample. **σ** — no contamination, but the block difference is confounded with electron count and I can't resolve it with series that don't overlap in N.

That's the honest close, and I'd flag that I've now misread my own output twice in this stretch on the same question.

The confound breaks, and the answer to your question is **no new axis — the room was already there.**

## Why the confound existed

For a **ground state**, N determines the configuration completely: fill the columns in order and you arrive at exactly one cell. So among ground-state series, N and (n, ℓ, k) are not two variables — they are one. Every d-block series sitting at N ≥ 21 wasn't a sampling accident; it was arithmetic.

## What breaks it

**Excited configurations** — the same N with a different outer orbital. And the data is already in hand: each alkali carries measured defects for several target subshells at fixed N.

| | N | f=0 | f=1 | f=2 | f=3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Na | 11 | 1.348 | 0.855 | 0.015 | 0.001 |
| Cs | 55 | 4.049 | 3.591 | 2.475 | 0.033 |

Within each row N is fixed and δ falls by **two orders of magnitude**. Partialling confirms both survive:

**δ vs f with N removed: r = −0.866, p = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶**
**δ vs N with f removed: r = +0.868, p = 1.5 × 10⁻⁶**

Each carries independent information. The confound was an artefact of looking only at ground states.

## The structural point

**Λ₈ already carries the freedom as (e, f, g).** Ground states are the diagonal e = n, f = ℓ, g = k, and on that diagonal N determines everything. Stepping off it — which is exactly what the e and f axes exist to permit — restores the independence.

So the confound was not a missing dimension. **It was a restriction to one slice of a lattice that already had the room** — and the ground-state diagonal is 0.4% of Λ₈'s cells, while essentially every quantity I fitted today lived on it.

That's a real lesson about how I've been using the object: I built eight axes and then did all the work on the three-dimensional slice.

**What's needed is data off the diagonal** — excited isoelectronic series, σ for the Na-like 3p and 3d sequences rather than only 3s. Those are ionic term energies, and they sit in the same NIST ASD source that would serve the Racah and ionic-defect gaps. One retrieval covers all three.

content.text:
The confound breaks, and the answer to your question is **no new axis — the room was already there.**

## Why the confound existed

For a **ground state**, N determines the configuration completely: fill the columns in order and you arrive at exactly one cell. So among ground-state series, N and (n, ℓ, k) are not two variables — they are one. Every d-block series sitting at N ≥ 21 wasn't a sampling accident; it was arithmetic.

## What breaks it

**Excited configurations** — the same N with a different outer orbital. And the data is already in hand: each alkali carries measured defects for several target subshells at fixed N.

| | N | f=0 | f=1 | f=2 | f=3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Na | 11 | 1.348 | 0.855 | 0.015 | 0.001 |
| Cs | 55 | 4.049 | 3.591 | 2.475 | 0.033 |

Within each row N is fixed and δ falls by **two orders of magnitude**. Partialling confirms both survive:

**δ vs f with N removed: r = −0.866, p = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶**
**δ vs N with f removed: r = +0.868, p = 1.5 × 10⁻⁶**

Each carries independent information. The confound was an artefact of looking only at ground states.

## The structural point

**Λ₈ already carries the freedom as (e, f, g).** Ground states are the diagonal e = n, f = ℓ, g = k, and on that diagonal N determines everything. Stepping off it — which is exactly what the e and f axes exist to permit — restores the independence.

So the confound was not a missing dimension. **It was a restriction to one slice of a lattice that already had the room** — and the ground-state diagonal is 0.4% of Λ₈'s cells, while essentially every quantity I fitted today lived on it.

That's a real lesson about how I've been using the object: I built eight axes and then did all the work on the three-dimensional slice.

**What's needed is data off the diagonal** — excited isoelectronic series, σ for the Na-like 3p and 3d sequences rather than only 3s. Those are ionic term energies, and they sit in the same NIST ASD source that would serve the Racah and ionic-defect gaps. One retrieval covers all three.

Two series, **both N = 11** — same electron count, same core, same nuclear charges. The only difference is which orbital the outer electron occupies.

**α differs by 54%, 1/β by 25%, at fixed N.** So the charge law's parameters depend on the subshell independently of electron count — which no ground-state series could ever have shown, because on that slice N *fixes* the subshell.

**3p: R² = 1.000000.** Successive differences in 1/δ are 0.22908, 0.22989, 0.22911 — constant to four decimals.

The 1/δ = α + βc law is **exact for the excited configuration and only approximate for the ground one.** That's the third independent route to the same conclusion: the ground state is the worst-conditioned point in the whole structure. The e-axis conditioning map said it, the ionic charge series said it at c = 0, and now the diagonal-versus-off-diagonal comparison says it.

## The caveat I want to keep visible

**Four transition energies, recalled not retrieved.** They're the astronomical standards — Na D, Mg II h/k, Al III, Si IV — and I'm confident in them to about 1%, but the α and β values inherit that. The *structure* of the result doesn't depend on their precision: a 1% error cannot manufacture a 54% difference in α or turn a drifting series into one constant to four decimals.

content.text:
The confound breaks, and the off-diagonal series does something unexpected.

## The test

Two series, **both N = 11** — same electron count, same core, same nuclear charges. The only difference is which orbital the outer electron occupies.

| | α | β | 1/β | c₀ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **f = 0** (3s, the diagonal) | 0.7337 | 0.1716 | 5.83 | 4.276 |
| **f = 1** (3p, off-diagonal) | 1.1328 | 0.2294 | 4.36 | 4.938 |

**α differs by 54%, 1/β by 25%, at fixed N.** So the charge law's parameters depend on the subshell independently of electron count — which no ground-state series could ever have shown, because on that slice N *fixes* the subshell.

## And the excited series obeys the law better

**3p: R² = 1.000000.** Successive differences in 1/δ are 0.22908, 0.22989, 0.22911 — constant to four decimals.

**3s: R² = 0.999319.** Differences 0.18281, 0.16955, 0.16301 — visibly drifting.

The 1/δ = α + βc law is **exact for the excited configuration and only approximate for the ground one.** That's the third independent route to the same conclusion: the ground state is the worst-conditioned point in the whole structure. The e-axis conditioning map said it, the ionic charge series said it at c = 0, and now the diagonal-versus-off-diagonal comparison says it.

## The caveat I want to keep visible

**Four transition energies, recalled not retrieved.** They're the astronomical standards — Na D, Mg II h/k, Al III, Si IV — and I'm confident in them to about 1%, but the α and β values inherit that. The *structure* of the result doesn't depend on their precision: a 1% error cannot manufacture a 54% difference in α or turn a drifting series into one constant to four decimals.

What it does mean is that the numerical parameters should be re-derived from retrieved values before anything is built on them.

We did answer it, and the decomposition is clean — with one correction to my own damping figure.

## The three error sources, separated

**Law error.** Given exact α and β, the law returns energies to **0.007% off-diagonal** and **0.64% on the ground state** — a factor of ninety between them.

**Parameter sensitivity.** Perturbing both by 10% gives **5.4%**, not the 2% I wrote in the ceiling table. The damping factor is roughly **0.5**, not 0.2. My summary understated it by 2.5×, so every figure in that ceiling list is optimistic by the same factor.

Corrected:

| Parameters known to | Energy accuracy |
|---|---|
| 30% | ~13% |
| 10% | ~5% |
| 3% | ~1.8% |
| **1%** | **~0.6%** |

**And α dominates β by roughly 4:1** — 4.49% versus 1.04% at a 10% perturbation. So effort spent pinning α is worth four times effort spent on β.

## What that says

The limit is **not** the lattice's integer coarseness, **not** the single Rydberg constant, and **not** the law. It is entirely **how well α and β can be predicted** — and α is the reciprocal of the neutral quantum defect, which is exactly the quantity the count rule produces.

1/β was already predicted to **2.4%** with a whole shell held out. If α could be reached at similar accuracy, the arithmetic gives roughly **1.5% energies off-diagonal** — three to five times better than anything today.

## The structural finding

**Every fit performed today was on the ground-state diagonal, where the law is 90× worse and the conditioning is worst.** That slice is 0.4% of Λ₈'s cells. We built an eight-dimensional object and did all the work on the one place where it performs least well.

That is the answer to the precision question, and it is a statement about method rather than about the framework's limits.

import numpy as np
R=13.6057
print("="*94)
print("THE PRECISION QUESTION, ANSWERED FROM THE OFF-DIAGONAL SERIES")
print("="*94)
print("""  All day the model has sat around 5–10 per cent, and I have treated that as the
  lattice's accuracy. But the 3p series shows the LAW is exact — so the 5–10 per
  cent was never the law's error. It was the ground state's conditioning plus the
  parameter fit. Separate the three and the ceiling becomes computable.""")
NA=[('Na',0,5.139077,2.104),('Mg⁺',1,15.03527,4.434),
    ('Al²⁺',2,28.44765,6.68),('Si³⁺',3,45.14215,8.90)]
c=np.array([x[1] for x in NA],float)
T3p=np.array([x[2]-x[3] for x in NA])
d3p=3-(c+1)*np.sqrt(R/T3p)
T3s=np.array([x[2] for x in NA]); d3s=3-(c+1)*np.sqrt(R/T3s)
print("\n  STEP 1 — how exactly does the law reproduce the ENERGIES, given exact α, β?")
for nm,T,d in [('3p (off-diagonal)',T3p,d3p),('3s (ground)',T3s,d3s)]:
    b=np.polyfit(c,1/d,1)
    dp=1/(b[1]+b[0]*c)
    Tp=R*(c+1)**2/(3-dp)**2
    e=np.abs(Tp-T)/T*100
    print(f"\n    {nm}")
    print(f"      {'c':>3}{'T observed':>13}{'T from law':>13}{'error %':>11}")
    for cc,to,tp,ee in zip(c,T,Tp,e):
        print(f"      {int(cc):>3}{to:>13.4f}{tp:>13.4f}{ee:>11.5f}")
    print(f"      mean {e.mean():.5f}%   max {e.max():.5f}%")
print("""
  So with the two parameters known, the law returns energies to about one part in
  ten thousand off the diagonal and one part in a thousand on it. The law is not
  the limit.""")
print()
print("="*94); print("STEP 2 — HOW MUCH PARAMETER ERROR CAN BE TOLERATED?"); print("="*94)
b=np.polyfit(c,1/d3p,1); a0,b0=b[1],b[0]
print(f"  3p series, true α = {a0:.4f}, β = {b0:.4f}. Perturb each and see.\n")
print(f"  {'perturbation':<16}{'α only':>12}{'β only':>12}{'both':>12}")
print("  "+"-"*54)
for pc in (0.001,0.01,0.03,0.10,0.30):
    out=[]
    for da,db in [(pc,0),(0,pc),(pc,pc)]:
        dp=1/(a0*(1+da)+b0*(1+db)*c)
        Tp=R*(c+1)**2/(3-dp)**2
        out.append(np.mean(np.abs(Tp-T3p)/T3p)*100)
    print(f"  {f'{100*pc:g}%':<16}{out[0]:>11.3f}%{out[1]:>11.3f}%{out[2]:>11.3f}%")
print("""
  The response is nearly linear and heavily damped: a 10 per cent error in both
  parameters gives about 2 per cent in the energy. That damping is why the model
  has been usable at all despite parameters fitted on a dozen series.""")
print()
print("="*94); print("STEP 3 — THE CEILING"); print("="*94)
print(f"""  Precision  =  (law error)  +  (parameter error × damping)  +  (conditioning)

    law error          0.003%   off-diagonal, measured above
    damping factor     ≈ 0.2    a 10% parameter error → 2% in energy
    conditioning       the ground state costs a further factor of ~5

  So the ceiling is set entirely by how well α and β can be predicted:

      parameters to 30%  →  ~6% energies      (roughly where we are)
      parameters to 10%  →  ~2%
      parameters to  3%  →  ~0.6%
      parameters to  1%  →  ~0.2%

  And 1/β was already predicted to 2.4% when a whole shell was held out. So the
  arithmetic says this construction should reach sub-per-cent accuracy off the
  diagonal — a factor of ten better than anything achieved today — and the reason
  it has not is that every fit was performed on the ground-state slice, where the
  law itself is only good to 0.1% and the conditioning is worst.""")
print("""
  That is the answer to the precision question. The limit is not the lattice's
  coarseness, not the single Rydberg constant, and not the law. It is that we
  have been standing on the one slice of Λ₈ where everything is hardest.""")
EOF

content.text:
We did answer it, and the decomposition is clean — with one correction to my own damping figure.

## The three error sources, separated

**Law error.** Given exact α and β, the law returns energies to **0.007% off-diagonal** and **0.64% on the ground state** — a factor of ninety between them.

**Parameter sensitivity.** Perturbing both by 10% gives **5.4%**, not the 2% I wrote in the ceiling table. The damping factor is roughly **0.5**, not 0.2. My summary understated it by 2.5×, so every figure in that ceiling list is optimistic by the same factor.

Corrected:

| Parameters known to | Energy accuracy |
|---|---|
| 30% | ~13% |
| 10% | ~5% |
| 3% | ~1.8% |
| **1%** | **~0.6%** |

**And α dominates β by roughly 4:1** — 4.49% versus 1.04% at a 10% perturbation. So effort spent pinning α is worth four times effort spent on β.

## What that says

The limit is **not** the lattice's integer coarseness, **not** the single Rydberg constant, and **not** the law. It is entirely **how well α and β can be predicted** — and α is the reciprocal of the neutral quantum defect, which is exactly the quantity the count rule produces.

1/β was already predicted to **2.4%** with a whole shell held out. If α could be reached at similar accuracy, the arithmetic gives roughly **1.5% energies off-diagonal** — three to five times better than anything today.

## The structural finding

**Every fit performed today was on the ground-state diagonal, where the law is 90× worse and the conditioning is worst.** That slice is 0.4% of Λ₈'s cells. We built an eight-dimensional object and did all the work on the one place where it performs least well.

That is the answer to the precision question, and it is a statement about method rather than about the framework's limits.

The comparison is decisive and holds for every atom.

## Diagonal versus whole structure

| Held out | Diagonal fit | Whole structure |
|---|---|---|
| Li | 0.353 | **0.124** |
| Na | 0.395 | **0.133** |
| K | 0.431 | **0.184** |
| Rb | 0.475 | **0.183** |
| Cs | 0.544 | **0.275** |

**Better for all five, by a factor of two to three.** And the diagonal-only fit applied to off-diagonal points gives mean |Δδ| = 0.587 with a worst case of 1.155 — larger than most of the defects it's trying to predict.

## The structural reason

**On the diagonal every point has f = 0.** The f-dependence isn't merely poorly estimated there; it is **invisible**. Range of f on the diagonal: 0 to 0. Range in the full set: 0 to 3.

So this isn't a refinement — the diagonal fit is *structurally incapable* of representing a dependence the data contains. It achieves R² = 0.9993 on its own five points and then fails by half a unit the moment it steps off.

That is the concrete cost of the slice, and it applies to everything fitted today.

## One thing to note honestly

The whole-structure fit has **lower R²** — 0.974 against 0.9993 — because it is fitting nineteen heterogeneous points rather than five collinear ones. The in-sample number gets *worse* while the out-of-sample number gets three times *better*.

That's the signature of the diagonal fit having been overfitted to a degenerate subspace all along, and it's a caution about every R² I've quoted today from a ground-state fit.

## Where this leaves the precision question

LOO on the whole structure is **0.213**, still well above the 0.075 the per-f stratified fit reached. So fitting off-diagonal fixes the *structural* blindness but hasn't yet delivered the precision ceiling — that needs the parameters pinned to a few per cent, and nineteen points across five atoms won't do it.

The direction is now unambiguous though: **more off-diagonal data, not more corrections.**

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
R=13.6057
AUF=[(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1),(4,0),(3,2),(4,1),(5,0),(4,2),(5,1),(6,0)]
def cnt(core,f):
    tot=0;c=0
    for (n,l) in AUF:
        cap=2*(2*l+1)
        if tot+cap<=core:
            if l==f: c+=1
            tot+=cap
        else: break
    return c
# atom : core electrons, ground n, and δ measured for each target subshell f
A={'Li':(2,2,{0:0.400,1:0.047,2:0.002}),
   'Na':(10,3,{0:1.348,1:0.855,2:0.015,3:0.001}),
   'K' :(18,4,{0:2.180,1:1.713,2:0.277,3:0.010}),
   'Rb':(36,5,{0:3.195,1:2.711,2:1.233,3:0.016}),
   'Cs':(54,6,{0:4.049,1:3.591,2:2.475,3:0.033})}
rows=[]
for a,(core,n,d) in A.items():
    for f,v in d.items():
        rows.append(dict(a=a,core=core,n=n,f=f,delta=v,cnt=cnt(core,f),
                         ground=(f==0)))
print("="*94)
print("FITTING AGAINST THE WHOLE STRUCTURE INSTEAD OF THE DIAGONAL")
print("="*94)
print(f"  {len(rows)} measured defects; {sum(r['ground'] for r in rows)} of them lie on the")
print(f"  ground-state diagonal (f = ℓ = 0), {sum(not r['ground'] for r in rows)} off it.\n")
print(f"  {'atom':<5}{'f':>3}{'count':>7}{'δ':>9}{'slice'}")
print("  "+"-"*36)
for r in rows:
    print(f"  {r['a']:<5}{r['f']:>3}{r['cnt']:>7}{r['delta']:>9.3f}   "
          f"{'diagonal' if r['ground'] else 'off'}")
print()
print("="*94); print("WHAT THE DIAGONAL ALONE CAN AND CANNOT SEE"); print("="*94)
g=[r for r in rows if r['ground']]
print(f"  On the diagonal every point has f = 0. So the f-dependence is not merely")
print(f"  hard to estimate — it is INVISIBLE. Range of f on the diagonal: "
      f"{min(r['f'] for r in g)}–{max(r['f'] for r in g)}.")
print(f"  Range of f in the whole set: {min(r['f'] for r in rows)}–{max(r['f'] for r in rows)}.")
print(f"\n  a diagonal-only fit of δ on the count:")
c=np.array([r['cnt'] for r in g],float); d=np.array([r['delta'] for r in g])
bg=np.polyfit(c,d,1)
print(f"    δ = {bg[1]:+.3f} {bg[0]:+.3f}·count    R² = "
      f"{1-np.sum((d-np.polyval(bg,c))**2)/np.sum((d-d.mean())**2):.4f}   (n = {len(g)})")
print(f"    applied to the OFF-diagonal points it gives:")
off=[r for r in rows if not r['ground']]
e1=[abs(np.polyval(bg,r['cnt'])-r['delta']) for r in off]
print(f"      mean |Δδ| = {np.mean(e1):.3f}   max {np.max(e1):.3f}")
print(f"\n  a whole-structure fit, count and f together:")
C=np.array([r['cnt'] for r in rows],float); F=np.array([r['f'] for r in rows],float)
D=np.array([r['delta'] for r in rows])
X=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(D)),C,F])
b,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X,D,rcond=None)
print(f"    δ = {b[0]:+.3f} {b[1]:+.3f}·count {b[2]:+.3f}·f    R² = "
      f"{1-np.sum((D-X@b)**2)/np.sum((D-D.mean())**2):.4f}   (n = {len(rows)})")
lo=[]
for i in range(len(D)):
    m=np.ones(len(D),bool); m[i]=False
    bb,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X[m],D[m],rcond=None); lo.append(abs(X[i]@bb-D[i]))
print(f"    LOO |Δδ| = {np.mean(lo):.3f}")
print()
print("="*94); print("HOLD OUT WHOLE ATOMS, FITTING ON THE FULL STRUCTURE"); print("="*94)
print(f"  {'held out':<8}{'from diagonal only':>22}{'from whole structure':>24}")
print("  "+"-"*56)
for t in A:
    tr=[r for r in rows if r['a']!=t]; te=[r for r in rows if r['a']==t]
    trg=[r for r in tr if r['ground']]
    cg=np.array([r['cnt'] for r in trg],float); dg=np.array([r['delta'] for r in trg])
    bgg=np.polyfit(cg,dg,1)
    e_diag=np.mean([abs(np.polyval(bgg,r['cnt'])-r['delta']) for r in te])
    Xt=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(tr)),[r['cnt'] for r in tr],[r['f'] for r in tr]])
    yt=np.array([r['delta'] for r in tr])
    bb,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(Xt,yt,rcond=None)
    Xe=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(te)),[r['cnt'] for r in te],[r['f'] for r in te]])
    e_full=np.mean(np.abs(Xe@bb-np.array([r['delta'] for r in te])))
    print(f"  {t:<8}{e_diag:>22.3f}{e_full:>24.3f}")
print(f"\n  Fitting the whole structure is not a refinement of the diagonal fit — the")
print(f"  diagonal fit cannot represent the f-dependence at all, because it has no")
print(f"  f-variation to learn from. That is the concrete cost of the slice.")
EOF

content.text:
The comparison is decisive and holds for every atom.

## Diagonal versus whole structure

| Held out | Diagonal fit | Whole structure |
|---|---|---|
| Li | 0.353 | **0.124** |
| Na | 0.395 | **0.133** |
| K | 0.431 | **0.184** |
| Rb | 0.475 | **0.183** |
| Cs | 0.544 | **0.275** |

**Better for all five, by a factor of two to three.** And the diagonal-only fit applied to off-diagonal points gives mean |Δδ| = 0.587 with a worst case of 1.155 — larger than most of the defects it's trying to predict.

## The structural reason

**On the diagonal every point has f = 0.** The f-dependence isn't merely poorly estimated there; it is **invisible**. Range of f on the diagonal: 0 to 0. Range in the full set: 0 to 3.

So this isn't a refinement — the diagonal fit is *structurally incapable* of representing a dependence the data contains. It achieves R² = 0.9993 on its own five points and then fails by half a unit the moment it steps off.

That is the concrete cost of the slice, and it applies to everything fitted today.

## One thing to note honestly

The whole-structure fit has **lower R²** — 0.974 against 0.9993 — because it is fitting nineteen heterogeneous points rather than five collinear ones. The in-sample number gets *worse* while the out-of-sample number gets three times *better*.

That's the signature of the diagonal fit having been overfitted to a degenerate subspace all along, and it's a caution about every R² I've quoted today from a ground-state fit.

## Where this leaves the precision question

LOO on the whole structure is **0.213**, still well above the 0.075 the per-f stratified fit reached. So fitting off-diagonal fixes the *structural* blindness but hasn't yet delivered the precision ceiling — that needs the parameters pinned to a few per cent, and nineteen points across five atoms won't do it.

The direction is now unambiguous though: **more off-diagonal data, not more corrections.**

The step back found a real contradiction and it resolves cleanly.

## The incoherence

I was using **two incompatible definitions of g**. Reading (a) — total occupancy of the target — is how I justified the axis, since a Rydberg state has one electron there and a ground state has k. Reading (b) — electrons *transferred* — is how I imposed conservation g ≤ q and pruned 62% of Λ₇ as unphysical.

A neutral ground state has q = 0, so (b) forces g = 0 while (a) requires g = k. I motivated the axis with one and constrained it with the other and never checked them against each other.

## The resolution

**Reading (b) is correct, and nothing is lost**, because the total occupancy is derived rather than discarded:

**G = g + k·[e = n][f = ℓ]**

The pre-existing occupancy is k when the target *is* the source subshell and zero otherwise, and both conditions are already coordinates. For a ground cell that gives G = 0 + k = k — reading (a) recovered exactly.

## Λ₈, stated properly

**Algebraically**: Λ₈ ≅ {(A, B, q, S) : A ∈ Λ, B ∈ Λ′, e(B) ≥ n(A), g(B) ≤ q ≤ k(A), 2S ≤ k(A)} — **two copies of the configuration lattice**, coupled by a partial order, with a transfer count and a coupling number. Every constraint has the form x ≤ φ(y) with φ non-decreasing in one coordinate, which is why it closes.

**Geometrically**: a pair of lattices joined along an order, with three regions — the **diagonal** (231 cells, 0.40%, ground states, the fixed-point set of the source-to-target map), the **excited wing** (41,540), and the **ionised wing** (45,144).

All six validity checks pass. Closure holds at 57,660 cells with zero join or meet failures.

## The thing worth keeping

**The diagonal is 0.40% of the object and every quantity in this work was fitted on it.** Moving off it in f broke the N–ℓ confound; moving off it in e made the 1/δ law exact to six figures. The framework's difficulty was never its coarseness — it was that we never left the fixed-point set.

The pre-existing occupancy is k when the target *is* the source subshell and zero otherwise, and both conditions are already coordinates. For a ground cell that gives G = 0 + k = k — reading (a) recovered exactly.

## Λ₈, stated properly

**Algebraically**: Λ₈ ≅ {(A, B, q, S) : A ∈ Λ, B ∈ Λ′, e(B) ≥ n(A), g(B) ≤ q ≤ k(A), 2S ≤ k(A)} — **two copies of the configuration lattice**, coupled by a partial order, with a transfer count and a coupling number. Every constraint has the form x ≤ φ(y) with φ non-decreasing in one coordinate, which is why it closes.

**Geometrically**: a pair of lattices joined along an order, with three regions — the **diagonal** (231 cells, 0.40%, ground states, the fixed-point set of the source-to-target map), the **excited wing** (41,540), and the **ionised wing** (45,144).

All six validity checks pass. Closure holds at 57,660 cells with zero join or meet failures.

## The thing worth keeping

**The diagonal is 0.40% of the object and every quantity in this work was fitted on it.** Moving off it in f broke the N–ℓ confound; moving off it in e made the 1/δ law exact to six figures. The framework's difficulty was never its coarseness — it was that we never left the fixed-point set.

Real off-diagonal data, and three things fall out of it.

## The Ritz condition holds

δ is constant along each series to a few thousandths — s: 1.0975, 1.0795, 1.0739, 1.0715 across four members; p: 0.7349, 0.7132, 0.7059; d: 0.0304, 0.0376.

**So δ genuinely is a property of the cell, not of the individual level.** That was assumed all day; it's now measured. And the limit of 121267.64 cm⁻¹ reproduces I₂(Mg) = 15.035 eV exactly, which validates the whole extraction.

## The recalled values were sound

Constructed from the recalled 280 nm line: **δ(3p) = 0.7343**. Retrieved from NIST levels: **0.7349**. Agreement to 0.0006.

So the off-diagonal result from two exchanges ago stands on retrieved data. That's worth having checked, given I flagged it as provisional.

## And the charge dependence of the count rule is now measured directly

| | Count slope | Intercept |
|---|---|---|
| Na I (c = 0) | 0.913 | −0.505 |
| **Mg II (c = 1)** | **0.547** | **+0.049** |

Same core, same counts, same N — **only the charge differs, and the slope drops by 40%.**

That is the first direct measurement of something I'd been inferring indirectly all day. The count rule isn't merely offset for ions; its **slope** changes with charge. Which explains why every attempt to patch the neutral rule with an additive correction failed — six of them — and why the ionic test came back at 329%.

## What this opens

The NIST Handbook has this table for **every element**, neutral and singly ionised. That's roughly 200 complete Rydberg series, all off-diagonal, all retrievable the same way. Each gives δ for several (e, f) at a known charge.

That is the dataset the whole construction has been short of, and it exists in a form I can actually reach.

# Electron-impact broadening of the 3s - 3p lines in low-Z Li-like ions

Yu. V. Ralchenko <sup>a,\*</sup>, H. R. Griem <sup>b</sup>, I. Bray <sup>c</sup>

<sup>a</sup>Faculty of Physics, Weizmann Institute of Science, Rehovot 76100, Israel

Maryland, College Park MD 20742

<sup>c</sup> Centre for Atomic, Molecular and Surface Physics, School of Mathematical and Physical Sciences, Murdoch University, Perth 6150, Australia

## Abstract

The collisional electron-impact line widths of the 3s-3p transitions in Li-like ions from B III to Ne VIII are calculated with the convergent close-coupling (CCC) method from the atomic collision theory. The elastic and inelastic contributions to the line broadening and their Z-scaling are discussed in detail, and comparisons with recent experimental and theoretical results are also presented. 

Thus, the existing data could when taken as a whole provide a diverse set of results for comparison of measurements and theory.

In continuation of the previous quantal calculations of line broadening in multiply-charged ions [3,5,6], we present here a quantum-mechanical calculation of the electron-impact line widths of the 3s - 3p transitions in Li-like ions from B III to Ne VIII. The paper is organized as follows. Section II contains the basic discussion of the theoretical method used for the present

calculation. The convergent close-coupling method is applied for determination of both inelastic and elastic contributions to the line widths. The results of calculations as well as the comparison with experimental data are presented in Sec. III. The following Section deals with the scaling properties of the line widths and finally the conclusions are drawn in the last Section.

content.text:
A Almodlej, H Alrashed, N Ben Nessib, M S Dimitrijević, Atomic structure for carbon-like ions from Na vi to Ar xiii, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, Volume 507, Issue 3, November 2021, Pages 3228–3237, https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stab2265 · We have calculated the energy levels, oscillator strengths, and transition probabilities for eight carbon-like ions (Na vi, Mg vii, Al viii, Si ix, P x, S xi, Cl xii and Ar xiii) using the Hartree–Fock pseudo-relativistic (HFR) and Thomas–Fermi–Dirac–Amaldi (TFDA) approaches. We used configuration expansions containing eight configurations, namely 2s2 2p2, 2s 2p3, 2s2 2p 3s, 2s2 2p 3p, 2s2 2p 3d, 2s2 2p 4s, 2s2 2p 4p, and 2s2 2p 5s. For each of the considered ions we obtained 59 energy levels, a number of which are not in the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) data base.

For the transition 2s2 2p23P − 2s 2p33Po, the two codes give nearly the same values. 

For the transition 2s2 2p23P − 2s2 2p 3s 3Po, the aS code reaches 3 per cent difference from NIST data base values. For all missing atomic structure values in the NIST data base, where there are no experimental data, we obtained new values with the codes cw and as, and we recommend the use of cw values, which are in better agreement with NIST data. We used a fitting form function of the gf versus atomic number Z, which allowed us to obtain values for missing data in the isoelectronic sequence. We recommend our new atomic structure results: they are expected to be very useful for studying laboratory and astrophysical plasmas; they cover the missing values in the literature; and we plan in the future to perform similar calculations for other isoelectronic sequence ions.

AUF=[(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1)]

C=[];D=[]
for f in (0,1,2,3):
    v=[d for nm,e,ff,T,d in rows if ff==f]
