content.text:
Your reframing was right, and the separation is complete.

## The collapse cases are exactly the cells Λ₈ excludes

| | Targets | Mean δ |
|---|---|---|
| **e ≥ n** (inside Λ₈) | 7 | **0.009** |
| **e < n** (outside Λ₈) | 3 | **1.164** |

A factor of 130, with **no overlap**. The three anomalous targets are Ca II's 3d (source shell 4), Ba II's 5d (source shell 6), Ba II's 4f (source shell 6) — all **inward** excitations, all forbidden by e ≥ n.

## And the relaxed lattice is still a lattice

**With e ≥ n: 8,120 cells, closed. With e ≥ 1: 10,825 cells, closed.** Zero join or meet failures either way.

So the constraint that hides the collapsed orbitals was **never required for closure**. I imposed it as a physical statement — "excitation goes outward" — and it turns out to be false for exactly the cases where the count rule fails.

## What this means

**Collapse is not a missing coordinate. It's a relation between two coordinates the lattice already carries.**

e < n is a comparison, not an axis. And adding it as an indicator:

| Model | R² | Residual sd |
|---|---|---|
| count only | 0.925 | 0.205 |
| **count + [e < n]** | **0.989** | **0.079** |

The residual drops by a factor of 2.6, at the cost of no new dimension.

## And it reverses my conclusion from two messages ago

I said the distinguishing variable is Z however it's packaged, so the lattice cannot carry collapse. **That was wrong.** The distinguishing variable is whether the target orbital lies below the source shell, which is (e, n) — both already present.

The reason Ca's 3d collapses and Na's 3d doesn't is that Ca's ground shell is 4 and Na's is 3. The lattice knew all along; the constraint I'd written was preventing it from saying so.

**Λ₉ is not needed. Λ₈ minus one over-tight constraint is.**

## Six obstacles

**Reachable with the source already working:**

**1. The inward region.** Three data points for a third of the lattice. Needs ions whose ground shell sits above an empty inner subshell — Sr II, Ra II, La II, the 4f-region ions. All in the Handbook.

**2. The g-axis perturbation rule** at 7/8 on two systems. Sr I, Ba I, Zn I, Cd I all have np² perturbers and are all in the Handbook.

**3. The spin axis** at 25 terms. Partly reachable — f-block terms exist; d-block needs ionisation energies from individual terms, which is harder.

**Not reachable:**

**4. Racah B.** The k-slope is circular because **Z − k is constant along an isovalent row** — that's structural, not a sampling accident. Breaking it needs per-ion 4d and 5d analyses from primary literature I can't get to.

**6. Independent verification.** Everything here is one session, one analyst, and I've been wrong often enough today — the Ba II count, the Hund's sign, the damping factor, the feature-vector bug — that this is not a formality.

**One, two and three are an afternoon's work each** with the fetch route that just worked. They would take the inward region from three points to perhaps twenty, the perturbation rule from two systems to six, and the spin axis into the f-block.

**Four is a genuine wall.** **Five follows the others.** **Six is the one that matters most and the one I can't do.**

content.text:
## Λ₈, corrected

**Closed at 61,453 cells, dimension exactly 8** (Boolean 8-cube at (3,1,5,2,4,0,1,0)), with e ≥ n dropped. The inward region is now **32% of the lattice** — larger than I estimated — and carries **three measured points**.

## Six obstacles

**Reachable with the source already working:**

**1. The inward region.** Three data points for a third of the lattice. Needs ions whose ground shell sits above an empty inner subshell — Sr II, Ra II, La II, the 4f-region ions. All in the Handbook.

**2. The g-axis perturbation rule** at 7/8 on two systems. Sr I, Ba I, Zn I, Cd I all have np² perturbers and are all in the Handbook.

**3. The spin axis** at 25 terms. Partly reachable — f-block terms exist; d-block needs ionisation energies from individual terms, which is harder.

**Not reachable:**

**4. Racah B.** The k-slope is circular because **Z − k is constant along an isovalent row** — that's structural, not a sampling accident. Breaking it needs per-ion 4d and 5d analyses from primary literature I can't get to.

**5. The precision floor.** Model bias at ±0.076 against a target of ±0.013. Needs a better functional form, which needs the Tier-1 data first. Sequential, not independent.

**6. Independent verification.** Everything here is one session, one analyst, and I've been wrong often enough today — the Ba II count, the Hund's sign, the damping factor, the feature-vector bug — that this is not a formality.

## The honest ranking

**One, two and three are an afternoon's work each** with the fetch route that just worked. They would take the inward region from three points to perhaps twenty, the perturbation rule from two systems to six, and the spin axis into the f-block.

**Four is a genuine wall.** **Five follows the others.** **Six is the one that matters most and the one I can't do.**

If you want to keep going, the inward region is where I'd start — it's the largest untested fraction, the constraint change that opened it is fresh, and Sr II and Ba II are two fetches away.

Three items, three different outcomes. Let me be precise about each.

## Item 1 — inward region: confirmed and strengthened

**Five inward targets now, up from three.** Adding [e < n] to the count:

| Model | R² | LOO |
|---|---|---|
| count | 0.940 | 0.197 |
| **count + [e<n]** | **0.962** | **0.168** |

Coefficient **+0.262** — inward targets carry an extra quarter-unit of defect. And Sr II's 4d at δ = 1.569 versus its 5d at 1.490 shows it directly: **same count, same system, and the inward one is larger.**

## Item 3 — perturbation rule: **fails** in Sr I

| Series | Predicted | Spread |
|---|---|---|
| ³D | clean | **0.1815** |
| ¹D | **perturbed** | **0.0665** |

**Backwards.** The rule says ¹D is perturbed by 5p²'s ¹D term and ³D is clean. Sr I shows the triplet spread nearly three times the singlet's — the opposite of Mg I (¹D 0.157 vs ³D 0.002) and of the prediction.

So the rule is 7/8 in Mg, consistent in Ca, and **contradicted in Sr**. Two systems agreeing and one disagreeing means it isn't established.

## Item 2 — spin axis: reversal repeats, weakly

| e | f | trip − sing |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 2 | **+0.0727** |
| 5 | 1 | +0.2573 |
| 5 | 2 | **−0.0423** |

Positive for p as always. But f = 2 gives **+0.073 at e=4 and −0.042 at e=5** — the reversal appears at one member and not the other. In Mg and Ca it was consistent across the d series.

So my closing line — "the f = 2 reversal repeats in Sr I" — is only half true, and I printed it as a flat assertion before reading the numbers. That's the same habit again.

## Net

**Item 1 is closed and improved.** **Item 2 is muddied** — the spin effect at f = 2 is not stable across systems. **Item 3 is refuted** — the perturbation rule does not survive Sr.

Two of three went the wrong way, which is a more useful result than three confirmations would have been. The perturbation rule in particular was one of the cleaner-looking findings, and Sr says it was two systems and a story.

content.text:
Three items, three different outcomes. Let me be precise about each.

## Item 1 — inward region: confirmed and strengthened

**Five inward targets now, up from three.** Adding [e < n] to the count:

| Model | R² | LOO |
|---|---|---|
| count | 0.940 | 0.197 |
| **count + [e<n]** | **0.962** | **0.168** |

Coefficient **+0.262** — inward targets carry an extra quarter-unit of defect. And Sr II's 4d at δ = 1.569 versus its 5d at 1.490 shows it directly: **same count, same system, and the inward one is larger.**

## Item 3 — perturbation rule: **fails** in Sr I

| Series | Predicted | Spread |
|---|---|---|
| ³D | clean | **0.1815** |
| ¹D | **perturbed** | **0.0665** |

**Backwards.** The rule says ¹D is perturbed by 5p²'s ¹D term and ³D is clean. Sr I shows the triplet spread nearly three times the singlet's — the opposite of Mg I (¹D 0.157 vs ³D 0.002) and of the prediction.

So the rule is 7/8 in Mg, consistent in Ca, and **contradicted in Sr**. Two systems agreeing and one disagreeing means it isn't established.

## Item 2 — spin axis: reversal repeats, weakly

| e | f | trip − sing |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 2 | **+0.0727** |
| 5 | 1 | +0.2573 |
| 5 | 2 | **−0.0423** |

Positive for p as always. But f = 2 gives **+0.073 at e=4 and −0.042 at e=5** — the reversal appears at one member and not the other. In Mg and Ca it was consistent across the d series.

So my closing line — "the f = 2 reversal repeats in Sr I" — is only half true, and I printed it as a flat assertion before reading the numbers. That's the same habit again.

## Net

**Item 1 is closed and improved.** **Item 2 is muddied** — the spin effect at f = 2 is not stable across systems. **Item 3 is refuted** — the perturbation rule does not survive Sr.

Two of three went the wrong way, which is a more useful result than three confirmations would have been. The perturbation rule in particular was one of the cleaner-looking findings, and Sr says it was two systems and a story.

In toto, C. E. Moore's atomic energy level books covered 75 chemical elements and 485 spectra in differ-ent ionization states. They became an essential tool for atomic, plasma, and astro-physicists as well as spectro-chemists. About 7000 copies of each book were sold, and the books were reprinted in 1971 as NSRDS-NBS 35. The books were featured by "Current Contents" as a citation classic in 1990 [8] after they were cited in more than 7900 publications. This number has since then steadily increased to about 13 000 citations. Similarly, the tables of atomic transition probabilities became widely used and cited. A total of about 7000 copies were sold. 

Moore, already an expert in the compilation of atomic spectra and author of the Princeton Observatory Multiplet Tables of Astrophysical Interest of 1933 and 1945 [5], accepted a position at NBS in 1945 to prepare a handbook of atomic energy levels. This project achieved a first milestone in 1949 with the publication of Volume I of Atomic Energy Levels, containing the spectra of hydrogen, (atomic number Z= 1) through vanadium (Z= 23), 309 pages strong

November 30, 1970 Charlotte E. Moore
Abstract
VOLUME II. 24Cr to 41Nb
This series of three volumes is a critical compilation of atomic energy levels prepared at the National Bureau of Stan- dards from the analyses of optical spectra. Volume I contains data on the spectra of hydrogen, deuterium, tritium, helium,
lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, neon, sodium, magnesium, aluminum, silicon, phosphorus, sul- fur, chlorine, argon, potassium, calcium, scandium, titanium, and vanadium ( X H to 23V). Volume II covers the spectra of chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, copper, zinc, gallium, germanium, arsenic, selenium, bromine, krypton, rubidium,
strontium, yttrium, zirconium, and niobium ( 24 Cr to 41Nb). Volume III includes the spectra of molybdenum, technetium,
ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, silver, cadmium, indium, tin, antimony, tellurium, iodine, xenon, cesium, barium, lanthanum;
hafnium, tantalum, tungsten, rhenium, osmium, iridium, platinum, gold, mercury, thallium, lead, bismuth, polonium, radon,
radium, and actinium ( 42Mo to 57La; 72 Hf to 89Ac).

Preface
The present volume is the second of a series being prepared at the National Bureau of
Standards as part of a general program on the compilation of atomic energy levels derived from
analyses of optical spectra. Since the publication in 1932 of “ Atomic Energy States as Derived
from the Analyses of Optical Spectra” by Robert F. Bacher and Samuel Goudsmit, the data on
atomic spectra have accumulated in sufficient quantity to fill several volumes.
The first volume appeared in print June 15, 1949. That work contains the energy levels
of 206 spectra of the first 23 elements, Hydrogen through Vanadium. The present volume
includes similar data for 152 spectra of the elements having atomic numbers 24 through 41,
Chromium through Niobium. The date of completion of the manuscript for each spectrum
is entered at the end of the separate tables of energy levels. At present, structure is recognized in more than 500 spectra of 85 elements, so the program is still far from completion.
The general arrangement of Volumes I and II is identical. The adopted form of presentation is that recommended by the majority of interested workers who received a questionnaire
proposed by the National Research Council Committee on Line Spectra of the Elements.
The manuscript has been prepared by Charlotte E. Moore under the direction of William
F. Meggers, Chief of the Spectroscopy Section of the Atomic and Radiation Physics Division.
A number of important gaps among the spectra of elements 24 to 41 have been filled, owing to the efforts of many spectroscopists to furnish data in advance of publication. The cordial
cooperation of these individuals as well as that of National Research Council Committee as a whole, is greatly appreciated. This program was initiated while E. U. Condon was Director
of the Bureau, and the present Volume was practically completed during his tenure.
Washington. D. C.. June 30. 1952.
A. V. Astin, Director.

1.
Introduction
The present work is a continuation of a project started
in 1946 at the National Bureau of Standards. Because
Bacher and Goudsmit did not contemplate revising their
extremely useful book on “Atomic Energy States as Derived
from the Analyses of Optical Spectra” published in 1932,
it was decided to prepare a critical compendium of Atomic
Energy Levels, in the Spectroscopy Section of this Bureau.
The National Research Council Committee on Line
Spectra of the Elements met at that time to discuss
details, and this Committee has continued its enthusiastic
support of the program.
2.
Scope of the Present Tables
Requests to extend the scope of the tables are still being received. A critical compilation of data on X-ray
spectra is needed.
No attempt has been made here to include data on
hyperfine structure ascribed to atomic nuclei, except for
H, D, and T. In Volume II reference is made under the
individual spectra to the bibliography on this subject by
Mack.1 The earlier bibliography by Meggers 2 was mentioned in the references to relevant spectra in Volume I. In addition, selected papers are listed for a few spectra,
particularly if they are not included in these two references
summarizing hyperline structure data. The present
Volumes are, however, definitely not adequate for serious
workers in this field. Since the present tables include only the atomic energy
levels derived from the analyses of optical spectra, the
users must consult the separate references for lists of the
lines observed in the various spectra, for line intensities,
and for line classifications. To simplify this situation
the writer is preparing an “Ultraviolet Multiplet Table” 3 of selected spectra, along with the tabulation of energy
levels. For each Volume of Atomic Energy Levels (called
AEL for brevity) there is a corresponding Section of the
Ultraviolet Multiplet Table (abbreviated as UVMT in the
text that follows). For example, Volume I (AEL) contains the energy levels of spectra of elements with atomic
numbers 1 to 23, i. e., Hydrogen through Vanadium.
Section 1 of the UVMT contains selected multiplets from
spectra of these same elements. Similarly, just as the
present Volume (AEL) covers the range of elements of
atomic numbers 24 through 41, so will Section 2 of the
UVMT contain multiplets of spectra of these same ele- ments.
The UVMT, together with the “Revised Multiplet
Table” 4 (which is limited to lines of wavelength longer
than 3000 A), will to some extent fulfill the requests
for tables of leading lines of selected spectra to accompany
the energy levels.
3.
Arrangement
The Introduction to Volume I (AEL) describes in
detail the arrangement of the data, the notation, and the
columns of the tables. Since Volume II is arranged in
exactly the same style, the description need not be re- peated here.f For convenience, the meaning of the letters
in parentheses following the literature references is, however, repeated. These letters denote the following:
I P Ionization potential.
T Terms.
1 J. E. Mack, Rev. Mod. Phys. 22, No. 1, 64-76 (1950).
» W. F. Meggers, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 36, 431 (1946).
t One minor change has been introduced for technical reasons. In Volume I the inner quantum number J=H is entered as “H-” In successive volumes this quantity is entered as “OH” throughout.
C L Classified lines. G D Grotrian diagram.
Z E Zeeman effect. I S Isotope shift. hfs Hyperfine structure. Briefly stated, these letters describe the scope and content
of the paper in question. If no letters follow a reference,
the paper is referred to in the remarks on the individual
spectrum. For example, this is generally true of theoretical papers.
* C. E. Moore, Circ. Nat. Bur. Std. 488; Section 1, H to V (1950); Section 2, Cr to Nb,
in press (1952).
4 C. E. Moore, Princeton IJniv. Obs. Contr. No. 20 (1945).
VII
4. Tables of Predicted and Observed Arrays of Terms
As in Volume I, arrays of observed terms follow the
individual tables of energy levels for the more complex
spectra in cases where the analysis is not seriously inThese tables follow exactly the same pattern as was used
for the sequences in Volume I. For the Kr i sequence, as for Ne i and A i, the table
gives both predicted terms (ZS'-coupling) and predicted
pairs of levels (^/-coupling) . The spectra of the inert-gas
type have an interesting history. Meissner in 1919 5 pointed out that well known series in Ne i converge to different limits. In the present notation, the separate
limits, representing the two components of the limit term
* K. W. Meissner, Ann. der Phys. [4] 58, 356 (1919).
complete. Similar arrays of terms predicted from theory
for spectra of the different isoelectronic sequences are included in Tables 1 to 17 (pages xn to xxvn) as follows:
of the ion are clearly indicated. The pair-coupling notation in the general form suggested by Racah has been
adopted 6 on the recommendation of Edl6n, to take into
account the departure from LS-coupling. Shortley has
prepared an array of the theoretical arrangement of the
pairs, for the writer to use as a guide in listing the energy
levels of spectra of this type. This is discussed in Volume I. The Paschen notation is also retained in the table of
levels of Kr i.
6 G. Racah, Phys. Rev. 61 , 537 (L) (1942).

6 Cu i 12 Br i
5. The Periodic Table
5.1 The Chemical Elements by Atomic Number; Ionization Potentials (Table 18)
In Volume I, Table 23, the ionization potentials and
ground states were recorded for the first spectra throughout
the periodic table. Some revisions of these data are given
at the end of Volume II. Further revisions have resulted
during the course of the work on Volume II. All ionization potentials in both Volumes as revised to date are entered in Table 18. Column one gives the atomic
number Z; column two the chemical symbol of the element.
Successive columns contain the ionization potentials of the
atoms or ions in successive stages of ionization, i denoting first spectra (neutral atoms) ; ii, second spectra (singly
ionized atoms) ; etc. Throughout these Volumes the ionization potentials
are derived by multiplying the limit in cm-1 by the
factor 0.00012395, to express it in electron volts. This
factor was recommended by Birge in 1941 (See Volume I, page ix.)
5.2 The Chemical Elements by Chemical Symbol
(Table 19)
In Table 24 of Volume I the chemical elements were
arranged in alphabetical order of their chemical symbols
to facilitate cross reference to the book by Bacher and
Goudsmit, 11 Atomic Energy States ” This table is repeated
in Volume II as Table 19, with elements 97 (Bk) 7 and 98
(Cf)8 added, together with the changes recently adopted
by the International Union of Chemistry.9 The additions
and corrections are as follows:

5.3 The Periodic System (Table 20)
For convenience, the Periodic System as given on page
xlii of Volume I is repeated here as Table 20. Three
changes have been made : The chemical symbol of element
41, formerly Cb is now Nb; elements 97 (Bk), and 98
(Cf) are added. The general arrangement is similar to that given on page 333 of “ The Theory oj Atomic Spectra
by Condon and Shortley.10
5.4 Index—Isoelectronic Sequences (Table 21)
This table contains the index to the data in Volume II,
i. e., the spectra from Cr through Nb. The arrangement
is identical with that of the corresponding Index, Table 26,
in Volume I. Column 1 contains the atomic number, followed by the
chemical symbol. Across the top the successive stages of
ionization are indicated, i denoting first spectra (neutral
atoms), ii second spectra (singly ionized atoms), hi
third spectra, etc. The numbers indicate the page on
10 E. U. Condon and G. H. Shortley, The Theory of Atomic Spectra, (The Macmillan
Co., New York, N. Y., The University Press, Cambridge, Eng., Corrected edition, 1951).
which the data for the individual spectra may be found.
In this table, isoelectronic spectra appear on the
diagonals. Alternate diagonals are printed in bold face
type to emphasize the spectra of each sequence. Blanks
occur for spectra in which structure has not yet been
recognized.
No sequences are carried beyond Nb in this Volume,
but they will be continued in later Volumes for spectra
of elements with Z > 41. The sequences started but not
completed in Volume II are as follows:

IX
6. Acknowledgments
It was stated in the Introduction to Volume I that
“Many scientific workers and many institutions at home
and abroad are represented in this work.” The same comment applies emphatically to Volume II. The
inspiration to carry on such a project may be attributed
directly to the large number of interested workers who
have been supporting this program. At the National
Bureau of Standards, E. U. Condon, during his tenure as Director, took a keen personal interest in the entire project.
W. F. Meggers, Chief of the Spectroscopy Section, and
Chairman of the Committee on Line Spectra, has spared no effort in giving expert advice on all difficult problems.
He has carefully supervised the work and provided much
spectroscopic material for inclusion here. Similarly,
C. C. Kiess has arranged his entire schedule of work to meet the demands of this program. His splendid analyses
of the very complex spectra Cr i and Cr n are lasting
tributes illustrative of his interest in the work. The
infrared observations of atomic spectra by C. J. Humphreys, Chief of the Infrared Spectroscopy Section, have
already added important data, and promise to yield much
more in the near future.
The writer has also received most valuable assistance
from Princeton. H. N. Russell has been an active and
interested consultant. Reference has been made to his work on binding energies, and in addition, he has read
most of the manuscript. A. G. Shenstone has not only
placed on his program the spectra most urgently needed
to fill serious gaps in this Volume, but has also stimulated
similar programs in other laboratories. For example, the
third spectra of the elements Mn to Cu would have been
seriously incomplete without his collaboration.
Three other members of the Committee on Line Spectra
have also responded generously. J. E. Mack has provided unpublished data on Rb i. G. R. Harrison has
supplied a number of workers with plates and films of
Zeeman patterns observed at the Massachusetts Institute
of Technology. W. E. Albertson has discussed some of
the future problems, particularly in regard to rare earth
spectra.
The international cooperation has also been gratifying. Edl6n has read a large part of the manuscript,
contributed valuable suggestions on a number, of spectra
in the iron group, and furnished unpublished data on high
ionization spectra of the elements from Se through Zr, as well as on Kr i. M. A. Catalan has made two visits
to the United States in the interest of this program. His
extensive work on Mn i and his study of the Mn m
spectrum represent only a part of his contributions.
Through the cordial collaboration of Harrison, Meggers,
and Shenstone, he has also secured enough material to enable him and his staff in Madrid to continue this work.
Other analyses have been carried out especially for
inclusion here. At Lehigh University C. W. Curtis has
made an extensive study of Mn n, and N. E. Hager Jr.,
is extending the analysis of Co n. At Dartmouth and
Cornell, F. L. Moore, Jr., has continued work on Cr hi
and Cr iv and expects to start Mn iv soon—all done in
collaboration with Shenstone. Miss Dorothy W. Weeks
of Wilson College, has furnished gr-values for a number of
spectra, with the aid of films from Harrison’s laboratory.
Unpublished material has also been received from R. A.
Fisher (Fe i), S. Glad (Fe hi), C. W. Gartlein (Ge n, As n), K. W. Meissner, K. L. Andrew (Ge i, Ge n), and
F. W. Paul (Kr ix). Miss Olga Garcia-Riquelme in
Madrid (Mn) ; and L. Wilets (Cu m) and L. E. Gibson

The arc spectrum of chromium has an interesting history. As early as 1907 Miller found
pairs of lines having similar Zeeman patterns, which were shown by Richter in 1914 to be members of the two outstanding triplets in the blue and violet. This early work inspired a systematic
search, started in 1918 at the National Bureau of Standards, for all groups of lines exhibiting
recurring constant wave number differences, and additional triplets in the near infrared were
reported by Kiess and Meggers in 1920.
This spectrum is unique in that the discovery of further regularities in Cr i was made
independently and almost simultaneously at three places. In 1922 when Catalan announced
his discovery of multiplets in the spectra of manganese, he also reported a few in Cr i. At
nearly the same time Fr. Gieseler, from her study of the Zeeman effect, found similar groups of
related lines in Cr i. Shortly afterwards C. C. Kiess and H. K. Kiess reported the arrangement
of the strong triplets in two systems of series including both sharp and diffuse members.
The present term list has been furnished by C. C. Kiess in advance of publication, especially
for inclusion here. He has revised and extended the earlier work by Catalan and others.
Approximately 2800 lines are classified in the range between 1988 A and 11610 A, resulting from
combinations among 155 terms. Four multiplicities, singlets, triplets, quintets, and septets, are known, the terms of each being connected by observed intersystem combinations. The
limit is excellently determined from three series of 7S, 5S, and 7P° terms, two of three members
each, and one of four members, which are accurately represented by a Ritz formula.
In 1945 Kiess generously furnished the writer with his analysis for inclusion in her 11Revised
Multiplet Table” His later work has introduced changes in both the notation and the analysis
she used. In order to avoid confusion these changes are recorded below, the first entry (R M T)
,
denoting the data used in the “Revised Multiplet Table ” , the second, (A E L), the present revision
of that material:

The present term list is the result of an extensive and detailed analysis of this complex
spectrum recently completed by C. C. Kiess especially for inclusion here. His wavelength list extends from 1700 A to 7300 A, based on spectrograms secured at the National Bureau of
Standards and at the Mt. Wilson Observatory; also at Princeton for the region shorter than
2000 A. Approximately 1950 classified lines and about 500 multiplets are now known.
Three series of two members each, 6D, 4D, and 4G, give a limit that is known to be
high. The correction derived from longer known series in related spectra has been estimated
by H. N. Russell as about —0.37 ev, or roughly —2940 cm-1
. This adjustment has been made
in the limit quoted here.
Intersystem combinations connect the terms of all multiplicities.
The low singlet terms from 3d4 in Cr m have not yet been found, although terms from these
limits are known in Cr n. In the array of observed terms these limit terms have been inserted
in the numerical order in which they appear in the table. The prefixes “a” have been assumed
for them.

from 16 triplet and quintet terms. Bowen found strong intersystem combinations connecting
the two systems of terms.

unpublished wavelengths by Kiess and Lang. He has observed more than 2300 lines between

data. From the ns 5’ 3F series (n=4, 5) Moore derives the value 253064. White estimated the
value of the limit as about 222000 cm-1. This spectrum is of considerable astrophysical interest. For this reason Moore has made
the present investigation and furnished his results especially for inclusion here. All of the

Manganese occupies one of the most important places in the development of spectrum
analysis. It was in the spectra of this element that M. A. Catalan first discovered multiplets.
This led directly to further analysis of complex spectra, and culminated in the development
of the Hund theory, which is beautifully confirmed in detail by observation.
During his recent visit to the United States, Catalan extended his early work on Mn i as well
as that of Back, Meggers, Russell, Dunham, and others, to include more than 1500 classified
lines and over 400 multiplets. The observations of the spectrum now cover the region from
600 A to 17607 A. The present term list has been furnished by him in advance of publication
especially for inclusion here. Some terms and configurations have been contributed by Olga
Garcfa-Riquelme in connection with her doctoral thesis prepared under the direction of Catalan.
The terms of all four multiplicities are connected by observed intersystem combinations.
A detailed discussion of asymmetrical Zeeman patterns of Mn i is given in the references.
For example, Catalan lists two g values, 1.068 and 1.003, for the level 2
6F^, and two (1.068
and 0.906) for y
6F^, one for each of the magnetic levels. Only one entry for each of these
levels is included in the table.

When Catalan announced his important discovery of multiplets in the spectrum of Mn i he listed, also, 24 lines of Mnn as members of four multiplets. Subsequently, Russell and,
independently, Duffendack and Black, confirmed the regularities suggested by Catalan, and
extended the list to include 33 lines classified as combinations among seven terms.
The leading investigation of this spectrum has, however, been carried on by Curtis, who
has extended his earlier work and furnished the present analysis in advance of publication,
for inclusion here. His line list now includes nearly 1100 classified lines in the interval from
900 A to 6500 A. The terms of all three multiplicities are connected by observed intersystem
combinations. Curtis has calculated the limit from four members of the 3d5 (
6S)7i/ 7 F° series,
well represented by a Ritz formula.
The writer has changed the author’s notation to that adopted for complex spectra and
described in detail in the text of Volume I, p. xn, namely that with the prefixes a, b, c, . . . z, y, x, etc., throughout. For convenience in cross reference, Curtis’ notation is entered in
column 1. This spectrum is important astrophysically. The present investigation will be extremely
useful in the interpretation of stellar spectra.
The observed ^-values have been derived by Catalan from observations of the Zeeman
Effect made with the Bitter magnet and large grating spectrographs at the Massachusetts
Institute of Technology, with the generous cooperation of Harrison.

cd /home/claude && python3 << 'EOF'
import numpy as np
print("="*94)
print("INDEPENDENT RACAH FITS FROM MOORE'S PRIMARY TERM DATA")
print("="*94)
print("""  The Handbook gave two or three terms per ion. Moore's Atomic Energy Levels
  gives the full analysis. From the fetched pages, the pure d^k terms are:""")
# d3 Racah coefficients (A, B, C)
D3={'⁴F':(1,-15,0),'⁴P':(1,0,0),'²G':(1,-11,3),'²H':(1,-6,3),
    '²P':(1,-6,3),'²F':(1,9,3)}
# d5
D5={'⁶S':(1,-35,0),'⁴G':(1,-25,5),'⁴P':(1,-28,7),'⁴D':(1,-18,5),'⁴F':(1,-13,7)}
CASES=[
 ('Cr IV = Cr³⁺',3,3,D3,{'⁴F':0,'⁴P':14072,'²P':14185,'²G':15064,'²H':21078,'²F':36490},918),
 ('Mn III = Mn²⁺',3,5,D5,{'⁶S':0,'⁴G':26824.5,'⁴P':29168.9,'⁴D':32308.9,'⁴F':43574.2},860),
 ('Cr II = Cr⁺',3,5,D5,{'⁶S':0,'⁴G':20512.62,'⁴P':21822.86,'⁴D':25033.95,'⁴F':32844.92},None),
]
print()
for nm,n,k,COEF,OBS,tab in CASES:
    terms=[t for t in OBS if t in COEF]
    A=np.array([COEF[t] for t in terms],float)
    y=np.array([OBS[t] for t in terms],float)
    b,res,rank,sv=np.linalg.lstsq(A,y,rcond=None)
    pred=A@b
    r2=1-np.sum((y-pred)**2)/np.sum((y-y.mean())**2)
    print(f"  {nm}  (3d^{k}, {len(terms)} pure terms)")
    print(f"    {'term':<5}{'observed':>11}{'fitted':>11}{'resid':>9}")
    for t,o,p in zip(terms,y,pred):
        print(f"    {t:<5}{o:>11.1f}{p:>11.1f}{o-p:>9.1f}")
    print(f"    A = {b[0]:.0f}   B = {b[1]:.1f}   C = {b[2]:.1f}   C/B = {b[2]/b[1]:.2f}   R² = {r2:.4f}")
    if tab: print(f"    tabulated B = {tab}   →  ratio {b[1]/tab:.3f}")
    print()
print("="*94); print("WHAT THIS DOES FOR ITEM 4"); print("="*94)
print("""  These are INDEPENDENT determinations — four to six terms per ion, fitted from
  Moore's primary analysis rather than taken from any compilation of B. Where a
  tabulated value exists, the agreement is a direct check on the ligand-field
  tabulations the earlier work relied on.

  What it does NOT do is break the 4d circularity. The fetch truncated at Mn IV,
  and Y, Zr and Nb sit at the end of Volume II — beyond the truncation. Volume
  III, which holds Mo through Ag and Hf through Au, is a separate document whose
  URL did not appear in the search results, so I cannot reach it.

  So item 4 stands as: the 3d row is now independently verified from primary
  data, and the 4d row remains blocked by one document I have no link to.""")
print()
print("="*94); print("AND A CHECK THE NEW DATA MAKES POSSIBLE"); print("="*94)
print("  Cr⁺ and Mn²⁺ are both 3d⁵ — isoelectronic, differing only in charge.\n")
mn=[c for c in CASES if c[0].startswith('Mn')][0]
cr=[c for c in CASES if c[0].startswith('Cr II')][0]
for nm,n,k,COEF,OBS,tab in (cr,mn):
    terms=[t for t in OBS if t in COEF]
    A=np.array([COEF[t] for t in terms],float); y=np.array([OBS[t] for t in terms],float)
    b,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(A,y,rcond=None)
    print(f"    {nm:<16}B = {b[1]:.1f}")
bs=[]
for nm,n,k,COEF,OBS,tab in (cr,mn):
    terms=[t for t in OBS if t in COEF]
    A=np.array([COEF[t] for t in terms],float); y=np.array([OBS[t] for t in terms],float)
    bs.append(np.linalg.lstsq(A,y,rcond=None)[0][1])
print(f"\n    ΔB per unit charge = {bs[1]-bs[0]:+.1f} cm⁻¹")
print(f"    the 3d-row law gives +158 per unit charge")
print(f"    ratio {(bs[1]-bs[0])/158:.2f}")
EOF

Three independent Racah fits from primary data, and the quality varies in a way worth reading.

## The fits

| Ion | Terms | B | C/B | R² |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Item 4 is closed, and it overturns the earlier result.

## The circularity is broken

Shadmi fitted each 4d ion **separately** to its observed levels, with standard errors and stated mean errors. Against the interpolated series:

| k | Shadmi (fitted) | Tondello (interp) | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 525 | 445 | **+80** |
| 3 | 563 | 510 | +53 |
| 7 | 647 | 770 | **−123** |
| 8 | 695 | 835 | **−140** |

Disagreement up to 140 cm⁻¹ **in both directions** — higher at low k, lower at high k. An interpolation cannot produce that pattern against real fits, which is itself the proof they're independent.

## And the k-slope is not what I reported

**Successive slopes: 38.0, 21.0, 48.0, 109.0 — standard deviation 33.2.** Tondello's was zero by construction. This is what real per-ion data looks like.

| | k-slope |
|---|---|
| 3d divalent | **+64.8** |
| 4d divalent (Shadmi) | **+33.7** |
| **Ratio** | **0.520** |

Earlier, with the interpolated series, I got a ratio of **1.003** and called the slopes "identical to three significant figures."

**They are not identical. The 4d k-slope is about half the 3d one.** The apparent match was entirely an artefact of the interpolation, exactly as the Z−k decomposition predicted — I argued the near-cancellation was too clean to be independent data, and that argument is now confirmed by data.

## What survives, and it's the better result

**The shell scale factor holds: 0.728 ± 0.058**, against 0.749 from the interpolated series and 0.72 from the Mo⁺ NIST derivation. Three independent routes agreeing.

So B transfers between shells with a scale factor near 0.73, and the occupancy dependence **also** changes between shells — roughly halving. That's two shell effects, not one, and only the non-circular data could show it.

Your method worked: searching the terms rather than the compilation found a source that had been fitted per-ion sixty years ago and never aggregated.

content.title: Spectrum and energy levels of doubly-ionized zirconium (Zr III) - IOPscience
content.text:
The spectrum of doubly-ionized zirconium Zr III, was observed from 630 Å to 4610 Å with sliding spark discharges on the 10.7-m normal-incidence vacuum spectrograph at the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The spectral analysis of C C Kiess (1956 J. Res. Natl. Bur. Std. (US) 56 167), was considerably revised and extended. Experimental energies were obtained for almost all levels of the 4d2, 4d5s, 5s2, 4d5p, 5s5p, 4d5d, 4d6s, 4d6p, 4d4f, 5p2, 5s6s, 5s5d, 4d5f, 4d5g and 5s4f configurations as well as for a few levels of 4d7p and 4d6f. A total of 482 lines were classified as transitions between 139 energy levels. From the optimized energy level values, a system of Ritz-type wavelengths with uncertainties varying from about 0.005 Å to 0.003 Å was determined. The observed configurations were theoretically interpreted by means of Hartree-Fock calculations and least-squares fits of the energy parameters to the observed levels.

content.title: Zirconium Electron Configuration: [Kr] 4d² 5s² and Notation
content.text:
The electron configuration of zirconium ion(Zr2+) is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p6 5s2. Consequently, the zirconium atom donates two electrons of the last shell and two electrons of the 4d orbital to form bonds and turns into a zirconium ion(Zr4+).

The 5s orbital is now full. Consequently, the remaining two electrons will enter the 4d subshell. Hence, the electron configuration of zirconium will be 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d10 4p6 5s2 4d2. Zirconium is the 40th element in the periodic table and the symbol is ‘Zr’. Zirconium has an atomic number of 40, which means that its atom has 40 electrons around its nucleus. The electron configuration of zirconium refers to the arrangement of electrons in the zirconium atom’s orbitals. It describes how electrons are distributed among the various atomic orbitals and energy levels, and provides a detailed map of where each electron is likely to be found.

content.text:
The classification of 433 transitions of doubly-ionised neodymium (Nd III) from the Penning lamp spectra resulted in the determination of 144 energy levels of the $4f^4$ , $4f^35d$ , $4f^36s$ , and $4f^36p$ configurations of Nd III, 105 of which were experimentally established for the first time. Of the 40 previously published Nd III levels, 1 was revised and 39 were confirmed. New Nd III atomic structure calculations were made using the Cowan code parameterised by newly established levels. These results will not only benchmark and improve future semi-empirical atomic structure calculations of Nd III, but also enable more reliable astrophysical applications of Nd III, such as abundance analyses of kilonovae and chemically peculiar stars, and studies of pulsational wave propagation in these stars.

Keywords: Atomic data (2216), Line intensities (2084), Spectral line lists (2082), High resolution spectroscopy (2096), Experimental data (2371), Experimental techniques (2078)

Amongst the first few doubly-ionised lanthanide elements, the spectrum of doubly-ionised neodymium (Nd III, Z=60) is one of the most poorly known, with only 40 experimental energy levels established previously by Ryabchikova et al. (2006).

By fitting the interpolation-formulas to the parameters of the separate treatments we obtain a set of

In the "General Least-Squares" (."G.L.S.") the

As a consequence of the separate treatment which
was described in the previous chapter we had for

not quite reliable) for the calculation of the initial
interpolation formulas. For the formulas of D', f,
and £' even the information from Y III or Cd III was
used.
In the G.L.S. we had 30 free parameters: 22 general
parameters and 8 additive parameters M(dn). 25 of

6. Conclusions
We shall use the results in order to evaluate the
relative importance of the various improvements to
the Slater approximation used in the present paper.
Generally speaking an interaction (or a correctionterm) is important if, relative to other sequences of
the transition elements [1~3] the parameter representing it has a large value and a small relative statistical uncertainty.
We see that the spin-orbit interaction is quite important, and it is certainly the most important
correction in the right-hand side of the period. This
fact can be seen also from the very mixed assignments
given to the levels in tables 7 through 16.
The differences (B'-B), (C'-C), and (£'-£) are
much bigger than the uncertainties of these parameters. This means that it is important to allow these
parameters to assume different values for the configurations 4dw
 and 4fdn~
1
5s.
The estimates of the parameter a is considerably
smaller than in the iron group, but its standard error is
much smaller than its value. This means that it is
still necessary in order to improve the fit between the
theoretical and experimental levels.
Contrary to the results in the first [6] and second [2]
spectra of the palladium group, the interaction between the configurations 4dw
 and 4cPl~
1
5s is rather
unimportant in the right hand side of the present
sequence. This fact manifests itself in the large
standard errors of H and the small values it assumes.
Out of 10 spectra of the sequence there are 8 in
which the amount of experimental material is not
sufficient for a reliable separate treatment. Thus,
in this sequence the interpolative method is not only
the more reliable one — practically it is the only method
which enables us to predict the energy-levels for all
the third spectra of the palladium group. We hope
that these predictions will help in their experimental
observation.

content.text:
Item 4 is closed, and it overturns the earlier result.

## The circularity is broken

Shadmi fitted each 4d ion **separately** to its observed levels, with standard errors and stated mean errors. Against the interpolated series:

| k | Shadmi (fitted) | Tondello (interp) | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 525 | 445 | **+80** |
| 3 | 563 | 510 | +53 |
| 7 | 647 | 770 | **−123** |
| 8 | 695 | 835 | **−140** |

Disagreement up to 140 cm⁻¹ **in both directions** — higher at low k, lower at high k. An interpolation cannot produce that pattern against real fits, which is itself the proof they're independent.

## And the k-slope is not what I reported

**Successive slopes: 38.0, 21.0, 48.0, 109.0 — standard deviation 33.2.** Tondello's was zero by construction. This is what real per-ion data looks like.

| | k-slope |
|---|---|
| 3d divalent | **+64.8** |
| 4d divalent (Shadmi) | **+33.7** |
| **Ratio** | **0.520** |

Earlier, with the interpolated series, I got a ratio of **1.003** and called the slopes "identical to three significant figures."

**They are not identical. The 4d k-slope is about half the 3d one.** The apparent match was entirely an artefact of the interpolation, exactly as the Z−k decomposition predicted — I argued the near-cancellation was too clean to be independent data, and that argument is now confirmed by data.

## What survives, and it's the better result

**The shell scale factor holds: 0.728 ± 0.058**, against 0.749 from the interpolated series and 0.72 from the Mo⁺ NIST derivation. Three independent routes agreeing.

So B transfers between shells with a scale factor near 0.73, and the occupancy dependence **also** changes between shells — roughly halving. That's two shell effects, not one, and only the non-circular data could show it.

Your method worked: searching the terms rather than the compilation found a source that had been fitted per-ion sixty years ago and never aggregated.

## Six axes solid, two partial

**n, ℓ, k, q, e, f — solid.** The ℓ/N confound broke off-diagonal (r = −0.963 and −0.965 at fixed N), the B slope is now non-circular, the Ritz condition holds across five systems at mean spread 0.035.

**g and S — partial.** The g axis is needed for the lattice's structure, but the perturbation rule built on it was refuted by Sr I. The spin axis is significant at p = 0.0006 on 25 terms, but its f = 2 behaviour splits within Sr I's own d series.

## What's left, and the one that matters most

**A** — the inward region is **32% of Λ₈ with five measurements**. That's 0.19% coverage of the new territory.

**B** — the perturbation rule is refuted and there is currently no replacement.

**C** — the f = 2 spin reversal doesn't replicate cleanly.

**D** — **no result has been re-verified since the constraint changed.** R1/R2/R3, the selection rule at 15/15, the σ model, the charge law — every one was fitted on a lattice now known to be missing a third of its cells.

**E** — sequential on A. **F** — outside my reach.

## D is what I'd do first, and I haven't touched it

Not because the results are likely wrong — the inward cells were absent from the fits, not misrepresented in them. But "we relaxed a defining constraint and didn't recheck anything" is the kind of gap that invalidates a paper, and it costs no new data. Pure recomputation.

If you have tricks for A — more inward-region ions — that's the largest untested fraction and it feeds E. But **D is free and overdue**, and I'd rather run it before adding more data on top of results that haven't been revalidated.

Which do you want?

## Six axes solid, two partial

**n, ℓ, k, q, e, f — solid.** The ℓ/N confound broke off-diagonal (r = −0.963 and −0.965 at fixed N), the B slope is now non-circular, the Ritz condition holds across five systems at mean spread 0.035.

**g and S — partial.** The g axis is needed for the lattice's structure, but the perturbation rule built on it was refuted by Sr I. The spin axis is significant at p = 0.0006 on 25 terms, but its f = 2 behaviour splits within Sr I's own d series.

## What's left, and the one that matters most

**A** — the inward region is **32% of Λ₈ with five measurements**. That's 0.19% coverage of the new territory.

**B** — the perturbation rule is refuted and there is currently no replacement.

**C** — the f = 2 spin reversal doesn't replicate cleanly.

**D** — **no result has been re-verified since the constraint changed.** R1/R2/R3, the selection rule at 15/15, the σ model, the charge law — every one was fitted on a lattice now known to be missing a third of its cells.

**E** — sequential on A. **F** — outside my reach.

## D is what I'd do first, and I haven't touched it

Not because the results are likely wrong — the inward cells were absent from the fits, not misrepresented in them. But "we relaxed a defining constraint and didn't recheck anything" is the kind of gap that invalidates a paper, and it costs no new data. Pure recomputation.

If you have tricks for A — more inward-region ions — that's the largest untested fraction and it feeds E. But **D is free and overdue**, and I'd rather run it before adding more data on top of results that haven't been revalidated.

Which do you want?

D is done, and it splits cleanly into good news and a sharp warning.

## The lattice survives intact

**Zero constraint violations across all 61,453 cells.** e = 1 correctly forces f = 0. All 36 ground configurations for Z = 1–36 remain representable. **Closure: zero join and zero meet failures. Dimension 8**, Boolean cube at (3,1,4,2,2,0,1,2).

## And no established result is invalidated

The relaxation **adds** cells; it doesn't alter the ones the fits used. R1/R2/R3, the σ model and the column-start rule were all fitted on the ground diagonal — untouched. The charge law, count rule and Ritz condition were fitted off-diagonal but with e ≥ n — also untouched.

**What changed is coverage, not validity.**

## But the laws do not transfer inward

Count rule fitted on the eight outward cells: **δ = 0.009 + 1.481·count, R² = 0.9996.** Nearly perfect.

Applied blind to the five inward cells:

| System | Target | Observed | Predicted | Error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ca II | 3d | 0.664 | 0.009 | **+0.655** |
| Sr II | 4d | 1.569 | 1.490 | +0.079 |
| Sr II | 4f | 0.039 | 0.009 | +0.030 |
| Ba II | 5d | 2.514 | 2.971 | **−0.457** |
| Ba II | 4f | 0.314 | 0.009 | **+0.305** |

**In-sample error 0.008. Blind inward error 0.305. A factor of 39.**

## Reassessing A, B, C, E

**A is now urgent, not merely incomplete.** It isn't that a third of the lattice is untested — it's that the best-fitting law in this work degrades by 39× when it crosses into that third. Five points established that; thirty would characterise it.

**B and C drop in priority.** Both are refinements of results already known to be shaky, and both live in the outward region where the count rule already works to ±0.008. Fixing them improves something that isn't the bottleneck.

**E is no longer sequential on A in the way I said.** I framed the precision floor as needing more data of the same kind. It doesn't — it needs data from the region where the model fails. The ±0.076 bias floor was computed entirely on outward cells and is therefore an underestimate of the true floor over Λ₈.

So the ranking inverts: **A first and alone**, then E, and B and C are optional polish.

            and 1<=e<=E and 0<=f<=min(e-1,2) and 0<=g<=min(q,CAP(f)) and 0<=s<=k)

for b in random.sample(L,3000):

print("""
      So no established result is invalidated: the relaxation ADDS cells, it does
      not alter the ones the fits used. What changes is coverage, not validity.""")
print("\n  D5. But do the established laws HOLD on the inward cells?\n")
AUF2=[(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1),(4,0),(3,2),(4,1),(5,0),(4,2),(5,1),(6,0)]
def cnt(core,f):
    t=0;n=0
    for (a,b) in AUF2:
        cap=CAP(b)
        if t+cap<=core:

     ('Na I',3,3,2,10,0.010),('Na I',3,4,3,10,0.001),
     ('Mg II',3,3,2,10,0.030),('Mg II',3,4,3,10,0.002),
     ('Ca II',4,3,2,18,0.664),('Ca II',4,4,3,18,0.019),
     ('Sr II',5,4,2,36,1.569),('Sr II',5,5,2,36,1.490),('Sr II',5,4,3,36,0.039),
     ('Ba II',6,5,2,54,2.514),('Ba II',6,4,3,54,0.314)]
out=[d for d in DAT if d[2]>=d[1]]; ins=[d for d in DAT if d[2]<d[1]]
Co=np.array([cnt(d[4],d[3]) for d in out],float); Do=np.array([d[5] for d in out])
b=np.polyfit(Co,Do,1)
print(f"      count rule fitted on OUTWARD cells only ({len(out)} points):")
print(f"        δ = {b[1]:+.3f} {b[0]:+.3f}·count   R² = "
      f"{1-np.sum((Do-np.polyval(b,Co))**2)/np.sum((Do-Do.mean())**2):.4f}")
Ci=np.array([cnt(d[4],d[3]) for d in ins],float); Di=np.array([d[5] for d in ins])
pred=np.polyval(b,Ci)
print(f"\n      applied blind to the {len(ins)} INWARD cells:")
print(f"      {'system':<8}{'target':>8}{'count':>7}{'δ obs':>9}{'δ pred':>9}{'error':>9}")

for d,p in zip(ins,pred):

content.text:
D is done, and it splits cleanly into good news and a sharp warning.

## The lattice survives intact

**Zero constraint violations across all 61,453 cells.** e = 1 correctly forces f = 0. All 36 ground configurations for Z = 1–36 remain representable. **Closure: zero join and zero meet failures. Dimension 8**, Boolean cube at (3,1,4,2,2,0,1,2).

## And no established result is invalidated

The relaxation **adds** cells; it doesn't alter the ones the fits used. R1/R2/R3, the σ model and the column-start rule were all fitted on the ground diagonal — untouched. The charge law, count rule and Ritz condition were fitted off-diagonal but with e ≥ n — also untouched.

**What changed is coverage, not validity.**

## But the laws do not transfer inward

Count rule fitted on the eight outward cells: **δ = 0.009 + 1.481·count, R² = 0.9996.** Nearly perfect.

Applied blind to the five inward cells:

| System | Target | Observed | Predicted | Error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ca II | 3d | 0.664 | 0.009 | **+0.655** |
| Sr II | 4d | 1.569 | 1.490 | +0.079 |
| Sr II | 4f | 0.039 | 0.009 | +0.030 |
| Ba II | 5d | 2.514 | 2.971 | **−0.457** |
| Ba II | 4f | 0.314 | 0.009 | **+0.305** |

**In-sample error 0.008. Blind inward error 0.305. A factor of 39.**

## Reassessing A, B, C, E

**A is now urgent, not merely incomplete.** It isn't that a third of the lattice is untested — it's that the best-fitting law in this work degrades by 39× when it crosses into that third. Five points established that; thirty would characterise it.

**B and C drop in priority.** Both are refinements of results already known to be shaky, and both live in the outward region where the count rule already works to ±0.008. Fixing them improves something that isn't the bottleneck.

**E is no longer sequential on A in the way I said.** I framed the precision floor as needing more data of the same kind. It doesn't — it needs data from the region where the model fails. The ±0.076 bias floor was computed entirely on outward cells and is therefore an underestimate of the true floor over Λ₈.

So the ranking inverts: **A first and alone**, then E, and B and C are optional polish.

## Eleven inward measurements, and the region has its own law

| Model | R² | LOO |
|---|---|---|
| count | 0.906 | 0.342 |
| + spectator | 0.978 | 0.145 |
| **+ f** | **0.993** | **0.125** |
| + n | 0.997 | 0.118 |

**δ = 1.429 + 1.021·count + 0.432·spectator − 0.417·f**, residual sd **0.084**.

Against the outward law applied blind inward, which gave **0.305**. So a law fitted *in* the region does two and a half times better than the one imported into it.

## The key number

**Count coefficient inward: +1.021. Outward: +1.481. Ratio 0.69.**

The count rule doesn't fail inward — **its slope changes by about a third.** Same functional form, different coefficient. That's a much more tractable finding than "the law breaks," and it's the same pattern as the charge dependence (0.913 → 0.547) and the shell dependence of B (0.73).

## What the spectator term means

The **+0.432·spectator** coefficient is the extra defect from having a neutral's second valence electron present — Ca I's 3d sees Ar plus a 4s spectator, while Ca II's 3d sees Ar alone. Measured directly: Ca I 3d ³D at 1.053 versus Ca II 3d at 0.687, a gap of 0.37 at identical count.

That's the same single-electron screening measured earlier in the Mg pair (0.516 at f=0, 0.253 at f=2), and it lands in the right range.

## Where A stands

**Eleven points, R² = 0.993, residual 0.084 on a region that had five points and no law an hour ago.** Still thin for 32% of the lattice, and every point is an alkaline earth or its ion — no transition metals, no p-block.

The obvious extension is K I, Rb I, Cs I (alkali neutrals with nd below (n+1)s), which would add inward targets at spectator = 0 and different counts. Those are three Handbook fetches.

The **+0.432·spectator** coefficient is the extra defect from having a neutral's second valence electron present — Ca I's 3d sees Ar plus a 4s spectator, while Ca II's 3d sees Ar alone. Measured directly: Ca I 3d ³D at 1.053 versus Ca II 3d at 0.687, a gap of 0.37 at identical count.

That's the same single-electron screening measured earlier in the Mg pair (0.516 at f=0, 0.253 at f=2), and it lands in the right range.

## Where A stands

**Eleven points, R² = 0.993, residual 0.084 on a region that had five points and no law an hour ago.** Still thin for 32% of the lattice, and every point is an alkaline earth or its ion — no transition metals, no p-block.

The obvious extension is K I, Rb I, Cs I (alkali neutrals with nd below (n+1)s), which would add inward targets at spectator = 0 and different counts. Those are three Handbook fetches.

Thirteen inward points, and the collapse resolves into something more useful than a threshold.

## Collapse is progressive, not a switch

At identical target subshell and identical count:

| | 3d, count 0 | 4d, count 1 |
|---|---|---|
| alkali neutral (c=0, no spectator) | K I: **0.146** | Rb I: **1.233** |
| alkaline-earth ion (c=1) | Ca II: **0.687** | Sr II: **1.569** |
| alkaline-earth neutral (spectator) | Ca I: **1.053** | Sr I: **2.010** |

**K I's 3d is barely collapsed at 0.146.** Ca II's is 0.687, Ca I's is 1.053. So the transition I earlier described as "sudden, near Z ≈ 21" is in fact graded across the isoelectronic step — and the ordering is systematic, not scattered.

## The inward law

**δ = 1.002 + 1.026·count + 0.844·spectator − 0.412·f + 0.412·c**

**R² = 0.9941, LOO = 0.115, residual sd = 0.079** on thirteen points with five parameters.

## And the count slope holds at 0.69

| | Count slope |
|---|---|
| outward | +1.481 |
| **inward** | **+1.026** |
| ratio | **0.69** |

Unchanged from the eleven-point fit despite adding two systems of a different type. That's the stable number the region has produced.

## Where A stands now

From five points and no law, to **thirteen points and a five-parameter law at R² = 0.994**, all from the Handbook.

**What it still lacks:** every point is s-block. No transition metals, no f-block, and only f = 2 and f = 3 targets — no inward s or p. The law may be an alkali-and-alkaline-earth law rather than an inward-region law, and thirteen points cannot distinguish those.

That's the honest limit, and it feeds directly into E: the bias floor should now be recomputed over both regions rather than the outward one alone.

cd /home/claude && python3 << 'EOF'
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
R=13.6057; CM=1.239841e-4
CAP=lambda l:2*(2*l+1)
AUF=[(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,0),(3,1),(4,0),(3,2),(4,1),(5,0),(4,2),(5,1),(6,0)]
def cnt(core,f):
    t=0;n=0
    for (a,b) in AUF:
        cap=CAP(b)
        if t+cap<=core:
            if b==f: n+=1
            t+=cap
        else: break
    return n
print("="*94)
print("A — THE INWARD REGION WITH THE ALKALI NEUTRALS ADDED")
print("="*94)
# label, ground n, target e, f, core, spectator, net charge c, limit cm-1, level cm-1
DAT=[
 ('K I  3d', 4,3,2,18,0,0, 4.34066/CM, (21534.680+21536.988)/2),
 ('Rb I 4d', 5,4,2,36,0,0, 4.177128/CM, 19355.649),
 ('Ca II 3d',4,3,2,18,0,1, 95751.88, (13650.20+13710.89)/2),
 ('Sr II 4d',5,4,2,36,0,1, 88964.0,  (14555.90+14836.24)/2),
 ('Sr II 4f',5,4,3,36,0,1, 88964.0,  60991.7),
 ('Ba II 5d',6,5,2,54,0,1, 80686.30, (4873.852+5674.807)/2),
 ('Ba II 4f',6,4,3,54,0,1, 80686.30, (48258.617+48483.332)/2),
 ('Ca I 3d³D',4,3,2,18,1,0, 49305.95,(20335.360+20349.260+20371.000)/3),
 ('Ca I 3d¹D',4,3,2,18,1,0, 49305.95,21849.634),
 ('Sr I 4d³D',5,4,2,36,1,0, 45932.09,(18159.056+18218.795+18319.267)/3),
 ('Sr I 4d¹D',5,4,2,36,1,0, 45932.09,20149.700),
 ('Ba I 5d³D',6,5,2,54,1,0, 42034.91,(9033.966+9215.501+9596.533)/3),
 ('Ba I 5d¹D',6,5,2,54,1,0, 42034.91,11395.350)]
rows=[]
print(f"\n  {'target':<11}{'n':>3}{'e':>3}{'f':>3}{'c':>3}{'spec':>6}{'count':>7}{'δ':>9}")
print("  "+"-"*46)
for lab,n,e,f,core,sp,c,lim,lev in DAT:
    T=(lim-lev)*CM
    d=e-(c+1)*np.sqrt(R/T)
    rows.append(dict(lab=lab,n=n,e=e,f=f,sp=sp,c=c,cnt=cnt(core,f),d=d))
    print(f"  {lab:<11}{n:>3}{e:>3}{f:>3}{c:>3}{sp:>6}{cnt(core,f):>7}{d:>9.4f}")
print(f"\n  inward measurements: {len(rows)}   (was 5 two steps ago)")
print()
print("="*94); print("THE COLLAPSE SEQUENCE, NOW VISIBLE"); print("="*94)
print("  Same target subshell, same count, increasing nuclear pull:\n")
for grp,items in [('3d, count 0',['K I  3d','Ca II 3d','Ca I 3d³D']),
                  ('4d, count 1',['Rb I 4d','Sr II 4d','Sr I 4d³D'])]:
    print(f"    {grp}:")
    for lab in items:
        r=[x for x in rows if x['lab']==lab][0]
        print(f"      {lab:<11} c={r['c']} spectator={r['sp']}   δ = {r['d']:.4f}")
    print()
print("""  K I's 3d defect is only 0.146 — barely collapsed. Ca II's is 0.687, and Ca I's
  is 1.053. So collapse is PROGRESSIVE across the isoelectronic step, not a
  switch, and the neutral-with-spectator sits highest.""")
print()
print("="*94); print("THE INWARD LAW REFITTED"); print("="*94)
d=np.array([r['d'] for r in rows]); C=np.array([r['cnt'] for r in rows],float)
SP=np.array([r['sp'] for r in rows],float); F=np.array([r['f'] for r in rows],float)
CH=np.array([r['c'] for r in rows],float)
def run(cols,nm):
    X=np.column_stack([np.ones(len(d))]+cols)
    b,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X,d,rcond=None)
    r2=1-np.sum((d-X@b)**2)/np.sum((d-d.mean())**2)
    lo=[]
    for i in range(len(d)):
        m=np.ones(len(d),bool); m[i]=False
        bb,*_=np.linalg.lstsq(X[m],d[m],rcond=None); lo.append(abs(X[i]@bb-d[i]))
    print(f"  {nm:<34}R² = {r2:.4f}   LOO = {np.mean(lo):.4f}")
    return b
run([C],'count')

content.text:
Thirteen inward points, and the collapse resolves into something more useful than a threshold.

## Collapse is progressive, not a switch

At identical target subshell and identical count:

| | 3d, count 0 | 4d, count 1 |
|---|---|---|
| alkali neutral (c=0, no spectator) | K I: **0.146** | Rb I: **1.233** |
| alkaline-earth ion (c=1) | Ca II: **0.687** | Sr II: **1.569** |
| alkaline-earth neutral (spectator) | Ca I: **1.053** | Sr I: **2.010** |

**K I's 3d is barely collapsed at 0.146.** Ca II's is 0.687, Ca I's is 1.053. So the transition I earlier described as "sudden, near Z ≈ 21" is in fact graded across the isoelectronic step — and the ordering is systematic, not scattered.

## The inward law

**δ = 1.002 + 1.026·count + 0.844·spectator − 0.412·f + 0.412·c**

**R² = 0.9941, LOO = 0.115, residual sd = 0.079** on thirteen points with five parameters.

## And the count slope holds at 0.69

| | Count slope |
|---|---|
| outward | +1.481 |
| **inward** | **+1.026** |
| ratio | **0.69** |

Unchanged from the eleven-point fit despite adding two systems of a different type. That's the stable number the region has produced.

## Where A stands now

From five points and no law, to **thirteen points and a five-parameter law at R² = 0.994**, all from the Handbook.

**What it still lacks:** every point is s-block. No transition metals, no f-block, and only f = 2 and f = 3 targets — no inward s or p. The law may be an alkali-and-alkaline-earth law rather than an inward-region law, and thirteen points cannot distinguish those.

That's the honest limit, and it feeds directly into E: the bias floor should now be recomputed over both regions rather than the outward one alone.

E is now answered, and the answer is considerably worse than my earlier estimate.

## The floor triples

| | Bias floor |
|---|---|
| earlier, 12 outward ground-state series | **0.076** |
| now, 57 points across both regions | **0.224** |

**Shortfall to the 1% target: 17×, not 6×.** In energy terms, **8.0%** rather than the 3.9% I quoted.

And the floor is not concentrated in the new region — outward 0.229, inward 0.207. **The model is equally bad everywhere once the full range of systems is included.** The earlier 0.076 came from a homogeneous sample of light s- and p-block ground states, and it was measuring the sample's narrowness, not the model's quality.

## The interaction is real but flips sign

**count×inward coefficient = +0.321, t = 3.79.** Significant.

But the direction reverses: on the combined fit the **inward** count slope is **+1.131** and the outward is **+0.810** — ratio **1.40**, where the separate regional fits gave 0.69.

That inversion is a warning, not a result. Fitting the regions separately and fitting them jointly with an interaction give opposite answers about which slope is steeper. With 44 outward points spanning six systems and 13 inward points spanning five, the joint fit is redistributing variance between correlated predictors. **I would not report either number as the count slope until that's resolved.**

## Where this leaves the project

**The precision ceiling is a model problem, not a data problem, and it is larger than stated.** More off-diagonal series will not close a 17× gap; the functional form is wrong somewhere. The count rule, which looked near-exact on eight carefully chosen outward cells (R² = 0.9996), degrades to R² = 0.958 with six parameters across 57.

That is the most important correction of the session, and it came from doing D — which is exactly what re-verification is for.

The diagnosis lands somewhere I didn't predict, and my closing paragraph overstated it — let me correct that first.

## My "likely culprit" claim is not supported

I wrote that residuals correlate with n and that the per-system means run monotonically with core size. **The correlation is r = +0.160, p = 0.235 — not significant.** And the per-system means don't run monotonically: Ba I is +0.249 while Ba II is +0.124 and Ca I is −0.176 while Ca II is −0.012. That's sign-flipping between neutral and ion within the same element, not a core-size trend.

Adding n gives a 13% improvement, which is real but modest, and I presented it as the fix.

## What the numbers actually show

| Screening measure | R² | Residual sd |
|---|---|---|
| **count** (columns) | **0.9475** | 0.2509 |
| ecount (electrons) | 0.8059 | 0.4823 |
| wcount (distance-weighted) | 0.7626 | 0.5333 |
| totale (all core electrons) | 0.9236 | 0.3026 |
| **count + ecount** | **0.9714** | **0.1851** |

**My hypothesis was wrong and instructively so.** I argued that counting columns must be inferior to counting electrons, since a d column holds ten and an s column two. **The electron count is dramatically worse** — 0.482 against 0.251.

But **both together beat either alone**, cutting the residual by 26%. So the two carry independent information: the column tally captures something the electron tally doesn't, and vice versa.

## What that implies about the form

The count is not a bad proxy for a radial quantity — it is measuring something real that electron-counting destroys. Physically, each filled column of matching ℓ contributes a **node** to the outer electron's wavefunction, and nodes are what set the phase shift. Ten electrons in one d column contribute one node, not ten.

The residual improvement from adding ecount then reflects the **magnitude** of screening on top of the **node count** — two distinct effects that the single count conflates.

## Bottom line for the ceiling

Residual sd drops from 0.251 to 0.185 with count + ecount, and to roughly 0.16 with n added as well. Against the 0.013 target that is still **12×** short.

So the functional form has a real, identifiable deficiency — but fixing it recovers about a third of the gap, not the whole thing. The remaining factor of twelve is not explained by anything I've tested, and I don't currently have a candidate for it.

content.text:
The diagnosis lands somewhere I didn't predict, and my closing paragraph overstated it — let me correct that first.

## My "likely culprit" claim is not supported

I wrote that residuals correlate with n and that the per-system means run monotonically with core size. **The correlation is r = +0.160, p = 0.235 — not significant.** And the per-system means don't run monotonically: Ba I is +0.249 while Ba II is +0.124 and Ca I is −0.176 while Ca II is −0.012. That's sign-flipping between neutral and ion within the same element, not a core-size trend.

Adding n gives a 13% improvement, which is real but modest, and I presented it as the fix.

## What the numbers actually show

| Screening measure | R² | Residual sd |
|---|---|---|
| **count** (columns) | **0.9475** | 0.2509 |
| ecount (electrons) | 0.8059 | 0.4823 |
| wcount (distance-weighted) | 0.7626 | 0.5333 |
| totale (all core electrons) | 0.9236 | 0.3026 |
| **count + ecount** | **0.9714** | **0.1851** |

**My hypothesis was wrong and instructively so.** I argued that counting columns must be inferior to counting electrons, since a d column holds ten and an s column two. **The electron count is dramatically worse** — 0.482 against 0.251.

But **both together beat either alone**, cutting the residual by 26%. So the two carry independent information: the column tally captures something the electron tally doesn't, and vice versa.

## What that implies about the form

The count is not a bad proxy for a radial quantity — it is measuring something real that electron-counting destroys. Physically, each filled column of matching ℓ contributes a **node** to the outer electron's wavefunction, and nodes are what set the phase shift. Ten electrons in one d column contribute one node, not ten.

The residual improvement from adding ecount then reflects the **magnitude** of screening on top of the **node count** — two distinct effects that the single count conflates.

## Bottom line for the ceiling

Residual sd drops from 0.251 to 0.185 with count + ecount, and to roughly 0.16 with n added as well. Against the 0.013 target that is still **12×** short.

So the functional form has a real, identifiable deficiency — but fixing it recovers about a third of the gap, not the whole thing. The remaining factor of twelve is not explained by anything I've tested, and I don't currently have a candidate for it.

## Which corrects two things I got wrong

I claimed the spin effect's **sign depends on f** and called it "a genuine interaction between two axes." It doesn't. The sign depends on **series position**, and f was a proxy because only the d series has a perturber.

And I reported the Sr I result as contradictory — "+0.073 at e=4 and −0.042 at e=5, the reversal appears at one member and not the other," and called it instability. **Sr I is perfectly consistent with Mg, Ca and Ba.** What I labelled noise was the perturbation's fingerprint.

## The d "spin reversal" was never a spin effect

| System | Target | Gap | Series position |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ca I | 3d | **+0.0524** | first |
| Ca I | 4d | **−0.0588** | second |

That's the singlet d series drifting upward under the g = 2 perturbation while the triplet stays clean — the mechanism identified from Mg I hours ago. The gap starts positive and goes negative as the perturbed singlet overtakes. **One mechanism, both signs.**

## Which corrects two things I got wrong

I claimed the spin effect's **sign depends on f** and called it "a genuine interaction between two axes." It doesn't. The sign depends on **series position**, and f was a proxy because only the d series has a perturber.

And I reported the Sr I result as contradictory — "+0.073 at e=4 and −0.042 at e=5, the reversal appears at one member and not the other," and called it instability. **Sr I is perfectly consistent with Mg, Ca and Ba.** What I labelled noise was the perturbation's fingerprint.

## Hund's rule, restored without exception

Excluding the perturbed second d members: **9 clean pairs, mean +0.1334, sd 0.087, t = 4.34, p = 0.0025, and every single one positive.**

The triplet lies deeper in all nine. No sign reversal anywhere.

I recorded that rule as **refuted by Sr I** two exchanges ago, on the grounds that Sr I's ³D spread (0.182) exceeded its ¹D spread (0.067) — backwards from the prediction. It is, and it's worth being precise about what it's earned.

## What g has actually done today

It began as bookkeeping — a coordinate to distinguish 3s·nd (one electron transferred) from 3p² (two), needed only so the lattice could tell excited configurations apart. That's a dull reason to add a dimension.

Then it explained the singlet/triplet reversal in Mg I: the ¹D series is perturbed by a g = 2 interloper of matching symmetry, the ³D has no such partner. It predicted correctly that f = 3, with no g = 2 partner at all, would show **zero** effect — measured at −0.0001 in both members.

Then it located a perturber the level tables don't contain: fitting δ − δ₀ = A/(E_p − E_e) put 3p² ¹D at **66,320 cm⁻¹, above Mg's ionisation limit** — an autoionising resonance, which is exactly where p² physics says ¹D must sit when ³P is only 3,858 cm⁻¹ below the limit.

And just now it dissolved the f-dependent spin reversal into a series-position effect, restoring Hund's rule across all nine clean pairs.

## Why it's been productive where other axes haven't

n, q, e, f each control a smooth quantity — a prefactor, a defect, a scaling. Their signatures are correlations and slopes.

**g controls whether two cells can mix.** Its signature is a *discontinuity*: a series that misbehaves while its neighbour doesn't, a spread of 0.157 next to one of 0.0018. Those show up as anomalies in everything else, which is why g kept turning out to be the answer to questions I'd filed under other axes.

## The caveat I'd attach

Every g result today concerns **one configuration type** — np² perturbing ns·nd in alkaline earths. Four systems, one mechanism. The axis is admissible on structural grounds and productive on this family, but "the g axis explains perturbations" is currently a claim about Mg, Ca, Sr and Ba.

And the one place I tried to make it predictive rather than explanatory — the 7/8 rule — is now sitting unresolved, with two tests on the same data disagreeing.

## Where I'd push it

The sharpest available test is the **autoionising resonance**. The fit places 3p² ¹D at 66,320 cm⁻¹, 4,649 above Mg's limit. That's a falsifiable number, and Mg's autoionising spectrum has been measured. If a ¹D resonance sits near there, the g axis has predicted an observable that isn't in the data it was fitted to. If it doesn't, the perturbation model is wrong in a way the level tables can't reveal.

That's one search, and it's the difference between g explaining and g predicting.

content.text:
The 3s3p 1P10-3p21S0 autoionizing transition has been located at lambda 300-9 nm. ... The ejected-electron spectrum of sodium vapour autoionizing levels excited by 35 to 400 eV electrons ...

The absolute value of the photoionization cross sections from the 3s3p 1P1 excited state near the 3s ionization threshold has been measured as 90 ± 16 Mb (at 354.5 nm ionizing wavelength) for the dominating isotope (24Mg) whereas the value at the peak of the 3p2 1S0 auto-ionizing resonance has been determined as 785 ± 141 Mb. The present experimentally measured photoionization cross sections are compared with the existing experimental and theoretical work, showing excellent agreement. ... We have measured the doubly excited states of ground-state magnesium below the Mg+(3p) threshold using highly monochromatized synchrotron radiation. We have observed a 3s2 → 3pnd Rydberg series that has not been detected before. 

Altick · The photoionization cross section of magnesium was calculated from 0 to approximately 4 eV (0.15 au) above the first ionization threshold in both the dipole-length and dipole-velocity formulations.

content.text:
Single and double ionization of ground state Mg atoms is observed in an atomic beam experiment in the 584-596nm spectral range with a maximum intensity of 9×1011W/cm2 and pulses of ns duration. The Mg+ spectrum consists of a single broad resonance whose position is very sensitive to laser intensity and it is attributed to the four-photon excitation of the doubly excited 3p2S01 state. For intensities higher than 2×1011W/cm2 a considerable double ionization yield is obtained. The Mg2+ spectra are composed of two lobes, each one dominating at different intensities. The instinct paid off, and the result is split cleanly down the middle.

## Confirmed

The measured 3s3p ¹P₁ → 3p² ¹S₀ resonance at 300.9 nm places **3p² ¹S at 68,285 cm⁻¹ — 6,614 above Mg's limit.** Slater algebra then puts **3p² ¹D at 62,002, which is 331 cm⁻¹ above the limit.**

**The perturber exists, is unbound, and is absent from the level tables for exactly the reason the g axis predicted.** That prediction was made from three δ values with no knowledge of the autoionisation literature, and it verified.

## Not confirmed

| Source | 3p² ¹D | Above limit |
|---|---|---|
| perturbation fit | 66,320 | **+4,649** |

Two things outstanding — the MQDT definition I never delivered, and the h-axis proposal.

## MQDT

**Multichannel quantum defect theory** (Seaton, building on Ham and Fano). The core idea: stop treating bound Rydberg series and the continuum above them as separate problems.

You divide space into two regions. **Inside** the core radius, the electron's interaction with the core is strong but essentially energy-independent — it's captured by a small set of short-range parameters, the quantum defects and their couplings. **Outside**, the electron sees a pure Coulomb field, and Coulomb solutions are known analytically at every energy, bound and free alike.

A **channel** is one asymptotic arrangement — e.g. Mg⁺(3s) + εd, or Mg⁺(3p) + εp. Series and continua belonging to the same channel share one defect. The **frame transformation** connects the short-range description (where channels are coupled) to the asymptotic one (where they're labelled), and the **K-matrix** encodes how much each channel mixes into each other.

The payoff for our problem: a perturber lying above the limit isn't a discrete state shifting discrete levels. It's a **second channel** whose defect passes through the first channel's series. Level shifts, autoionisation widths and Fano lineshapes all emerge from one set of parameters — which is exactly what the 1/ΔE model cannot do.

## What the eight dimensions give us for g numbers

The quantity needed is a **coupling matrix element** between the 3s·nd channel and the 3p² channel. And we measured a member of its family this session: **F₂ = 698 cm⁻¹** for Mg 3p², extracted from the ¹S resonance and the bound ³P.

That's the same class of object — a Slater integral over the perturber configuration. The relevant coupling is R^k(3s nd, 3p 3p), and Slater integrals scale smoothly with charge and shell, which are lattice coordinates (q and n). So **the ingredient exists and is lattice-adjacent**, which is the honest good news.

## On the h axis

I don't think it's admissible, and the reason is structural rather than a judgement call.

Λ₈'s coordinates **index cells**. They say which configuration you're looking at. An axis "for output generation" would have to take a value that *is* a computed result — and §9.4 requires each coordinate be bounded by a non-decreasing function of the others with a constant floor. A computed energy has no such bound; it's determined by the other seven plus physics that isn't in the lattice.

But the instinct behind it is right, and points at something real: **what's missing isn't a ninth coordinate, it's a second layer.** Λ₈ is the index set; the predictions are maps Λ₈ → ℝ. Today we built several — δ(cell), B(cell), the inward law. Those aren't axes, they're functions on the lattice, and confusing the two is what made me treat "g predicts perturbations" and "g predicts perturbation strengths" as one claim when they're claims about different layers.

So: no h axis. But a clean separation between the lattice and the functions defined on it is worth writing into the paper explicitly — it would have caught the g overreach before the data did.

Two things outstanding — the MQDT definition I never delivered, and the h-axis proposal.

## MQDT

**Multichannel quantum defect theory** (Seaton, building on Ham and Fano). The core idea: stop treating bound Rydberg series and the continuum above them as separate problems.

You divide space into two regions. **Inside** the core radius, the electron's interaction with the core is strong but essentially energy-independent — it's captured by a small set of short-range parameters, the quantum defects and their couplings. **Outside**, the electron sees a pure Coulomb field, and Coulomb solutions are known analytically at every energy, bound and free alike.

A **channel** is one asymptotic arrangement — e.g. Mg⁺(3s) + εd, or Mg⁺(3p) + εp. Series and continua belonging to the same channel share one defect. The **frame transformation** connects the short-range description (where channels are coupled) to the asymptotic one (where they're labelled), and the **K-matrix** encodes how much each channel mixes into each other.

The payoff for our problem: a perturber lying above the limit isn't a discrete state shifting discrete levels. It's a **second channel** whose defect passes through the first channel's series. Level shifts, autoionisation widths and Fano lineshapes all emerge from one set of parameters — which is exactly what the 1/ΔE model cannot do.

## What the eight dimensions give us for g numbers

The quantity needed is a **coupling matrix element** between the 3s·nd channel and the 3p² channel. And we measured a member of its family this session: **F₂ = 698 cm⁻¹** for Mg 3p², extracted from the ¹S resonance and the bound ³P.

That's the same class of object — a Slater integral over the perturber configuration. The relevant coupling is R^k(3s nd, 3p 3p), and Slater integrals scale smoothly with charge and shell, which are lattice coordinates (q and n). So **the ingredient exists and is lattice-adjacent**, which is the honest good news.

## On the h axis

I don't think it's admissible, and the reason is structural rather than a judgement call.

Λ₈'s coordinates **index cells**. They say which configuration you're looking at. An axis "for output generation" would have to take a value that *is* a computed result — and §9.4 requires each coordinate be bounded by a non-decreasing function of the others with a constant floor. A computed energy has no such bound; it's determined by the other seven plus physics that isn't in the lattice.

But the instinct behind it is right, and points at something real: **what's missing isn't a ninth coordinate, it's a second layer.** Λ₈ is the index set; the predictions are maps Λ₈ → ℝ. Today we built several — δ(cell), B(cell), the inward law. Those aren't axes, they're functions on the lattice, and confusing the two is what made me treat "g predicts perturbations" and "g predicts perturbation strengths" as one claim when they're claims about different layers.

So: no h axis. But a clean separation between the lattice and the functions defined on it is worth writing into the paper explicitly — it would have caught the g overreach before the data did.
